We can navigate between tabs using CONTROL + TAB or SHIFT + CONTROL + TAB on Windows and CONTROL + [ or CONTROL + ] on Mac. We can also click on the tabs with the mouse.</p> <p>The scene tab contains the camera and the items in the game. In it, we can control the camera properties, delete items, or find them in the scene. In contrast, the Palette Tab contains images or models that can be placed inside of a scene. There are default (open licensed) art objects that can be used freely in any project as a starting point. This provides a way to add, for 2D games, basic tiles for dirt, water, stone, monsters, and other items for use in a potential game. In each case, the art is appropriately labeled so that users can see the image and get accessible information about it. All default art is child-appropriate and should be usable in or out of a classroom.</p> <h5 id="the-2d-grid-editor">The 2D Grid Editor</h5> <p>Modern computer gaming uses both 2D and 3D graphics. To say the least, 2D is simpler for many reasons, especially the math behind the scenes. The metaphor used in many scene editors is one of a grid. In 2D, we have x and y coordinates and in 3D we add z. This means that for 2D, we can add items to any horizontal and vertical value. For 3D, it is the same idea, except a z coordinate can push the item forward (positive z) or backward (negative z), by default. Computer games use numbers not integers, so 1.5 or 1 are both fine.</p> <p>Consider an example. In the image below, there are horizontal and vertical lines. They are drawn on the screen for the editor, but do not show up in your game. By default, these lines are spaced 32 ‘units’ apart from each other, which for this 2D editor is pixels. This default is set because many open-source art tilesets have a fixed size. Basically, the system then stores many images with many items in them. They may use 32 or 16-pixel squares for map layout.</p> <p>Past this, the image below has a green section, which is a layout a person added for their game. In this case, the tiles are just images in a row, but this highlights why scene editors are helpful. A human writing down each coordinate of each item in code is time consuming. Having a tool let you place them around is easier. In the editor, each, so-called, tile can be adjusted in many ways.</p> <p>The math to find the position of each square on the grid can be a little tricky. Suppose there is a grid cell size of P, where P is 32 pixels. This means that to determine the grid coordinate, we always take the grid cell and multiply by P. For example, a cell at position (10, 10) would be (P*10, P*10), or (320, 320). This is important when setting properties to objects in a 2D scene.</p> <h5 id="the-3d-grid-editor">The 3D Grid Editor</h5> <p>Placing items in 3D is similar to 2D. Just like in 2D, you can select items and put them in the scene at an x, y, and now z position. Just like before, x means left and right, y means up and down, and z now means forward (positive) or backward (negative) in relation to the camera. The camera may be pointed in a direction of your choice, but by default it is on the y-axis looking down.</p> <p>This idea, that z moves you forward in relation to the camera if positive is critical to understand. That the camera can be pointed in any direction is thus confusing but also important. In computer science, there is a fancy name for it called the left-handed rule. Different areas of science uses different rules for z (e.g., physics right, pilots z goes down).</p> <p>One common sense way to think about the z coordinate in 3D is to put your arm or leg in front of you. That is a positive z if you are the camera looking out. Putting your arm or leg behind you is a negative coordinate. In graphics, this means that if the item is in front of the camera, a larger z would make an item look smaller because it is farther away. A smaller z would make the item look larger because it is closer. Too far away or behind the camera makes the item disappear. The camera is the same but can also look at things, called its direction. For example, it might be at an x, y, z position and looking at a different one.</p> <p>Consider the image below. In it, there are a series of walls and a spaceship. The camera is pointed at the spaceship from above at an angle. For the grid, there are a series of lines extending to infinity on the x and z axis, forming a plane. The up and down, or y axis, does not have gridlines but has the same unit measurements and movement as x and z. By default, these lines are spaced 1 ‘unit’ apart from each other. In 2D, pixels has no physical meaning, but in 3D, one unit is a meter. The reason for this is we can then set properties on items and use real-time physics in our game. The meaning matches that of the physical world. The camera in this game is the editor camera. Your game can use any kind of camera it wants. As such, you must it in your game if you want it to be the same as it is in the editor.</p> <p>The math to find the position of each square on the grid can be a little tricky. Suppose there is a grid cell size of P, where P is 32 meters. This means that to determine the grid coordinate, we always take the grid cell and multiply by P. For example, a cell at position (10, 10, 10) would be (P*10, P*10, P*10), or (320, 320, 320). This is important when setting properties to objects in the scene.</p> <h5 id="next-tutorial-105">Next Tutorial</h5> <p>In the next tutorial, we will discuss Add and Remove Items in Scenes, which describes adding and removing items in scenes in Quorum Studio.</p> <p>Go BackNext Tutorial</p> <h5 id="on-this-page-122">On this page</h5> <h3 id="what-is-a-scene-editor">What is a Scene Editor?</h3> <h5 id="scene-editing-9">Scene Editing</h5> <h5 id="scene-editor-overview">Scene Editor Overview</h5> <p>Making computer games can be hard for many reasons. One more innovation over decades has been the creation of so-called scene editors. Examples of such editors include those in Unity3D, Unreal, and many other engines. The basic idea is to allow visual, or hopefully accessible, manipulation of pictures, sounds, and the like without having to write code for everything. This kind of visual approach is common all throughout computer science. In 3D modeling, for example, tools like Maya or Blender can be used to let users manipulate one 3D object. Scene libraries tend to manipulate more.</p> <p>Beyond 3D, scene editing is also used in 2D games. The most famous is likely the one used in Scratch. Instead of coding everything, the visual aspect of the system can be manipulated directly and the code then changes what it does. Others like Tiled have made it easier to create 2D map layouts for games, again using visual metaphors. Libraries for scientific computing, 3D printing, and many other applications have followed a similar path of development in using graphics to better afford ease of use. Quorum Studio’s approach here is in the tradition of many of these tools, except we obsess about trying to make it all accessible to people with disabilities.</p> <h5 id="next-tutorial-106">Next Tutorial</h5> <p>In the next tutorial, we will discuss Creating a scene project, which describes creating a scene project in Quorum Studio.</p> <h5 id="on-this-page-123">On this page</h5> <h2 id="charts-and-data-visualisation">Charts and data visualisation</h2> <h3 id="additional-functions-in-charts">Additional Functions in Charts</h3> <h5 id="charts-2">Charts</h5> <p>This tutorial introduces additional useful chart functions in Quorum</p> <h5 id="additional-useful-functions">Additional Useful Functions</h5> <p>As a data scientist, we always want to present our data to help viewers understand and draw conclusions from the data. These functions listed below are additional resources to help us customize our data visualizations even further. All the functions described will work with any chart type.</p> <table> <colgroup> <col style="width: 20%" /> <col style="width: 60%" /> <col style="width: 18%" /> </colgroup> <thead> <tr> <th>Function</th> <th>Description</th> <th>Usage</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>SetYAxisMinimum(number num)</td> <td>This function sets the minimum value of the chart on the y axis</td> <td>chart:SetYAxisMinimum(5)</td> </tr> <tr> <td>SetYAxisMaximum(number num)</td> <td>This function sets the maximum value of the chart on the y axis</td> <td>chart:SetYAxisMaximum(200)</td> </tr> <tr> <td>SetXAxisMinimum(number num)</td> <td>This function sets the minimum value of the chart on the x axis</td> <td>chart:SetXAxisMinimum(0)</td> </tr> <tr> <td>SetXAxisMaximum(number num)</td> <td>This function sets the maximum value of the chart on the x axis</td> <td>chart:SetXAxisMaximum(600)</td> </tr> <tr> <td>FlipOrientation()</td> <td>This function takes in no parameters, and this function will swap the places of the x and y axis</td> <td>chart:FlipOrientation()</td> </tr> <tr> <td>SetFontSize(integer size)</td> <td>This function will adjust the font size on all areas of the chart based on points (pt) given</td> <td>chart:SetFontSize(20)</td> </tr> <tr> <td>SetLegendLabelFontSize(integer size)</td> <td>This function will adjust the font size of the labels on the legend of the chart based on points (pt) given</td> <td>chart:SetLegendLabelFontSize(10)</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Additional Useful Functions</p> <h5 id="next-tutorial-107">Next Tutorial</h5> <p>In the next tutorial, we will discuss multiple examples of a variety of chart types, which describes multiple examples of a variety of chart types.</p> <p>Go BackNext Tutorial</p> <h5 id="on-this-page-124">On this page</h5> <h3 id="bar-charts">Bar Charts</h3> <h5 id="charts-3">Charts</h5> <h5 id="making-a-bar-chart">Making a Bar Chart</h5> <p>The first chart type we will be using a new type of dataset to make a Bar Chart. Bar charts are useful for data scientists to compare the quantities of different types of groups. This dataset being used showcases the costs of night out activities around different parts of the country. We will be using it to compare how much total these activities cost per country.</p> <p>First step to this process is that we will need to load in the dataset and format it. It is best to keep track of where we are storing our data files. For this tutorial, we will have our dataset inside of a Data folder contained in another internal folder called “Miscellaneous.”</p> <p>To follow along, we can download the WorldNightOut.csv dataset <a href="https://github.com/qorf/quorum-website/blob/main/QuorumWebsite/html/data/WorldNightOut.csv">here</a>.</p> <p>Here is a snippet of what the dataset should look like:</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Category</th> <th>City</th> <th>Country</th> <th>Item</th> <th>Cost</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>Date night</td> <td>Barcelona</td> <td>Spain</td> <td>Dinner</td> <td>69.38</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Date night</td> <td>Barcelona</td> <td>Spain</td> <td>Dinner and Dessert</td> <td>21.28</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Date night</td> <td>Barcelona</td> <td>Spain</td> <td>Cinema entry</td> <td>11.87</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Date night</td> <td>Barcelona</td> <td>Spain</td> <td>Taxi</td> <td>10.92</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Date night</td> <td>Barcelona</td> <td>Spain</td> <td>Big Mac</td> <td>4.75</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>World Night Out CSV</p> <h5 id="loading-and-formatting">Loading and Formatting</h5> <p>As mentioned previously, to load and read in the dataset, we will need a DataFrame. Using the frame, we use the Load function and type in the file path of the Night Outs CSV. A comma separated file (CSV) file is a plain text file that separates data with commas.</p> <pre><code>use Libraries.Compute.Statistics.DataFrame use Libraries.Interface.Controls.Charts.BarChart // Create a dataframe to hold the data. DataFrame frame // Load your data file into the frame. frame:Load("data/WorldNightOut.csv")</code></pre> <p>In a chart, we typically want to categorize / separate our data in a way where we can see a relationship or draw comparisons from. An example of this is trying to find the profit out of grocery store items; instead of having each item be its own category (ex. milk products such as ice cream, cheese, etc), we can group food items to see the overall profit (ex. dairy). We approach our categories of data using this approach through factoring. Later we will be examining an action that allows us to categorize our data, sorting each entry into its respective factor.</p> <p>For this next part, we will want to select two columns of the dataset that we are comparing: Country and Cost. For Country, we will categorize this data because there are multiple activities listed for one country. This helps format the totals in which we will use Cost to add how much these activities cost per country. To select the Country column in our dataset, we would want to use the function, AddSelectedFactors(text textHeader). This will put countries listed on the x-axis. Adding an additional factor will separate our bar chart even further into smaller bars that can categorize items based on a broader factor, such as countries. We will also be extracting “Items” from the dataset and this will separate each activity from the country and display on the legend.</p> <p>Similarly, to get the Cost column from the dataset, we use the action AddSelectedColumns(“Cost”). This will add up the totals of these columns based on the categorized country and display them on the y axis. We will also briefly describe these two functions below in a table.</p> <table> <colgroup> <col style="width: 14%" /> <col style="width: 74%" /> <col style="width: 10%" /> </colgroup> <thead> <tr> <th>Function</th> <th>Description</th> <th>Usage</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>dataFrameObject:AddSelectedColumns(text heading)</td> <td>AddSelectedFactors() takes in a string that matches a column heading from our dataset. This function is used to format our legend and separate our data into categories For this tutorial, we will be calling this function twice and extract “Country” and “Item”</td> <td>frame:AddSelectedFactors(“heading”)</td> </tr> <tr> <td>dataFrameObject:AddSelectedColumns(text heading)</td> <td>AddSelectedColumns() takes in a string that matches a column heading from our dataset. This function is used to format our axises. For this tutorial, we will extract “Cost”</td> <td>frame:AddSelectedColumns(“heading”)</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>DataFrame Data Extraction Actions</p> <pre><code>// Select data from the frame that you wish to use in your bar chart. // Note: In Bar Charts, factors are used as the independent data, and Columns are used as the dependent data. // For this example we will be categorizing by "Country" and "Item" and calculating the bar value by "Cost". frame:AddSelectedFactors("Country") frame:AddSelectedFactors("Item") frame:AddSelectedColumns("Cost")</code></pre> <p>Now we create a bar chart object:</p> <pre><code>// Using the frame, create a BarChart object. BarChart chart = frame:BarChart() // Display your bar chart. chart:Display()</code></pre> <p>Calling the Display() function will give us a pop-up of our formatted data so far. We still need to give meaning to our data, therefore, the following steps will show us how to label and customize our chart.</p> <h5 id="labeling-the-bar-chart">Labeling the Bar Chart</h5> <p>We have successfully created our BarChart object! Now it is time to add features and tidy it up so we are able to present our data to viewers and have them understand what they are looking at. We will now be setting the title, the x axis title, and the y axis title. We will also be setting the font size so our data chart can be read easily.</p> <p>To label the titles, we must call the following functions now using our “chart” component: SetTitle(text title), SetXAxisTitle(text title), and SetYAxisTitle(text title). SetTitle(text title) takes in a string as the parameter so we can come up with a title that briefly describes our comparisons; in this case our title can be “How Expensive are Night Outs Per Country.” The next part is about labeling the x axis and y axis.</p> <p>For the x axis, we again will call our SetXAxisTitle(text title) function from our chart component which takes in a string; we should label this “Countries” and put it inside the parameter. The same process follows for SetYAxisTitle(text title) in which it should be labeled as “Cost (in USD $)” because our data calculates the cost in US dollars.</p> <p>We should also add a subtitle in our chart so we give clarity for our viewers of what the chart is about. This can be any small description or any useful / additional information. In this case, we would call SetSubtitle(text title) and insert a string inside the parameters. We will make our string “Various nightly activities cost in different countries.”</p> <p>We should have the following code:</p> <pre><code>// Give the chart a descriptive title. chart:SetTitle("How Expensive are Night Outs Per Country?") // Add a subtitle for further description. chart:SetSubtitle("Various nightly activities cost in different countries") // Give the x axis a descriptive title. chart:SetXAxisTitle("Countries") // Give the y axis a descriptive title. chart:SetYAxisTitle("Cost (in USD $)")</code></pre> <h5 id="customizing-the-bar-chart">Customizing the Bar Chart</h5> <p>With our bar chart, we are also able to change the color palette, the legend title, and the legend location. Before we display our chart, let us take a look at how to further customize this bar chart. For this tutorial, we will be selecting the Colorgorical palette.</p> <pre><code>// If needed, you can change the color palette to a predefined palette or create a custom one. // By default, the palette is set to Colorgorical which helps give our graphs aesthetic and discriminable elements. chart:SetColorPaletteToColorgorical()</code></pre> <p>Lastly, we will play around with the legend. Labeling our legend is important so that it provides clarity for the data, especially giving meaning to our categories created in the bar chart. To label the legend, we must call the SetLegendTitle(text title) function which takes in a string value, which we will label as “Countries.” Next we can change the position of the legend; by default, it is displayed on the right side, but it can be positioned at top, bottom, and left as well. Let us call the function, SetLegendLocationToBottom() which will set the location to the bottom of the chart.</p> <p>We should have the following code:</p> <pre><code>// If needed, you can change the legend location to either left, right, top or bottom. // By default, the legend is displayed on the right when showing. chart:SetLegendLocationToBottom() // Give the legend a descriptive title. chart:SetLegendTitle("Activity")</code></pre> <h5 id="displaying-the-chart">Displaying The Chart</h5> <p>Congratulations, our bar chart is constructed! Now we can display our chart with the Display() function. There are two ways to do this, letting it automatically display and specifying a specific window size. By doing chart:Display() it will display in a size equal to the screen size. By doing chart:Display(num, num), it will display the chart in a respected constraint window size. We will be using the default display to show the bar chart.</p> <pre><code>chart:Display()</code></pre> <p>Now, feel free to clean, build, and run the program and we shortly should see a Game window pop-up. This is our Bar Chart! To view the entire code, click <a href="https://github.com/qorf/curriculum/blob/main/Reference/DataScience/Charts%20(New)/DataScienceCurric/SourceCode/BarChartExample.quorum">here</a> to view the file.</p> <h5 id="try-it-yourself-15">Try it Yourself!</h5> <p>Press the blue run button to execute the code in the code editor. Press the red stop button to end the program. Your program will work when the console outputs “Build Successful!”</p> <pre><code>chart:Display()</code></pre> <h5 id="final-chart">Final Chart</h5> <h5 id="further-useful-bar-chart-functions">Further Useful Bar Chart Functions</h5> <table style="width:100%;"> <colgroup> <col style="width: 10%" /> <col style="width: 79%" /> <col style="width: 10%" /> </colgroup> <thead> <tr> <th>Function</th> <th>Description</th> <th>Usage</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>StackBars(boolean)</td> <td>StackBars() will stack bars on top of each other when a group contains multiple bars. They are not stacked by default.</td> <td>chart:StackBars(true)</td> </tr> <tr> <td>SortByBarSize()</td> <td>SortByBarSize() takes in no parameters and will sort the bars from largest bar to smallest bar. Note that it only will work with one factor added.</td> <td>chart:SortByBarSize()</td> </tr> <tr> <td>SeparateByFactor(integer)</td> <td>SeparateByFactor() will separate the chart into a grid of subcharts based on the bar groups. It takes in an integer as the number of columns in the grid. If empty, it results in a single-column grid.</td> <td>chart:SeparateByFactor(4)</td> </tr> <tr> <td>SeparateBySeries(integer)</td> <td>SeparateBySeries() will separate the chart into a grid of subcharts based on the legend (series). It takes in an integer as the number of columns in the grid. If empty, it results in a single-column grid.</td> <td>chart:SeparateBySeries(4)</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>DataFrame Data Extraction Actions</p> <p>To view more examples with charts, we can reference the Quorum Curriculum Repository for <a href="https://github.com/qorf/curriculum/tree/main/Reference/DataScience/Charts%20(New)/DataScienceCurric/SourceCode">charts</a>.</p> <h5 id="next-tutorial-108">Next Tutorial</h5> <p>In the next tutorial, we will discuss creating a histogram, which describes how to use the histogram chart in quorum.</p> <p>Go BackNext Tutorial</p> <h5 id="on-this-page-125">On this page</h5> <h3 id="box-plot">Box Plot</h3> <h5 id="charts-4">Charts</h5> <h5 id="making-a-box-plot">Making a Box Plot</h5> <p>The next chart to learn about is the box plot. For data scientists, box charts are useful to display data distribution separated by quartiles, meaning highlighting upper, lower, and middle ranged values. Box plots also show viewers data outliers in relation to the upper and lower extremes so we can examine what is different from the norm. Box plots are a great resource for data analytics in order to see the distribution of numerical data, similar to a Histogram.</p> <p>In this dataset, we will compare the height of males and females in the world. It will compare the height between the sexes based on the data from 199 countries collected in 2022.</p> <p>To follow along, we can download the Height of Male and Female by Country 2022 dataset <a href="https://github.com/qorf/curriculum/blob/4846bad77582e8d1da8325669b4de932b659e965/Reference/DataScience/Charts%20(New)/Data/Population/Height%20of%20Male%20and%20Female%20by%20Country%202022.csv">here</a>.</p> <p>Here is a snippet of what the dataset should look like:</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Country Name</th> <th>Male Height in Cm</th> <th>Female Height in Cm</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>Netherlands</td> <td>183.78</td> <td>170.36</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Montenegro</td> <td>183.30</td> <td>169.96</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Estonia</td> <td>182.79</td> <td>168.66</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Bosnia and Herzegovina</td> <td>182.47</td> <td>167.47</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Iceland</td> <td>182.10</td> <td>168.91</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Height of Male and Female by Country 2022 CSV</p> <h5 id="loading-and-formatting-1">Loading and Formatting</h5> <p>As mentioned previously, to load and read in the dataset, we will need to create a DataFrame component named ‘frame’. Using the frame, we must use the Load function and type in the file path of the insurance CSV. Recall that a CSV is a comma separated text file that holds in data.</p> <pre><code>use Libraries.Compute.Statistics.DataFrame use Libraries.Interface.Controls.Charts.BoxPlot /* This is an example of a simple box plot in quorum. The data collected is the average height of 2 sexes in 199 countries. */ // create dataframe to read in data DataFrame frame frame:Load("../Data/Population/Height of Male and Female by Country 2022.csv")</code></pre> <p>Note that, we stored this dataset in a Data folder, and contained in that folder is an inner folder named Population.</p> <p>Once the data has been loaded in, we will now extract this data to use in the data chart. We will be using two functions from our frame component, AddSelectedColumns(text header), and AddSelectedFactors(text header) where the columns will be used to label our x-axis, signifying the groups we are observing and the factor will be used to label our y-axis, signifying the change over time. AddSelectedColumn(text header) and AddSelectedFactor(text header) take in a parameter of either the column number or the column label in the CSV file. We will be using the column number to demonstrate.</p> <p>Please note that for a BoxPlot, we will only be using the AddSelectedColumns(text header) because of the simplicity of the dataset and this type of chart. This goes for other datasets as well, in which we will not be modifying the y axis. AddSelectedColumns(text header) will take a string as the parameter which represents the text header in the data file.</p> <table> <colgroup> <col style="width: 12%" /> <col style="width: 76%" /> <col style="width: 11%" /> </colgroup> <thead> <tr> <th>Function</th> <th>Description</th> <th>Usage</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>frame:AddSelectedColumns(text heading)</td> <td>AddSelectedColumns() takes in a string that matches a column heading from our dataset. This function is used to format our axises. For this tutorial, we will be calling this function twice and extract “Male Height in Cm” and “Female Height in Cm.”</td> <td>frame:AddSelectedColumns(“heading”)</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Adding CSV columns onto Charts</p> <p>We should have the following code:</p> <pre><code>// pull out selected data, for this we will be categorizing by Male and Female Height frame:AddSelectedColumns("Male Height in Cm") frame:AddSelectedColumns("Female Height in Cm")</code></pre> <p>Now it is time to create the Box Plot which can be done with the following code. This creates a chart object from our DataFrame component, frame. For the rest of this lesson, we will be using the chart object we have created to change and format the rest of our line chart.</p> <pre><code>// using the data frame, format data by creating a box plot chart component BoxPlot chart = frame:BoxPlot() chart:Display()</code></pre> <p>Calling the Display() function will give us a pop-up of our formatted data so far. We still need to give meaning to our data, therefore, the following steps will show us how to label and customize our chart.</p> <h5 id="labeling-the-box-plot">Labeling the Box Plot</h5> <p>In order for viewers to understand our data, labels give a clear comprehension of what is being presented. This means that we will be labeling the x axis, y axis, legend, and giving our chart a title that describes the dataset. To do so, we will call the following functions with our chart object: SetTitle(), SetXAxisTitle(), SetYAxisTitle(), SetLegendTitle(), and SetSubtitle(). Here is a brief description on what each function does and what it takes in.</p> <table style="width:100%;"> <colgroup> <col style="width: 7%" /> <col style="width: 73%" /> <col style="width: 19%" /> </colgroup> <thead> <tr> <th>Function</th> <th>Description</th> <th>Usage</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>SetTitle(text name)</td> <td>SetTitle() takes in a string as a parameter, which would be the title of the chart. For this example, we will name the chart “Height of Male and Female in the World”</td> <td>chart:SetTitle(“Height of Male and Female in the World”)</td> </tr> <tr> <td>SetXAxisTitle(text name)</td> <td>SetXAxisTitle() takes in a string as a parameter, which would be the label of the x axis. For this example, we will label this section “Sex”</td> <td>chart:SetXAxisTitle(“Sex”</td> </tr> <tr> <td>SetYAxisTitle(text name)</td> <td>SetYAxisTitle() takes in a string as a parameter, which would be the label of the y axis. For this example, we will label this section “Height (cm).”</td> <td>chart:SetYAxisTitle(“Height (cm)”)</td> </tr> <tr> <td>SetLegendTitle(text name)</td> <td>SetLegendTitle() takes in a string as a parameter, which would label the legend of the chart. The legend identifies the separate ages for the dots. For this example, we will label the legend “Average Height of a Human”</td> <td>chart:SetLegendTitle(“Average Height of a Human”)</td> </tr> <tr> <td>SetSubtitle(text title)</td> <td>SetSubtitle() takes in a string as a parameter which would set a subtitle under the title. This can be any short description or any other necessary information for our chart. For this example, we will label the subtitle “What is the average height of the population by sex?”</td> <td>chart:SetSubtitle(“What is the average height of the population by sex?”)</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Box Plot Labeling Functions</p> <pre><code>// label your box plot chart:SetXAxisTitle"Sex") chart:SetYAxisTitle("Height (cm)") chart:SetLegendTitle("Average Height of a Human") chart:SetSubtitle("What is the average height of the population by sex?") chart:SetTitle("Height of Male and Female in the World")</code></pre> <p>Note, if we would like to see the data chart so far, we can type “chart:Display()” to view it with the labels we created.</p> <h5 id="customizing-the-box-plot">Customizing the Box Plot</h5> <p>Now that we have our data labeled, we can customize our data to our liking, such as adjusting the intervals, changing starting values, and changing the color. We will be playing around with all these features and to do so, we will be again, using our chart object to call these functions. The functions we will be using for this would be: SetLegendLocationToBottom(), SetColorPaletteToDisurbing(), SetFontSize(integer size), and FlipOrientation(). Here are brief descriptions on what each function does and how to use it.</p> <table> <colgroup> <col style="width: 8%" /> <col style="width: 82%" /> <col style="width: 9%" /> </colgroup> <thead> <tr> <th>Function</th> <th>Description</th> <th>Usage</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>SetLegendLocationToBottom()</td> <td>SetLegendLocationToBottom() takes in no parameters, which would be the directions, but will place the legend in a specificed place. For this example, we will place the legend on the bottom. Alternatively, you could also use SetLegendLocationToTop(), SetLegendLocationToLeft() or SetLegendLocationToRight().</td> <td>chart:SetLegendLocationToBottom()</td> </tr> <tr> <td>SetFontSize(integer size)</td> <td>SetFontSize() takes in an integer as a parameter and will set the font size on all text based on the desired input. For this tutorial, we will insert 30 as the font size.</td> <td>chart:SetFontSize(20)</td> </tr> <tr> <td>SetColorPaletteToDisurbing()</td> <td>SetColorPaletteToDisurbing() takes in no parameters, but will adjust the color palette based off of yellows, browns, oranges, and greens</td> <td>chart:SetColorPaletteToDisturbing()</td> </tr> <tr> <td>FlipOrientation()</td> <td>FlipOrientation() takes in no parameters, and this function will swap the places of the x and y axis.</td> <td>chart:FlipOrientation()</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Other Useful Box Plot Functions</p> <pre><code>// set the legend location, choices are left, right, top and bottom chart:SetLegendLocationToBottom() // color palette contains yellows, oranges, browns, and greens chart:SetColorPaletteToDisturbing() // adjust font size by preference, here we set it to 30 pt chart:SetFontSize(20) // if we would like to switch the x and y axis chart:FlipOrientation()</code></pre> <h5 id="displaying-the-chart-1">Displaying The Chart</h5> <p>Congratulations, our Box Chart is constructed! Now we can display our chart with the Display() function. There are two ways to do this, letting it automatically display and specifying a specific window size. By doing chart:Display() it will display in a size equal to the screen size. By doing chart:Display(num, num), it will display the chart in a respected constraint window size. We will be using the default display.</p> <pre><code>chart:Display(1000, 750)</code></pre> <p>Now, feel free to clean, build, and run our program and we shortly should see a Game window pop-up. This is our Box Chart! To view the entire code, click <a href="https://github.com/qorf/curriculum/blob/main/Reference/DataScience/Charts%20(New)/DataScienceCurric/SourceCode/BoxExample1.quorum">here</a> to view the file.</p> <h5 id="try-it-yourself-16">Try it Yourself!</h5> <p>Press the blue run button to execute the code in the code editor. Press the red stop button to end the program. Your program will work when the console outputs “Build Successful!”</p> <h5 id="final-chart-1">Final Chart</h5> <h5 id="further-useful-box-plot-functions">Further Useful Box Plot Functions</h5> <p>To view more examples with charts, we can reference the Quorum Curriculum Repository for <a href="https://github.com/qorf/curriculum/tree/main/Reference/DataScience/Charts%20(New)/DataScienceCurric/SourceCode">charts</a>.</p> <table> <colgroup> <col style="width: 12%" /> <col style="width: 70%" /> <col style="width: 17%" /> </colgroup> <thead> <tr> <th>Function</th> <th>Description</th> <th>Usage</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>HideOutliers()</td> <td>This function does not take any parameters and it will hide the outliers from the chart.</td> <td>chart:HideOutliers()</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Other Useful Box Plot Actions</p> <h5 id="next-tutorial-109">Next Tutorial</h5> <p>In the next tutorial, we will discuss violin plot, which describes how to use the violin plot chart in quorum.</p> <p>Go BackNext Tutorial</p> <h5 id="on-this-page-126">On this page</h5> <h3 id="chart-gallery">Chart Gallery</h3> <h5 id="charts-5">Charts</h5> <p>Quorum features a variety of chart types to suit different needs for data visualization. <td>No</td> <td>No</td> <td>No</td> <td>No</td> <td>No</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Can you use SeparateBySeries with these inputs?</p> <h5 id="next-tutorial-110">Next Tutorial</h5> <p>In the next tutorial, we will discuss general usage charts functions, which describes how to customize data charts even further.</p> <p>Go BackNext Tutorial</p> <h5 id="on-this-page-128">On this page</h5> <h3 id="charts-overview">Charts Overview</h3> <h5 id="charts-7">Charts</h5> <p>This tutorial introduces how to make Charts in Quorum</p> <h5 id="overview-on-the-charts-library">Overview on the Charts Library</h5> <p>When data is cleaned and ready to be presented, scientists show their data to others. When scientists do this, it is rare that they just hand a community or person a data set. Looking at the raw data can be difficult for many reasons (e.g., it is huge, it is difficult to understand). Thus, we often use charts to represent summaries of the information in our data.</p> <p>Consider an example. We will take this example from a dataset about different dog breeds and their attributes such as maximum/minimum lifespan, maximum/minimum height, and maximum/minimum weight. Suppose we want to create a visualization about the heights of dogs based on their height from shortest to tallest by creating a line chart. It would be very clear that the Irish Wolfhound would be the tallest dog while the Yorkshire Terrier would be the shortest dog. All other dogs in the dataset would fall in-between this line. As data scientists we can observe any indication of the purpose of their breed type based on height. Data to make these predictions would be more difficult to see with just a data table. We will start by learning to load our data for the charts system.</p> <h5 id="loading-and-formatting-data">Loading and Formatting Data</h5> <p>Running our program on Quorum Studio is recommended for best practice.</p> <p>To follow along, we can download the Dog.csv dataset <a href="https://github.com/qorf/curriculum/blob/main/Reference/DataScience/Charts%20(New)/Data/Animals/Dogs.csv">here</a>.</p> <p>For the data to be read in, we use the DataFrame component to read in the Dogs CSV file. To do that, we include the DataFrame library and create a DataFrame:</p> <pre><code>use Libraries.Compute.Statistics.DataFrame DataFrame frame frame:Load("../Data/Animals/Dogs.csv")</code></pre> <p>Note that the file structure for this tutorial is that the dog CSV file is contained in a separate Data folder contained in an internal Animals folder for organization of datasets. The Data folder should be in a separate outside the project folder but inside the main parent directory.</p> <p>To format the data, we can select certain columns from our CSV file to consider in our chart. Let us try pull out the min and maximum height and weight as well as the breed group:</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Breed Group</th> <th>Max Weight</th> <th>Min Weight</th> <th>Max Height</th> <th>Min Height</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>Toy</td> <td>13</td> <td>6</td> <td>12</td> <td>9</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Hound</td> <td>60</td> <td>50</td> <td>27</td> <td>25</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Terrier</td> <td>65</td> <td>40</td> <td>23</td> <td>21</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Working</td> <td>120</td> <td>90</td> <td>34</td> <td>28</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Working</td> <td>115</td> <td>65</td> <td>28</td> <td>24</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Preview of Dogs.CSV file</p> <p>Taking our frame component, we use the AddSelectedFactors to create the x-axis for the chart. For the y-axis, AddSelectedColumns will be used as the comparison data to display the different data points taken from the data table. Think of this as the contents of the bars, lines, etc. of the chart. AddSelectedColumns() and AddSelectedFactors() both take in strings as a parameter or the table column number. In this example, we use the defined text headers to extract our data.</p> <pre><code>frame:AddSelectedFactors("Breed Group") // this will pull out the breed group from table and label on the x axis frame:AddSelectedColumns("Maximum Weight") // this will pull out the max weight from table and label on the y axis frame:AddSelectedColumns("Minimum Weight") frame:AddSelectedColumns("Maximum Height") frame:AddSelectedColumns("Minimum Height")</code></pre> <p>Let us run this example below!</p> <h5 id="try-it-yourself-17">Try it Yourself!</h5> <p>Press the blue run button to execute the code in the code editor. Press the red stop button to end the program. Your program will work when the console outputs “Build Successful!”</p> <p>Now that we have demonstrated let’s use the data we have read in and transform our data into a chart. For this example, we will be creating a chart object. The chart we will be constructing is a bar chart in which we will need to create a ‘chart’ object. We will formally learn more about bar charts and how to properly construct them, but for this tutorial, we want to learn how to combine data frames with the charts.</p> <h5 id="next-tutorial-111">Next Tutorial</h5> <p>In the next tutorial, we will discuss color accessibility, which describes color accessibility with charts.</p> <h5 id="on-this-page-129">On this page</h5> <h3 id="color-accessibility">Color Accessibility</h3> <h5 id="charts-8">Charts</h5> <p>This tutorial introduces how to make Charts in Quorum</p> <h5 id="color-accessibility-on-charts">Color Accessibility on Charts</h5> <p>Accessible features include discriminable color palettes in order to provide better contrasting visualizations as well as screen reader enabling. Contrasting choices were developed through using the <a href="https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27875168/">Colorgorical</a> palette picker noting that the chosen colors compare to current industry standards by balancing the importance of discriminability and aesthetic preference [1]. Other colors can also be manipulated by user preference such as converting colors to grayscale, negatives, warm tones, or cool tones as well. This small example will feature code on constructing color palettes for a bar chart. <strong>By default, the palette on the charts is based off of the Colorgorical palette.</strong> We can view how colorgorical works <a href="https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27875168/">here</a>.</p> <p>Other color palettes we considered were based off of the application between perceptual color properties (hue, chroma and lightness), palette composition (hue clusters, color frequency) and certain types of affect [2]. From this, the additional palettes were based off of eight affects, where four of them are core affects: Calm, Exciting, Positive, and Negative and four pragmatic affects: Serious, Playful, Trustworthy, and Disturbing. These affects relate the emotions users feel in relation to these palettes in order to have meaningful colors in data representations. Calm, Playful, and Positive palettes are in the lightest scales and most saturated while Serious, Disturbing, and Negative palettes are in the darkest scales and have more muted tones. Trustworthy palettes have more blue-green hues with a yellow to link, while Exciting had a similar palette, but more strongly saturated. The imporant aspect of this is learning how to give meaning to the colors we choose when creating our charts. <strong>These color palettes are focus more on the emotional design on viewers while maintaining discriminable palettes, similar to Colorgorical.</strong></p> <p>To change the color we can simply call a function such as SetColorPaletteToColorgorical() from our chart component which is a color palette that focuses on making distinguishable color palettes, providing accessibility for visually impaired viewers. Other color palettes we are able to choose from are as follows:</p> <pre><code>SetColorPaletteToColorgorical() SetColorPaletteToCalm() SetColorPaletteToCoolScale() SetColorPaletteToWarmScale() SetColorPaletteToDisturbing() SetColorPaletteToExciting() SetColorPaletteToMagma() SetColorPaletteToNegative() SetColorPaletteToPlayful() SetColorPaletteToPositive() SetColorPaletteToSerious() SetColorPaletteToTrustworthy() SetCurrentPaletteToGrayScale() // This one applies a grayscale filter to whichever other palette is currently being used. SetColorPalette(Color A) SetColorPalette(Color A, Color B) SetColorPalette(Color A, Color B, Color C) SetColorPalette(Array colors)</code></pre> <p>Here is example code of using the palettes which can be run on Quorum Studios:</p> <pre><code>BarChart chart = frame:BarChart() chart:SetColorPaletteToCalm() // will create a softer and cooler color palette chart:SetColorPaletteToColorgorical() // uses the constructed color palettes references by article chart:SetColorPaletteToExciting() // will create a bright and vibrant color palette</code></pre> <p>Color palettes can be manipulated by the user to best fit contrast levels in relation to the data. Below we will have examples on what each color palette looks like.</p> <h5 id="try-it-yourself-colorgorical-palette">Try it Yourself: Colorgorical Palette</h5> <p>Press the blue run button to execute the code in the code editor. Press the red stop button to end the program. Your program will work when the console outputs “Build Successful!”</p> <pre><code>SetColorPaletteToColorgorical()</code></pre> <h5 id="try-it-yourself-cool-palette">Try it Yourself: Cool Palette</h5> <p>Press the blue run button to execute the code in the code editor. Press the red stop button to end the program. Your program will work when the console outputs “Build Successful!”</p> <pre><code>SetColorPaletteToCoolScale()</code></pre> <h5 id="try-it-yourself-warm-palette">Try it Yourself: Warm Palette</h5> <p>Press the blue run button to execute the code in the code editor. Press the red stop button to end the program. Your program will work when the console outputs “Build Successful!”</p> <pre><code>SetColorPaletteToWarmScale()</code></pre> <h5 id="try-it-yourself-disturbing-palette">Try it Yourself: Disturbing Palette</h5> <p>Press the blue run button to execute the code in the code editor. Press the red stop button to end the program. Your program will work when the console outputs “Build Successful!”</p> <pre><code>SetColorPaletteToDisturbing()</code></pre> <h5 id="try-it-yourself-exciting-palette">Try it Yourself: Exciting Palette</h5> <p>Press the blue run button to execute the code in the code editor. Press the red stop button to end the program. Your program will work when the console outputs “Build Successful!”</p> <pre><code>SetColorPaletteToExciting()</code></pre> <h5 id="try-it-yourself-magma-palette">Try it Yourself: Magma Palette</h5> <p>Press the blue run button to execute the code in the code editor. Press the red stop button to end the program. Your program will work when the console outputs “Build Successful!”</p> <pre><code>SetColorPaletteToMagma()</code></pre> <h5 id="try-it-yourself-negative-palette">Try it Yourself: Negative Palette</h5> <p>Press the blue run button to execute the code in the code editor. Press the red stop button to end the program. Your program will work when the console outputs “Build Successful!”</p> <pre><code>SetColorPaletteToNegative()</code></pre> <h5 id="try-it-yourself-playful-palette">Try it Yourself: Playful Palette</h5> <p>Press the blue run button to execute the code in the code editor. Press the red stop button to end the program. Your program will work when the console outputs “Build Successful!”</p> <pre><code>SetColorPaletteToPlayful()</code></pre> <h5 id="try-it-yourself-positive-palette">Try it Yourself: Positive Palette</h5> <p>Press the blue run button to execute the code in the code editor. Press the red stop button to end the program. Your program will work when the console outputs “Build Successful!”</p> <pre><code>SetColorPaletteToPositive()</code></pre> <h5 id="try-it-yourself-serious-palette">Try it Yourself: Serious Palette</h5> <p>Press the blue run button to execute the code in the code editor. Press the red stop button to end the program. Your program will work when the console outputs “Build Successful!”</p> <pre><code>SetColorPaletteToSerious()</code></pre> <h5 id="try-it-yourself-trustworthy-palette">Try it Yourself: Trustworthy Palette</h5> <p>Press the blue run button to execute the code in the code editor. Press the red stop button to end the program. Your program will work when the console outputs “Build Successful!”</p> <pre><code>SetColorPaletteToTrustworthy()</code></pre> <p>Test out the different types of colors with the data being presented. Note that this chart may not fit the format of what to consider with making good charts.</p> <h5 id="references">References</h5> <p>[1]: Gramazio CC, Laidlaw DH, Schloss KB. Colorgorical: Creating discriminable and preferable color palettes for information visualization. IEEE Trans Vis Comput Graph. 2017 Jan;23(1):521-530. doi: 10.1109/TVCG.2016.2598918. PMID: 27875168. <code>https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/7539386</code>.</p> <p>[2]: Lyn Bartram, Abhisekh Patra, and Maureen Stone. 2017. Affective Color in Visualization. In Proceedings of the 2017 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI ’17). Association for Computing Machinery, New York, NY, USA, 1364 1374. DOI: <code>https://doi.org/10.1145/3025453.3026041</code>.</p> <h5 id="next-tutorial-112">Next Tutorial</h5> <p>In the next tutorial, we will discuss accessible navigation, which describes how to use keyboard navigation and screen reader with charts.</p> <p>Go BackNext Tutorial</p> <h5 id="on-this-page-130">On this page</h5> <h3 id="csvs-and-charts">CSVs and Charts</h3> <h5 id="charts-9">Charts</h5> <p>This tutorial introduces how download a CSV to use in a Chart</p> <h5 id="downloading-csvs-for-our-charts">Downloading CSVs for Our Charts</h5> <p>This tutorial will teach you how to download the Comma Separated Values files that we use in our examples. For this tutorial we will be downloading one file - <a href="https://github.com/qorf/curriculum/blob/main/Reference/DataScience/Charts%20(New)/Data/Miscellaneous/Christmas%20spending.csv">Christmas Spending</a>.</p> <p>First, let’s open the link by clicking on Christmas Spending above. This will take us to the GitHub page. You will have a Christmas spending.csv shown to you with 3 different columns and 24 rows. At the top of the CSV preview, there is the following information: the number of lines, the size of the file, two options, Raw and Blame, and the other four options. You want to click the “Raw” option that is located to the left of the “Blame” option.</p> <p>After you click that, the button will take you to a page with a lot of text. This is the raw data of the comma separated value file. You need to right-click anywhere on the page and select a “Save as…” option to save it. This will open a download menu; select the folder you would like to download the file to and make sure that Save as type is “Comma Separated Value File (*.csv).” Click “Save,” and this will download the comma separated value file to the folder you selected.</p> <h5 id="next-tutorial-113">Next Tutorial</h5> <p>In the next tutorial, we will discuss Bar Charts in Quorum, which describes how to make a simple bar chart in Quorum.</p> <p>Go BackNext Tutorial</p> <h5 id="on-this-page-131">On this page</h5> <h3 id="good-charts">Good Charts</h3> <h5 id="charts-10">Charts</h5> <h5 id="how-to-make-good-charts">How to Make Good Charts</h5> <p>The best practice of making any type of good chart is to give clear and concise context to the viewer, but what this means is at least partially subjective. Data visualization lacks in this area where many elements are inconsistent with the entire design. Design flaws with data visualizations include lacking meaningful captions and issues with visualizations being difficult to understand.</p> <p>Simon et al. [1] suggest issues such as line width, alignment, lack of meaningful descriptions, etc. can all impact comprehension, meaning that they are not readily interpreted. Examining reports from ITiCSE and full papers, they noticed that data visualizations for computing education were difficult to understand due to unorganization and lack of context.</p> <p>This means considering line width, number alignment, meaningful text, no [confusing] acronyms, and having a large font size contribute to understanding such charts. According to Simon et al. [2] a good rule of thumb when it comes to visualizing data is that for any diagrams, tables, and graphs, be sure to check whether they contain any text or numbers that are smaller than the text of the paper’s copyright notice. If it is smaller, it is a good indication that the graph we made will not be readable to the viewer.</p> <p>It is also worth noting that the information presented should also be meaningful, therefore it is not advised to over complicate data portrayals. It is better to have multiple simple graphs than one complex graph. The caption of charts should be to the point and give viewers an idea of what this data is without having to refer back to the text.</p> <p>Another aspect to consider is the choice of colors when designing a chart. Color palettes should be meaningful as well as distinguishable from each other, especially if they are adjacent. As an example, if a scientist is recording average temperatures in various states in the U.S., such as warm colors to signify hot temperatures.</p> <p>The following is a reference on when to use differing data representations [3]:</p> <table> <colgroup> <col style="width: 15%" /> <col style="width: 84%" /> </colgroup> <thead> <tr> <th>Type of Chart</th> <th>When should this chart be used?</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>Bar Graphs</td> <td>To compare categorical data or summary statistics from 1+ groups</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Line Graphs</td> <td>To depict a single variable or multiple variables with respect to change over time</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Histograms</td> <td>To portray sampling distribution with continuous independent variables</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Box Plot</td> <td>To show the distribution of data of 1+ groups</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Pie Chart</td> <td>To show frequencies or percentages</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Scatter Plot</td> <td>To determine if two varibles have a relationship or correlation</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Violin Plot</td> <td>To visualize peaks and distibutions in numerical data</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Chart References</p> <h5 id="references-1">References</h5> <p>[1]: Simple Simon, Brett A. Becker, Sally Hamouda, Robert McCartney, Kate Sanders, and Judy Sheard. 2019. Visual Portrayals of Data and Results at ITiCSE. In Proceedings of the 2019 ACM Conference on Innovation and Technology in Computer Science Education (ITiCSE ’19). Association for Computing Machinery, New York, NY, USA, 51 57. DOI: <code>https://doi.org/10.1145/3304221.3319742</code>.</p> <p>[2]: Franzblau LE, Chung KC. Graphs, tables, and figures in scientific publications: the good, the bad, and how not to be the latter. J Hand Surg Am. 2012 Mar;37(3):591-6. doi: 10.1016/j.jhsa.2011.12.041. Epub 2012 Feb 2. PMID: 22305731. <code>http://people.eku.edu/ritchisong/tables\_tigures.pdf</code>.</p> <h5 id="next-tutorial-114">Next Tutorial</h5> <p>In the next tutorial, we will discuss downloading CSVs, which describes how to download CSVs to use the data in the tutorials.</p> <p>Go BackNext Tutorial</p> <h5 id="on-this-page-132">On this page</h5> <h3 id="histograms">Histograms</h3> <h5 id="charts-11">Charts</h5> <h5 id="making-histograms">Making Histograms</h5> <p>A very common chart for visualizing numeric data is through a histogram. Histograms are typically used to represent the distribution of numerical data. The variable we observe is divided into different intervals where as a whole, we can examine the shape of the graph whether it is skewed, normal, uniform, bimodal [two distinct curves], etc. and draw conclusions about the data. Typical datasets to look out for when wanting to construct a histogram would be datasets featuring costs, ages, GPAs, and test scores. Note that datasets with non-numeric data are not recommended for histograms.</p> <p>For this lesson, we will examine the costs of various AirBnB per night in NYC in 2019. We can examine how expensive it is to rent an AirBnB and can make a conclusion if using the app is worth it or not.</p> <p>First step to this process is that we will need to properly load in the dataset and format it. It is best to keep track of where we are storing our data files. For this tutorial, we will have our dataset inside of a Data folder contained in another internal folder called “Other.”</p> <p>To follow along, we can download the NYC Airbnb dataset <a href="https://github.com/qorf/curriculum/blob/main/Reference/DataScience/Charts%20(New)/Data/Other/AB_NYC_2019.csv">here</a>.</p> <p>Here is a snippet of what the dataset should look like:</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Category</th> <th>City</th> <th>Country</th> <th></th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>Brooklyn</td> <td>Kensington</td> <td>Private room</td> <td>149</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Brooklyn</td> <td>Kensington</td> <td>Private room</td> <td>149</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Brooklyn</td> <td>Kensington</td> <td>Private room</td> <td>149</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Brooklyn</td> <td>Kensington</td> <td>Private room</td> <td>149</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Manhattan</td> <td>East Harlem</td> <td>Entire home/apt</td> <td>80</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Airbnb Prices in NYC CSV</p> <h5 id="loading-and-formatting-2">Loading and Formatting</h5> <p>As mentioned previously, to load and read in the dataset, we will need to create a DataFrame component named “frame”. Using the frame, we must use the Load function and type in the file path of the Airbnb CSV.</p> <pre><code>use Libraries.Compute.Statistics.DataFrame use Libraries.Interface.Controls.Charts.Histogram // Create a DataFrame to hold the data. DataFrame frame // Load your data file into the frame. frame:Load("data/AB_NYC_2019.csv")</code></pre> <p>Once the data has been loaded in, we will now extract this data to use in the data chart. We will be using two functions from our frame component, AddSelectedColumns(text header) and AddSelectedFactors(text header) where the columns will be used to label our x axis, signifying the groups we are observing and the factor will be used to label our y axis, signifying the change over time. AddSelectedColumn and AddSelectedFactor take in a parameter of either the column number or the column label in the CSV file. We will be using the column number to demonstrate.</p> <p>Notice in our data that we do have a lot of columns, but feel free to ignore them, the only column we will be pulling are the prices. Please note that for a Histogram, we will only be using the AddSelectedColumns(text header) because we would like to count the totals of each cost range for AirBnBs. This goes for other datasets as well, in which we will not be modifying the y axis. AddSelectedColumns(text header) will take a string as the parameter which represents the text header in the data file.</p> <p>We should have the following code:</p> <pre><code>// Select data from the frame that you wish to use in your histogram. // Note: In Histograms, factors and non-numerical columns are not supported. // For this example we will be using the numerical column "price". frame:AddSelectedColumns("price")</code></pre> <p>Now it is time to create the Histogram which can be done with the following code. This creates a chart object from our DataFrame component, frame. The rest of this lesson, we will be using the chart object we have created to change and format the rest of our line chart.</p> <pre><code>// Using the frame, create a Histogram object. Histogram chart = frame:Histogram() // Display your histogram. chart:Display()</code></pre> <p>Calling the Display() function will give us a pop-up of our formatted data so far. We still need to give meaning to our data, therefore, the following steps will show us how to label and customize our chart.</p> <h5 id="labeling-the-histogram">Labeling the Histogram</h5> <p>In order for viewers to understand our data, labels give a clear comprehension of what is being presented. This means that we will be labeling the x axis, y axis, legend, and giving our chart a title that describes the dataset. To do so, we will call the following functions with our “chart” object: SetTitle(text title), SetXAxisTitle(text title), SetYAxisTitle(text title), SetLegendTitle(text title), and SetSubtitle(text title). Here is a brief description on what each function does and what it takes in.</p> <table> <colgroup> <col style="width: 6%" /> <col style="width: 78%" /> <col style="width: 15%" /> </colgroup> <thead> <tr> <th>Function</th> <th>Description</th> <th>Usage</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>SetTitle(text name)*</td> <td>SetTitle() takes in a string as a parameter, which would be the title of the chart. For this example, we will name the chart “Price per night with AirBnB in 2019 (NYC)”</td> <td>chart:SetTitle(“Price per night with AirBnB in 2019 (NYC)”)</td> </tr> <tr> <td>SetXAxisTitle(text name)</td> <td>SetXAxisTitle() takes in a string as a parameter, which would be the label of the x axis. For this example, we will label this section “Price (<span class="math inline">$)" because this is the time frame we are observing | chart:SetXAxisTitle("Price ($</span>)”)</td> <td></td> </tr> <tr> <td>SetYAxisTitle(text name)</td> <td>SetYAxisTitle() takes in a string as a parameter, which would be the label of the y axis. For this example, we will label this section “Number of Stays” because this is the factor used for comparison between the different countries. This is also a good section to label the unit we are comparing, such as dollars</td> <td>chart:SetYAxisTitle(“Number of Stays”)</td> </tr> <tr> <td>SetLegendTitle(text name)</td> <td>SetLegendTitle() takes in a string as a parameter, which would label the legend of the chart. The legend identifies the separate countries into different lines. For this example, we will label the legend “Cost per night”</td> <td>chart:SetLegendTitle(“Cost per Night”)</td> </tr> <tr> <td>SetSubtitle(text title)</td> <td>SetSubtitle() takes in a string as a parameter which would set a subtitle under the title. This can be any short description or any other necessary information for our chart. For this example, we will label the subtitle “How expensive is it to stay in NYC?”</td> <td>chart:SetSubtitle(“How expensive is it to stay in NYC?”)</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Histrogram Labeling Functions</p> <pre><code>// Give the chart a descriptive title. chart:SetTitle("Price per night with AirBnB in 2019 (NYC)") // Add a subtitle for further description. chart:SetSubtitle("How expensive is it to stay in NYC?") // Give the x axis a descriptive title. chart:SetXAxisTitle("Price ($)") // Give the y axis a descriptive title. chart:SetYAxisTitle("Number of Stays")</code></pre> <p>*Note: We will also be adjusting the font size for the title as well so it fits nicely with our histogram. For this, we will be calling the function SetTitleFontSize(integer size) with our chart object. This takes in an integer (size) as the parameter, so for this case, we will insert 20 as our parameter.</p> <h5 id="customizing-the-histogram">Customizing the Histogram</h5> <p>Now that we have our data labeled, we can customize our data to our liking, such as adjusting the intervals, changing starting values, and changing the color. We will be playing around with all these features and to do so, we will be again, using our chart object to call these functions. The functions we will be using for this would be: SetXTickInterval(integer num), SetXAxisMinimum(integer num), and SetColorPaletteToWarmScale().</p> <table> <colgroup> <col style="width: 11%" /> <col style="width: 75%" /> <col style="width: 13%" /> </colgroup> <thead> <tr> <th>Function</th> <th>Description</th> <th>Usage</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>SetXTickInterval(number setX)</td> <td>SetXTickInterval() takes in a number as a parameter and sets the interval in multiples of the setX value given. For this tutorial, we will insert 50 as the tick interval</td> <td>chart:SetXTickInterval(50)</td> </tr> <tr> <td>SetXAxisMinimum(number min)</td> <td>SetXAxisMinimum() takes in a number as a parameter and adjusts the starting point for the x axis. For this tutorial, we will insert 0 as our minimum so we can see the price ranges from 0-50, 50-100, etc.</td> <td>chart:SetXAxisMinimum(0)</td> </tr> <tr> <td>SetColorPaletteToWarmScale()</td> <td>SetColorPaletteToWarmScale() changes the color palette to warmer colors such as yellows, reds, and oranges.</td> <td>chart:SetColorPaletteToWarmScale()</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Other Useful Histogram Functions</p> <pre><code>// You can hide the legend, as it is not needed for this example. chart:ShowLegend(false) // If needed, you can change the color palette to a predefined palette or create a custom one. chart:SetColorPaletteToWarmScale() // Set a custom interval along the x axis to 50 for a better display. // Alternatively, you can use SetBinWidth(50) for the same result. chart:SetXTickInterval(50) // Start the x axis at 0 for a better display. chart:SetXAxisMinimum(0)</code></pre> <h5 id="displaying-the-chart-2">Displaying The Chart</h5> <p>Congratulations, our Histogram is constructed! Now we can display our chart with the Display() function. There are two ways to do this, letting it automatically display and specifying a specific window size. By doing chart:Display() it will display in a size equal to the screen size. By doing chart:Display(num, num), it will display the chart in a respected constraint window size. We will be using the default display to show the histogram.</p> <pre><code>chart:Display()</code></pre> <p>Now, feel free to clean, build, and run our program and we shortly should see a Game window pop-up. This is our Histogram! To view the entire code, click <a href="https://github.com/qorf/curriculum/blob/main/Reference/DataScience/Charts%20(New)/DataScienceCurric/SourceCode/HistogramExample2.quorum">here</a> to view the file.</p> <h5 id="try-it-yourself-18">Try it Yourself!</h5> <p>Press the blue run button to execute the code in the code editor. Press the red stop button to end the program. Your program will work when the console outputs “Build Successful!”</p> <h5 id="final-chart-2">Final Chart</h5> <h5 id="further-useful-histogram-functions">Further Useful Histogram Functions</h5> <table> <colgroup> <col style="width: 10%" /> <col style="width: 78%" /> <col style="width: 11%" /> </colgroup> <thead> <tr> <th>Function</th> <th>Description</th> <th>Usage</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>StackBars(boolean)</td> <td>StackBars() will stack bars on top of each other when a group contains multiple bars. They are not stacked by default.</td> <td>chart:StackBars(true)</td> </tr> <tr> <td>OverlayBars(boolean)</td> <td>OverlayBars() will overlay bars on top of each other when a group contains multiple bars. They are not overlayed by default.</td> <td>chart:OverlayBars(true)</td> </tr> <tr> <td>SetBinWidth(number)</td> <td>SetBinWidth() will override the auto-calculated bin width with a user determined interval.</td> <td>chart:SetBinWidth(10)</td> </tr> <tr> <td>SeparateBySeries(integer)</td> <td>SeparateBySeries() will separate the chart into a grid of subcharts based on the legend (series). It takes in an integer as the number of columns in the grid. If empty, it results in a single-column grid.</td> <td>chart:SeparateBySeries(4)</td> </tr> <tr> <td>SeparateBySeries(boolean)</td> <td>SeparateBySeries() will separate the chart into a grid of subcharts based on the legend (series). If set to false, it will combined the subcharts to one histogram.</td> <td>chart:SeparateBySeries(false)</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Other Useful Histogram Actions</p> <p>To view more examples with charts, we can reference the Quorum Curriculum Repository for <a href="https://github.com/qorf/curriculum/tree/main/Reference/DataScience/Charts%20(New)/DataScienceCurric/SourceCode">charts</a>.</p> <h5 id="next-tutorial-115">Next Tutorial</h5> <p>In the next tutorial, we will discuss Creating a Pie Chart, which describes how to use pie charts in Quorum Studio.</p> <p>Go BackNext Tutorial</p> <h5 id="on-this-page-133">On this page</h5> <h3 id="keyboard-accessibility">Keyboard Accessibility</h3> <h5 id="charts-12">Charts</h5> <p>This tutorial introduces how to control charts with the keyboard</p> <h5 id="navigating-charts-on-the-keyboard">Navigating Charts on the Keyboard</h5> <p>Users can navigate through the chart using the computer arrow keys. If a screen reader is enabled, this will describe the contents of the chart, such as the x-axis, y-axis, and data points.</p> <h5 id="general-chart-keys">General Chart Keys</h5> <table> <colgroup> <col style="width: 10%" /> <col style="width: 8%" /> <col style="width: 80%" /> </colgroup> <thead> <tr> <th>Name</th> <th>Keys</th> <th>Description</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>Move Between Areas</td> <td>Page Up</td> <td>Page up: moves from legend to y-axis to x-axis. If missing a feature, just skips it and moves onto the next. Does not loop, so returns to overview after x-axis.</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Move Between Areas</td> <td>Page Down</td> <td>Page down: moves from x-axis to y-axis to legend. If missing a feature, just skips it and moves onto the next. Does not loop, so won’t move past legend.</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Chart Data Access</td> <td>Tab</td> <td>Move from anywhere in the graph to the main chart area, allowing access to specific data.</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Return to Overview</td> <td>Shift + Tab</td> <td>Return to overview from anywhere in the chart.</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Zoom in</td> <td>Enter</td> <td>Move to the first data point or subgroup in the chart, or first data point in subgroup.</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Zoom Out</td> <td>Shift + Enter</td> <td>Without subgroups or from subgroup overview: move to general chart data area. Within subgroups: move to subgroup overview.</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Multi-Chart Movement</td> <td>Up Arrow Key</td> <td>Down the list of charts.</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Multi-Chart Movement</td> <td>Down Arrow Key</td> <td>Up the list of charts.</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Multi-Chart Movement</td> <td>Left Arrow Key</td> <td>Up the list of charts.</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Multi-Chart Movement</td> <td>Right Arrow Key</td> <td>Down the list of charts.</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>General Chart Hotkeys</p> <h5 id="box-and-violin-plot-keys">Box and Violin Plot Keys</h5> <table> <colgroup> <col style="width: 13%" /> <col style="width: 9%" /> <col style="width: 77%" /> </colgroup> <thead> <tr> <th>Name</th> <th>Keys</th> <th>Description</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>Move Through Specifics</td> <td>Up Arrow Key</td> <td>Minimum to maximum movement. Full list of data: Minimum, interquartile range, first quartile, median, third quartile, maximum, outliers.</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Move Through Specifics</td> <td>Down Arrow Key</td> <td>Maximum to minimum movement. Full list of data: Minimum, interquartile range, first quartile, median, third quartile, maximum, outliers.</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Move Through Specifics</td> <td>Left Arrow Key</td> <td>Maximum to minimum movement. Full list of data: Minimum, interquartile range, first quartile, median, third quartile, maximum, outliers.</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Move Through Specifics</td> <td>Right Arrow Key</td> <td>Minimum to maximum movement. Full list of data: Minimum, interquartile range, first quartile, median, third quartile, maximum, outliers.</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Box and Violin Plots Keys</p> <h5 id="histogram-and-pie-chart-keys">Histogram and Pie Chart Keys</h5> <table> <colgroup> <col style="width: 22%" /> <col style="width: 22%" /> <col style="width: 54%" /> </colgroup> <thead> <tr> <th>Name</th> <th>Keys</th> <th>Description</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>X-Axis Movement</td> <td>Up Arrow Key</td> <td>Move towards origin.</td> </tr> <tr> <td>X-Axis Movement</td> <td>Down Arrow Key</td> <td>Move away from origin.</td> </tr> <tr> <td>X-Axis Movement</td> <td>Left Arrow Key</td> <td>Move away from origin.</td> </tr> <tr> <td>X-Axis Movement</td> <td>Right Arrow Key</td> <td>Move towards origin.</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Value Movement</td> <td>Page Up</td> <td>Towards largest value point movement.</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Value Movement</td> <td>Page Down</td> <td>Towards smallest valued point movement.</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Hisrogram and Pie Chart Keys</p> <h5 id="bar-chart-line-chart-and-scatter-plot-keys">Bar Chart, Line Chart, and Scatter Plot Keys</h5> <table> <colgroup> <col style="width: 23%" /> <col style="width: 15%" /> <col style="width: 60%" /> </colgroup> <thead> <tr> <th>Name</th> <th>Keys</th> <th>Description</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>X-Axis Movement</td> <td>Up Arrow Key</td> <td>Move towards origin.</td> </tr> <tr> <td>X-Axis Movement</td> <td>Down Arrow Key</td> <td>Move away from origin.</td> </tr> <tr> <td>X-Axis Movement</td> <td>Left Arrow Key</td> <td>Move away from origin.</td> </tr> <tr> <td>X-Axis Movement</td> <td>Right Arrow Key</td> <td>Move towards origin.</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Value Movement</td> <td>Page Up</td> <td>Towards smallest valued point movement.</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Value Movement</td> <td>Page Down</td> <td>Towards smallest valued point movement.</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Subgroup to Data Points</td> <td>Enter</td> <td>Move to specific data within a subgroup from the subgroup list.</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Bar Chart, Line Chart, and Scatter Plot Keys</p> <h5 id="accessible-data-by-chart-type">Accessible Data by Chart Type</h5> <table> <colgroup> <col style="width: 13%" /> <col style="width: 86%" /> </colgroup> <thead> <tr> <th>Chart Type</th> <th>Value Data Provided</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>Bar Chart</td> <td>Bar values, subgroup overview.</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Histogram</td> <td>Bin values.</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Pie Chart</td> <td>Slice values.</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Scatter Plot</td> <td>Data point values, subgroup overview.</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Line Chart</td> <td>Data point values, line overview.</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Box Plot</td> <td>Minimum, interquartile range, first quartile, median, third quartile, maximum, outliers.</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Violin Plot</td> <td>Minimum, interquartile range, first quartile, median, third quartile, maximum.</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Accessible Data by Chart Type</p> <h5 id="try-it-yourself-19">Try it Yourself!</h5> <p>Press the blue run button to execute the code in the code editor. Press the red stop button to end the program. Your program will work when the console outputs “Build Successful!”</p> <p>This runnable example demonstrates how to use the accessibility features with charts. Note that we must have screen reader enabled to go through all the individial parts of the chart.</p> <p>For this example, the data may not make sense to the chart type. However, we will be discussing what makes a good chart in the next section.</p> <h5 id="next-tutorial-116">Next Tutorial</h5> <p>In the next tutorial, we will discuss Good Charts, which describes how to make good charts as a data scientist.</p> <p>Go BackNext Tutorial</p> <h5 id="on-this-page-134">On this page</h5> <h3 id="line-charts">Line Charts</h3> <h5 id="charts-13">Charts</h5> <h5 id="making-a-line-chart">Making a Line Chart</h5> <p>The next chart type to learn how to create is a line chart. Line charts are a great visualization tool to use when presenting trends over time. Scientists typically use line charts to emphasize patterns of change in one or more variables of data. The dataset that we will be using for this lesson describes how much people in the US and the UK spend on Christmas on average over the years. With this graph, we can see how expensive (or inexpensive) shopping has been from 1999 to present day, and can draw conclusions about overall spending habits and price adjustments.</p> <p>First step to this process is that we will need to properly load in the dataset and format it. It is best to keep track of where we are storing our data files. For this tutorial, we will have our dataset inside of a Data folder contained in another internal folder called “Miscellaneous.”</p> <p>To follow along, we can download the Christmas spending dataset <a href="https://github.com/qorf/curriculum/blob/main/Reference/DataScience/Charts%20(New)/Data/Miscellaneous/Christmas%20spending.csv">here</a>.</p> <p>Here is a snippet of what the dataset should look like:</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Year</th> <th>Christmas Spending in US</th> <th>Christmas Spending in UK</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>1999</td> <td>857</td> <td>945</td> </tr> <tr> <td>2000</td> <td>817</td> <td>926</td> </tr> <tr> <td>2001</td> <td>794</td> <td>845</td> </tr> <tr> <td>2002</td> <td>690</td> <td>760</td> </tr> <tr> <td>2003</td> <td>734</td> <td>832</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Airbnb Prices in NYC CSV</p> <h5 id="loading-and-formatting-3">Loading and Formatting</h5> <p>As mentioned previously, to load and read in the dataset, we will need to create a DataFrame component named ‘frame’. Using the frame, we must use the Load function and type in the file path of the Christmas Spending CSV. Recall that a CSV is a comma separated text file that holds in data.</p> <pre><code>use Libraries.Compute.Statistics.DataFrame use Libraries.Interface.Controls.Charts.LineChart /* This is an example of a Line Chart built in quorum. The dataset we will be working with examines how much spending people in the US and the UK have spent on Christmas over the years. */ // create dataframe to read in data DataFrame frame frame:Load("../Data/Miscellaneous/Christmas spending.csv")</code></pre> <p>Note that, we stored this dataset in a Data folder and contained in that folder is an inner folder named Science.</p> <p>Once the data has been loaded in, we will now extract this data to use in the data chart. We will be using two functions from our frame component, AddSelectedColumn(text header) and AddSelectedFactor(text header) where the columns will be used to label our x axis, signifying the groups we are observing and the factor will be used to label our y axis, signifying the change over time. AddSelectedColumn(text header) and AddSelectedFactor(text header) take in a parameter of either the column number or the column label in the CSV file. We will be using the column number to demonstrate.</p> <p>In our dataset, we have a total of three columns: the year (0), spending in the US (1), and spending in the UK (2). The numbers correspond to the columns which we will extract using AddSelectedColumns(text header) and AddSelectedFactor(text header). For this, we would call AddSelectedFactor(text header) and type in 0 inside the parameter, which grabs the year. Similarly, we would call AddSelectedColumn() and inside the parameters type 1 and 2. Note that AddSelectedColumn(text header) must be called twice to separate column 1 and column 2 from each other. The usage of these functions is shown below:</p> <table style="width:100%;"> <colgroup> <col style="width: 11%" /> <col style="width: 78%" /> <col style="width: 10%" /> </colgroup> <thead> <tr> <th>Function</th> <th>Description</th> <th>Usage</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>frame:AddSelectedColumns(text heading)</td> <td>AddSelectedColumns() takes in a string that matches a column heading from our dataset. This function is used to format our axises. For this tutorial, we will be selecting two columns, specifically column 1 (spending values in the US) and column 2 (spending values in the UK).</td> <td>frame:AddSelectedColumns(“heading”)</td> </tr> <tr> <td>frame:AddSelectedFactors(text heading)</td> <td>AddSelectedFactors() takes in a string that matches a column heading from our dataset. This function is used to label our dots and form the legend based off of the two variables we are comparing. For this tutorial, we will be extracting factor in column 0 (the year)</td> <td>frame:AddSelectedFactors(“heading”)</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Adding CSV columns onto Charts</p> <p>We should have the following code:</p> <pre><code>// grabs the average spending values and place as y-axis frame:AddSelectedColumn(1) frame:AddSelectedColumn(2) // grabs the year values and place as x-axis frame:AddSelectedFactor(0)</code></pre> <p>Now it is time to create the Line chart which can be done with the following code. This creates a chart object from our DataFrame component, frame. Because we want both the UK and the US data to be on the same chart, we will be calling the function SeparateByFactor(bool) and put in ‘false’ as the parameter to get us started. By default, the line chart will separate each line with its own graph, so to adjust that setting, we will just want to simply call the function. The rest of this lesson, we will be using the chart object we have created to change and format the rest of our line chart.</p> <pre><code>// create chart component inherited from the line chart library LineChart chart = frame:LineChart() // creates only 1 chart but both lines are on same chart chart:SeparateByFactor(false) chart:Display()</code></pre> <p>Calling the Display() function will give us a pop-up of our formatted data so far. We still need to give meaning to our data, therefore, the following steps will show us how to label and customize our chart.</p> <h5 id="labeling-the-line-chart">Labeling the Line Chart</h5> <p>In order for viewers to understand our data, labels give a clear comprehension of what is being presented.
