This means that we will be labeling the x axis, y axis, legend, and giving our chart a title that describes the dataset. To do so, we will call the following functions with our ‘chart’ object: SetTitle(text name), SetXAxisTitle(text name), SetYAxisTitle(text name), SetLegendTitle(text name), and SetSubtitle(text name). Here is a brief description on what each function does and what it takes in.</p> <table> <colgroup> <col style="width: 6%" /> <col style="width: 72%" /> <col style="width: 21%" /> </colgroup> <thead> <tr> <th>Function</th> <th>Description</th> <th>Usage</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>SetTitle(text name)</td> <td>SetTitle() takes in a string as a parameter, which would be the title of the chart. For this example, we will name the chart “How Much the US and UK Spend During Christmas”</td> <td>chart:SetTitle(“How Much the US and UK Spend During Christmas”)</td> </tr> <tr> <td>SetXAxisTitle(text name)</td> <td>SetXAxisTitle(text name): SetXAxisTitle takes in a string as a parameter, which would be the label of the x axis. For this example, we will label this section “Year” because this is the time frame we are observing.</td> <td>chart:SetXAxisTitle(“Year”)</td> </tr> <tr> <td>SetYAxisTitle(text name)</td> <td>SetYAxisTitle() takes in a string as a parameter, which would be the label of the y axis. For this example, we will label this section “Money Spent (in $)” because this is the factor used for comparison between the different countries. This is also a good section to label the unit we are comparing, such as dollars.</td> <td>chart:SetYAxisTitle(“Money Spent (in $)”)</td> </tr> <tr> <td>SetLegendTitle(text name)</td> <td>SetLegendTitle takes in a string as a parameter, which would label the legend of the chart. The legend identifies the separate countries into different lines. For this example, we will label the legend “Christmas Shopping Spending.”</td> <td>chart:SetLegendTitle(“Christmas Shopping Spending”)</td> </tr> <tr> <td>SetSubtitle(text title)</td> <td>SetSubtitle takes in a string as a parameter which would set a subtitle under the title. This can be any short description or any other necessary information for our chart. For this example, we will label the subtitle “Overtime, shopping costs have increased over the years in XMAS shopping”</td> <td>chart:SetSubtitle(“Overtime, shopping costs have increased over the years in XMAS shopping”)</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Line Chart Labeling Functions</p> <pre><code>// label your line chart chart:SetXAxisTitle("Year") chart:SetYAxisTitle("Money Spent (in $)") chart:SetLegendTitle("Christmas Shopping Spending") chart:SetLegendLocationToTop() chart:SetTitle("How Much the US and UK Spend During Christmas")</code></pre> <p>Note, if we would like to see the data chart so far, we can type “chart:Display()” to view it with the labels we created.</p> <h5 id="customizing-the-line-chart">Customizing the Line Chart</h5> <p>Now that we have our data labeled, we can customize our data to our liking, such as adjusting the intervals, changing starting values, and changing the color. We will be playing around with all these features and to do so, we will be again, using our chart object to call these functions. The functions we will be using for this would be: SetLegendLocationToTop(), SetColorPaletteToDisurbing(), SetFontSize(integer size), FlipOrientation(), and ShowLinearRegression(bool). Here are brief descriptions on what each function does and how to use it.</p> <table> <colgroup> <col style="width: 13%" /> <col style="width: 71%" /> <col style="width: 14%" /> </colgroup> <thead> <tr> <th>Function</th> <th>Description</th> <th>Usage</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>SetXTickInterval(integer count)</td> <td>SetXTickInterval() takes in an integer as a parameter and sets the interval in multiples of the setX value given. For this tutorial, we will insert 5 as the tick count.</td> <td>chart:SetXTickInterval(5)</td> </tr> <tr> <td>SetFontSize(integer size)</td> <td>SetFontSize() takes in an integer as a parameter and will set the font size on all text based on the desired input. For this tutorial, we will insert 20 as the font size.</td> <td>chart:SetFontSize(20)</td> </tr> <tr> <td>SetLineDensity(number size)</td> <td>SetLineDensity(number size) takes in an integer as a parameter and will adjust the thickness of the lines within the chart. For this tutorial, we will insert 4 for the density.</td> <td>chart:SetColorPaletteToDisturbing()</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Other Useful Line Chart Functions</p> <pre><code>/* this will divide up the years by 5 from all years from 1999 to 2021 */ chart:SetXTickInterval(5) // makes font size bigger chart:SetFontSize(20) // creates a thicker line for graph chart:SetLineDensity(4) // changes the color palette chart:SetColorPaletteToCalm()</code></pre> <h5 id="displaying-the-chart-3">Displaying The Chart</h5> <p>Congratulations, our line chart is constructed! Now we can display our chart with the Display() function. There are two ways to do this, letting it automatically display and specifying a specific window size. By doing chart:Display() it will display in a size equal to the screen size. By doing chart:Display(number width, number height), it will display the chart in a respected constraint window size. We will be using the specified chart display for this. In this case, inside the Display parameters, we will put 1500 as the first parameter and 750 as the second parameter which will construct a display based on those dimensions.</p> <p>Now, feel free to clean, build, and run our program and we shortly should see a Game window pop-up. This is our Line Chart! To view the entire code, click <a href="https://github.com/qorf/curriculum/blob/main/Reference/DataScience/Charts%20(New)/DataScienceCurric/SourceCode/LineChartExample.quorum">here</a> to view the file.</p> <pre><code>chart:Display(1500, 750)</code></pre> <h5 id="try-it-yourself-20">Try it Yourself!</h5> <p>Press the blue run button to execute the code in the code editor. Press the red stop button to end the program. Your program will work when the console outputs “Build Successful!”</p> <h5 id="final-chart-3">Final Chart</h5> <p>To view more examples with charts, we can reference the Quorum Curriculum Repository for <a href="https://github.com/qorf/curriculum/tree/main/Reference/DataScience/Charts%20(New)/DataScienceCurric/SourceCode">charts</a>.</p> <h5 id="next-tutorial-117">Next Tutorial</h5> <p>In the next tutorial, we will discuss scatter plot, which describes how to use the scatter plot chart in quorum.</p> <p>Go BackNext Tutorial</p> <h5 id="on-this-page-135">On this page</h5> <h3 id="pie-charts">Pie Charts</h3> <h5 id="charts-14">Charts</h5> <h5 id="making-a-pie-chart">Making a Pie Chart</h5> <p>The next chart to learn is the pie chart. Pie charts are used to see parts-to-whole relationships such as totaling the favorite types of movie genres out of a survey of 100 people. Pie charts divide up a circle into various slices in which each slice represents a percentage of the total variable being represented. The dataset that we will be using for this lesson describes wine reviews in which we can observe the various popular wine types.</p> <p>First step to this process is that we will need to properly load in the dataset and format it. It is best to keep track of where we are storing our data files. For this tutorial, we will have our dataset inside of a Data folder contained in another internal folder called “Miscellaneous.”</p> <p>To follow along, we can download the wineReviews.csv dataset <a href="https://github.com/qorf/curriculum/blob/main/Reference/DataScience/Charts%20(New)/Data/Miscellaneous/wineReviews.csv">here</a>.</p> <p>Here is a snippet of what the dataset should look like:</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Province</th> <th>Region 1</th> <th>Variety</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>California</td> <td>Napa Valley</td> <td>Cabernet Sauvignon</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Northern Spain</td> <td>Toro</td> <td>Tinta de Toro</td> </tr> <tr> <td>California</td> <td>Knights Valley</td> <td>Sauvignon Blanc</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Oregon</td> <td>Willamette Valley</td> <td>Pinot Noir</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Provence</td> <td>Bandol</td> <td>Provence red blend</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Airbnb Prices in NYC CSV</p> <h5 id="loading-and-formatting-4">Loading and Formatting</h5> <p>As mentioned previously, to load and read in the dataset, we will need to create a DataFrame component named “frame”. Using the frame, we must use the Load function and type in the file path of the wine reviews CSV. Recall that a CSV is a comma separated text file that holds in data.</p> <pre><code>use Libraries.Compute.Statistics.DataFrame use Libraries.Interface.Controls.Charts.PieChart // create dataframe to read in data DataFrame frame frame:Load("../Data/Miscellaneous/wineReviews.csv")</code></pre> <p>Once the data has been loaded in, we will now extract this data to use in the data chart. We will be using the function, AddSelectedFactors(text header) to format our data into the pie chart. AddSelectedFactors(text header) will take in a string value that matches a column header to the dataset. For instance, we will be extracting the “variety” column from the dataset.</p> <pre><code>// pull out selected data, for this we will be categorizing by wine type frame:AddSelectedFactors("variety")</code></pre> <p>Now it is time to create the Pie Chart which can be done with the following code. This creates a chart object from our DataFrame component, frame. The rest of this lesson, we will be using the chart object we have created to change and format the rest of our line chart.</p> <pre><code>// pull out selected data, for this we will be categorizing by wine type frame:AddSelectedFactors("variety") // create chart component inherited from the line chart library PieChart chart = frame:PieChart() chart:Display()</code></pre> <h5 id="labeling-the-pie-chart">Labeling the Pie Chart</h5> <p>Pie charts are unique because there actually is no need to label an x axis or y axis. The different variables within the genre group we are using separates into parts that we can examine as a whole. For this part, we will focus on learning how to label our chart title and our legend title. Additionally, we will also change the orientation of our legend within the pie chart. The functions we would be using in this case are: SetTitle(text title), SetLegendTitle(text title), SetLegendLocationToBottom(), and SetSubtitle(text title). Here is a brief description of what each function takes in.</p> <table style="width:100%;"> <colgroup> <col style="width: 7%" /> <col style="width: 78%" /> <col style="width: 14%" /> </colgroup> <thead> <tr> <th>Function</th> <th>Description</th> <th>Usage</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>SetTitle(text name)</td> <td>SetTitle() takes in a string as a parameter, which would be the title of the chart. For this example, we will name the chart “Top Wine Reviews Based on Type.”</td> <td>chart:SetTitle(“Title Name”)</td> </tr> <tr> <td>SetLegendTitle(text name)</td> <td>SetLegendTitle() takes in a string as a parameter, which would label the legend of the chart. The legend identifies the separate countries into different lines. For this example, we will label the legend “Variety.”</td> <td>chart:SetLegendTitle(“Legend Description”)</td> </tr> <tr> <td>SetLegendLocationToBottom()</td> <td>SetLegendLocationToBottom() takes in no parameters, which would be the directions, but will place the legend in a specificed place. For this example, we will place the legend on the bottom. Alternatively, you could also use SetLegendLocationToTop(), SetLegendLocationToLeft() or SetLegendLocationToRight().</td> <td>chart:SetLegendLocationToBottom()</td> </tr> <tr> <td>SetSubtitle(text title)</td> <td>SetSubtitle takes in a string as a parameter which would set a subtitle under the title. This can be any short description or any other necessary information for our chart. For this example, we will label the subtitle “Praised wine categorized by type”</td> <td>chart:SetSubtitle(“Praised wine categorized by type”)</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Pie Chart Labeling Functions</p> <pre><code>// create title to describe graph chart:SetTitle("Top Wine Reviews Based on Type") // label your legend to show users what is being categorized chart:SetLegendTitle("Variety") chart:SetSubtitle("Praised wine categorized by type") // set the legend location, choices are left, right, top and bottom chart:SetLegendLocationToBottom()</code></pre> <h5 id="customizing-the-pie-chart">Customizing the Pie Chart</h5> <p>Now that we have our data labeled, we can customize our data to our liking, such as adjusting the font size, changing the color palette, and creating a hole in the middle of our pie chart. We will be playing around with all these features and to do so, we will be again, using our chart object to call these functions. The functions we will be using for this would be: SetDonutHolePercent(), SetFontSize(), and SetColorPaletteToPositive()</p> <table> <colgroup> <col style="width: 9%" /> <col style="width: 72%" /> <col style="width: 17%" /> </colgroup> <thead> <tr> <th>Function</th> <th>Description</th> <th>Usage</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>SetDonutHolePercent(float percent)</td> <td>SetDonutHolePercent() takes in a decimal value which will adjust the size of the hole in relation to the size of the pie chart. Larger percentages will make the hole bigger and smaller percentages will make the hole smaller. For this tutorial, let us make our hole 10%</td> <td>chart:SetDonutHolePercent(0.6) // sets hole size to 60% of chart</td> </tr> <tr> <td>SetColorPaletteToPositive()</td> <td>SetColorPaletteToPositive() takes in no parameters, but will adjust the color palette based on a positive color scale including bright oranges, greens, pinks, and yellows</td> <td>chart:SetColorPaletteToPositive()</td> </tr> <tr> <td>SetFontSize(integer size)</td> <td>SetFontSize() takes in an integer as a parameter and will set the font size on all text based on the desired input. For this tutorial, we will insert 20 as the font size.</td> <td>chart:SetFontSize(20)</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Other Useful Pie Chart Functions</p> <pre><code>// creates a hole in the middle of the pie chart (optional feature) chart:SetDonutHolePercent(0.1) // adjust font size by preference, here we set it to 20 pt chart:SetFontSize(20) /* change color palette if needed, this color palette is set to Colorgorical which helps give our graphs aesthetic and discriminable color palettes */ //chart:SetColorPaletteToNegative() //chart:SetColorPaletteToCalm() //chart:SetColorPaletteToMagma() //chart:SetColorPaletteToColorgorical() chart:SetColorPaletteToPositive()</code></pre> <h5 id="displaying-the-chart-4">Displaying The Chart</h5> <p>Congratulations, our Pie Chart is constructed! Now we can display our chart with the Display() function. There are two ways to do this, letting it automatically display and specifying a specific window size. By doing chart:Display() it will display in a size equal to the screen size. By doing chart:Display(num, num), it will display the chart in a respected constraint window size. We will be using the default display to show the histogram.</p> <pre><code>chart:Display()</code></pre> <p>Now, feel free to clean, build, and run our program and we shortly should see a Game window pop-up. This is our Pie Chart! To view the entire code, click <a href="https://github.com/qorf/curriculum/blob/main/Reference/DataScience/Charts%20(New)/DataScienceCurric/SourceCode/PieChartExample3.quorum">here</a> to view the file.</p> <h5 id="try-it-yourself-21">Try it Yourself!</h5> <p>Press the blue run button to execute the code in the code editor. Press the red stop button to end the program. Your program will work when the console outputs “Build Successful!”</p> <h5 id="final-chart-4">Final Chart</h5> <h5 id="further-useful-pie-chart-functions">Further Useful Pie Chart Functions</h5> <table> <colgroup> <col style="width: 10%" /> <col style="width: 79%" /> <col style="width: 10%" /> </colgroup> <thead> <tr> <th>Function</th> <th>Description</th> <th>Usage</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>SeparateByFactor(integer)</td> <td>SeparateByFactor() will separate graphs based on number of columns we want in the grid of subcharts. It takes in an integer, but could be left empty. If empty, by default, it would leave it as a single chart</td> <td>chart:SeparateByFactor(4)</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Other Useful Pie Chart Actions</p> <p>To view more examples with charts, we can reference the Quorum Curriculum Repository for <a href="https://github.com/qorf/curriculum/tree/main/Reference/DataScience/Charts%20(New)/DataScienceCurric/SourceCode">charts</a>.</p> <h5 id="next-tutorial-118">Next Tutorial</h5> <p>In the next tutorial, we will discuss line chart, which describes how to use the line chart in quorum.</p> <p>Go BackNext Tutorial</p> <h5 id="on-this-page-136">On this page</h5> <h3 id="saving-a-chart">Saving a Chart</h3> <h5 id="charts-15">Charts</h5> <h5 id="saving-our-charts">Saving Our Charts</h5> <p>Now that we have learned how to construct all these charts, we can also save them onto our computer for easier access. All charts should be saved as an SVG (Scalable Vector Graphic), meaning the chart should contain its resolution when zoomed in or out. The importance of using an svg is that the image would not be rasterized, meaning a loss of pixels, and they are still accessible and can be parsed through a screen reader.</p> <p>The first task we should do before being able to save our charts, we also would need to display them. We can do this simply by calling the Display() function with the chart object we have been using as follows:</p> <pre><code>chart:Display()</code></pre> <p>To save our charts we will need to call the Save(text fileName) function and it will save onto our project’s parent folder. Here is a brief explanation of the Save() function.</p> <table> <colgroup> <col style="width: 10%" /> <col style="width: 78%" /> <col style="width: 10%" /> </colgroup> <thead> <tr> <th>Function</th> <th>Description</th> <th>Usage</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>chart:Save(text fileName)</td> <td>Save() takes in a string as a parameter which saves our charts as actual images on our computer. The file name should always have the .svg extension included in order to have a successful save.</td> <td>chart:Save(“chart1.svg”)</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Using the Save() function</p> <p>This will create a file called ‘chart1.svg’ inside the parent folder. Now we can save any of the charts we have created!</p> <p>Below is a snippet of code to use to save a chart using the Save() function:</p> <pre><code>use Libraries.Compute.Statistics.DataFrame use Libraries.Interface.Controls.Charts.LineChart // create the data frame to read in data DataFrame frame frame:Load("../Data/Miscellaneous/Christmas spending.csv") // grabs the average spending values and place as x axis frame:AddSelectedColumn(1) // spending values in US frame:AddSelectedColumn(2) // spending values in UK // grabs the year values and place as y axis frame:AddSelectedFactor(0) // create chart component inherited from the line chart library LineChart chart = frame:LineChart() // sets title for chart at the top, this should give the chart meaning chart:SetTitle("How Much the US and UK Spend During Christmas") // displays chart in a specified window size chart:Display(1500, 750) // save chart image chart:Save("linechart1.svg")</code></pre> <p>Alternatively, we can also display our chart’s data onto the Quorum Studio terminal in which we would call the function ConvertToScalableVectorGraphics() and also use the ‘output’ function in order to translate our data into text form. Here is a brief explanation on the ConvertToScalableVectorGraphics() function.</p> <table> <colgroup> <col style="width: 17%" /> <col style="width: 65%" /> <col style="width: 17%" /> </colgroup> <thead> <tr> <th>Function</th> <th>Description</th> <th>Usage</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>chart:ConvertToScalableVectorGraphics()</td> <td>chart:ConvertToScalableVectorGraphics() takes in no parameters and will convert the chart we have created (after calling the Display() function) as an SVG.</td> <td>chart:ConvertToScalableVectorGraphics()</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Displaying charts on the terminal</p> <p>Below is a snippet of code to use to display onto the terminal:</p> <pre><code>output chart:ConvertToScalableVectorGraphics()</code></pre> <p>The SVG file relies on web hosted files to be navigated accessibly. The SVG file can be added inline to a webpage which imports the Javascript (used to handle the keystrokes necessary for navigation) and Cascading Stylesheet (used to show which element is focused on the image).</p> <p>To more easily share our charts, we can call the Share(text fileName) function instead of the Save() function and it will save a Hypertext Markup Language (HTML) file onto our project’s parent folder. Here is a brief explanation of the Share() function.</p> <table> <colgroup> <col style="width: 10%" /> <col style="width: 78%" /> <col style="width: 10%" /> </colgroup> <thead> <tr> <th>Function</th> <th>Description</th> <th>Usage</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>chart:Share(text fileName)</td> <td>Share() takes in a string as a parameter which saves our charts as a page with the image on our computer. The file name should always have the .html extension included in order to have a successful save.</td> <td>chart:Share(“chart1.html”)</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Using the Share() function</p> <p>This will create a file called ‘chart1.html’ inside the parent folder. This file can be opened in the browser and navigated accessibly. Now we can save and share any of the charts we have created!</p> <p>Below is a snippet of code to use to save a chart using the Share() function:</p> <pre><code>use Libraries.Compute.Statistics.DataFrame use Libraries.Interface.Controls.Charts.LineChart // create the data frame to read in data DataFrame frame frame:Load("../Data/Miscellaneous/Christmas spending.csv") // grabs the average spending values and place as x axis frame:AddSelectedColumn(1) // spending values in US frame:AddSelectedColumn(2) // spending values in UK // grabs the year values and place as y axis frame:AddSelectedFactor(0) // create chart component inherited from the line chart library LineChart chart = frame:LineChart() // sets title for chart at the top, this should give the chart meaning chart:SetTitle("How Much the US and UK Spend During Christmas") // displays chart in a specified window size chart:Display(1500, 750) // save chart image chart:Share("linechart1.html")</code></pre> <h5 id="next-tutorial-119">Next Tutorial</h5> <p>In the next tutorial, we will discuss Chart Separation, which describes How to split data into multiple charts for the same plot display..</p> <p>Go BackNext Tutorial</p> <h5 id="on-this-page-137">On this page</h5> <h3 id="scatter-plot">Scatter Plot</h3> <h5 id="charts-16">Charts</h5> <h5 id="making-a-scatter-plot">Making a Scatter Plot</h5> <p>The next chart we will be learning to create would be a scatter plot. Scatter plots are used to observe relationships between two variables. An example of this would be comparing the heights and diameters of trees, where the position of each dot correlates to that specified height and diameter. The data as a whole can represent a relationship: strong positive/negative linear, moderate positive/negative linear, or no relationship. As a data scientist, one of the most important patterns is seeing how points cluster from other points, if there are any gaps within the dataset, and identifying outliers for within the set. We focus on these aspects to make predictions on future datasets and understand trends.</p> <p>This next dataset we are using to create a scatter plot is about dog breeds and their traits. The chart will compare maximum life spans to maximum weights to see how they’re related.</p> <p>To follow along, we can download the dogs dataset <a href="https://github.com/qorf/quorum-website/blob/main/QuorumWebsite/html/data/Dogs.csv">here</a>.</p> <p>Here is a snippet of what the dataset should look like:</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Breeding Group</th> <th>Maximum Life Span</th> <th>Maximum Life Span</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>Toy</td> <td>12</td> <td>13</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Hound</td> <td>13</td> <td>60</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Terrier</td> <td>13</td> <td>65</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Working</td> <td>12</td> <td>120</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Working</td> <td>14</td> <td>115</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Dog CSV</p> <h5 id="loading-and-formatting-5">Loading and Formatting</h5> <p>As mentioned previously, to load and read in the dataset, we will need to create a DataFrame component named frame. Using the frame, we must use the Load function and type in the file path of the dogs CSV. Recall that a CSV is a comma separated text file that holds in data.</p> <pre><code>use Libraries.Compute.Statistics.DataFrame use Libraries.Interface.Controls.Charts.ScatterPlot DataFrame frame frame:Load("data/Dogs.csv")</code></pre> <p>Note that, we stored this dataset in a data folder.</p> <p>Once the data has been loaded in, we will now extract this data to use in the data chart. We will be using two functions from our frame component, AddSelectedColumns(text heading) and AddSelectedFactors(text heading). In this instance, because scatter plots need two data variables for comparisons, we will be extracting the maximum life span and weight for the dogs using our AddSelectedColumns(text header) function. We will also be extracting dog breeds with our AddSelectedFactors(text header) function to discriminate the two variables through the dots. The usage of these two functions are shown below:</p> <table> <colgroup> <col style="width: 12%" /> <col style="width: 76%" /> <col style="width: 11%" /> </colgroup> <thead> <tr> <th>Function</th> <th>Description</th> <th>Usage</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>frame:AddSelectedColumns(text heading)</td> <td>AddSelectedColumns() takes in a string that matches a column heading from our dataset. This function is used to format our axises. For this tutorial, we will be calling this function twice and extract “Maximum Life Span” and “Maximum Weight.”</td> <td>frame:AddSelectedColumns(“heading”)</td> </tr> <tr> <td>frame:AddSelectedFactors(text heading)</td> <td>AddSelectedFactors() takes in a string that matches a column heading from our dataset. This function is used to label our dots and form the legend based off of the two variables we are comparing. For this tutorial, we will be extracting “Breed Group.”</td> <td>frame:AddSelectedFactors(“heading”)</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Adding CSV columns onto Charts</p> <p>We should have the following code:</p> <pre><code>// pull out selected data frame:AddSelectedFactors("Breed Group") frame:AddSelectedColumns("Maximum Life Span") frame:AddSelectedColumns("Maximum Weight")</code></pre> <p>Now it is time to create the Scatter Plot which can be done with the following code. This creates a chart object from our DataFrame component, frame. The rest of this lesson, we will be using the chart object we have created to change and format the rest of our scatter plot.</p> <pre><code>// using the data frame, format data by creating a scatter plot chart component ScatterPlot chart = frame:ScatterPlot() chart:Display()</code></pre> <p>Calling the Display() function will give us a pop-up of our formatted data so far. We still need to give meaning to our data, therefore, the following steps will show us how to label and customize our chart.</p> <h5 id="labeling-the-scatter-plot">Labeling the Scatter Plot</h5> <p>In order for viewers to understand our data, labels give a clear comprehension of what is being presented. This means that we will be labeling the x axis, y axis, legend, and giving our chart a title that describes the dataset. To do so, we will call the following functions with our “chart” object: SetTitle(text name), SetXAxisTitle(text name), SetYAxisTitle(text name), SetLegendTitle(text name), and SetSubtitle(text name). Here is a brief description on what each function does and what it takes in.</p> <table> <colgroup> <col style="width: 7%" /> <col style="width: 74%" /> <col style="width: 18%" /> </colgroup> <thead> <tr> <th>Function</th> <th>Description</th> <th>Usage</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>SetTitle(text name)</td> <td>SetTitle() takes in a string as a parameter, which would be the title of the chart. For this example, we will name the chart “Dog Weight and Life Span”</td> <td>chart:SetTitle(“Dog Weight and Life Span”)</td> </tr> <tr> <td>SetXAxisTitle(text name)</td> <td>SetXAxisTitle() takes in a string as a parameter, which would be the label of the x axis. For this example, we will label this section “Maximum Life Span”</td> <td>chart:SetXAxisTitle(“Maximum Life Span”</td> </tr> <tr> <td>SetYAxisTitle(text name)</td> <td>SetYAxisTitle() takes in a string as a parameter, which would be the label of the y axis. For this example, we will label this section “Maximum Weight (pounds).” This is also a good section to label the unit we are comparing, such as pounds.</td> <td>chart:SetYAxisTitle(“Maximum Weight”)</td> </tr> <tr> <td>SetLegendTitle(text name)</td> <td>SetLegendTitle() takes in a string as a parameter, which would label the legend of the chart. The legend identifies the separate ages for the dots. For this example, we will label the legend “Breed Group”</td> <td>chart:SetLegendTitle(“Breed Group”)</td> </tr> <tr> <td>SetSubtitle(text title)</td> <td>SetSubtitle() takes in a string as a parameter which would set a subtitle under the title. This can be any short description or any other necessary information for our chart. For this example, we will label the subtitle “Does weight correlate to life span for dogs?”</td> <td>chart:SetSubtitle(“Does weight correlate to life span for dogs?”)</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Scatter Plot Labeling Functions</p> <pre><code>// label your scatter plot chart:SetXAxisTitle"Maximum Life Span (years)") chart:SetYAxisTitle("Maximum Weight (pounds)") chart:SetLegendTitle("Breed Group") chart:SetSubtitle("Does weight correlate to life span for dogs?") chart:SetTitle("Dog Weight and Life Span")</code></pre> <p>Note, if we would like to see the data chart so far, we can type “chart:Display()” to view it with the labels we created.</p> <h5 id="customizing-the-scatter-plot">Customizing the Scatter Plot</h5> <p>Now that we have our data labeled, we can customize our data to our liking, such as adjusting the intervals, changing starting values, and changing the color. We will be playing around with all these features and to do so, we will be again, using our chart object to call these functions. The functions we will be using for this would be: SetLegendLocationToBottom(), SetColorPaletteToDisurbing(), SetFontSize(integer size), FlipOrientation(), and ShowLinearRegression(bool). Here are brief descriptions on what each function does and how to use it.</p> <table> <colgroup> <col style="width: 8%" /> <col style="width: 81%" /> <col style="width: 9%" /> </colgroup> <thead> <tr> <th>Function</th> <th>Description</th> <th>Usage</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>SetLegendLocationToBottom()</td> <td>SetLegendLocationToBottom() takes in no parameters, which would be the directions, but will place the legend in a specificed place. For this example, we will place the legend on the bottom. Alternatively, you could also use SetLegendLocationToTop(), SetLegendLocationToLeft() or SetLegendLocationToRight().</td> <td>chart:SetLegendLocationToBottom()</td> </tr> <tr> <td>SetFontSize(integer size)</td> <td>SetFontSize() takes in an integer as a parameter and will set the font size on all text based on the desired input. For this tutorial, we will insert 30 as the font size.</td> <td>chart:SetFontSize(30)</td> </tr> <tr> <td>SetColorPaletteToDisurbing()</td> <td>SetColorPaletteToDisurbing() takes in no parameters, but will adjust the color palette based off of yellows, browns, oranges, and greens</td> <td>chart:SetColorPaletteToDisturbing()</td> </tr> <tr> <td>ShowLinearRegression(boolean)</td> <td>takes in a true or false value (boolean), and wll show the regression lines and equations for the chart</td> <td>chart:ShowLinearRegression(true)</td> </tr> <tr> <td>FlipOrientation()</td> <td>FlipOrientation() takes in no parameters, and this function will swap the places of the x and y axis.</td> <td>chart:FlipOrientation()</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Other Useful Scatter Plot Functions</p> <pre><code>// set the legend location, choices are left, right, top and bottom chart:SetLegendLocationToBottom() // color palette contains yellows, oranges, browns, and greens chart:SetColorPaletteToDisturbing() // adjust font size by preference, here we set it to 30 pt chart:SetFontSize(30) // if we would like to switch the x and y axis chart:FlipOrientation()</code></pre> <h5 id="displaying-the-chart-5">Displaying The Chart</h5> <p>Congratulations, our Scatter Plot is constructed! Now we can display the chart with the Display() function. There are two ways to do this, letting it automatically display and specifying a specific window size. By doing chart:Display() it will display in a size equal to the screen size. By doing chart:Display(num, num), it will display the chart in a respected constraint window size. We will be using the specified display.</p> <pre><code>chart:Display(1000, 750)</code></pre> <p>Now, feel free to clean, build, and run our program and we shortly should see a Game window pop-up. This is our Scatter Plot! To view the entire code, click <a href="https://github.com/qorf/curriculum/blob/main/Reference/DataScience/Charts%20(New)/DataScienceCurric/SourceCode/ScatterPlotExample.quorum">here</a> to view the file.</p> <h5 id="try-it-yourself-22">Try it Yourself!</h5> <p>Press the blue run button to execute the code in the code editor. Press the red stop button to end the program. Your program will work when the console outputs “Build Successful!”</p> <h5 id="final-chart-5">Final Chart</h5> <h5 id="further-useful-scatter-plot-functions">Further Useful Scatter Plot Functions</h5> <table> <colgroup> <col style="width: 20%" /> <col style="width: 62%" /> <col style="width: 17%" /> </colgroup> <tbody> <tr> <td>SetPointDestiny(integer num)</td> <td>This function takes in an integer that will adjust the size of the dots of the scatter plot</td> <td>chart:SetPointDensity(5)</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Other Useful Scatter Plot Actions</p> <p>To view more examples with charts, we can reference the Quorum Curriculum Repository for <a href="https://github.com/qorf/curriculum/tree/main/Reference/DataScience/Charts%20(New)/DataScienceCurric/SourceCode">charts</a>.</p> <h5 id="next-tutorial-120">Next Tutorial</h5> <p>In the next tutorial, we will discuss box plot, which describes how to use the box plot chart in quorum.</p> <p>Go BackNext Tutorial</p> <h5 id="on-this-page-138">On this page</h5> <h3 id="violin-plots">Violin Plots</h3> <h5 id="charts-17">Charts</h5> <h5 id="making-a-violin-plot">Making a Violin Plot</h5> <p>The next chart that we will discuss is a Violin Plot. A violin plot is a mix of 2 plots, a box plot and a density plot. Violin plots are used to visualize the distribution of numerical data. Because the violin plot is a mixture of two plots, it can show summary statistics and the density of each variable. Let’s talk about the structure of a violin plot: the white dot represents the median of the dataset, the thick black bar represents the interquartile range, and a thin black bar represents the rest of the distribution, except for the outliers. On each side of the black bar is a density estimation that shows the shape of the data’s distribution. The skinnier sections of the violin plot represent a lower probability, while wider sections represent a higher probability.</p> <p>The dataset that we will use in this example to create a violin plot is about the minimum and maximum lifespan of the various cat breeds.</p> <p>To follow along, we can download the Cats dataset <a href="https://github.com/qorf/curriculum/blob/main/Reference/DataScience/Charts%20(New)/Data/Animals/Cats.csv">here</a>.</p> <p>Here is a snippet of what the dataset should look like:</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Name</th> <th>Minimum Life Span</th> <th>Maximum Life Span</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>Abyssinian</td> <td>14.0</td> <td>15.0</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Aegean</td> <td>9.0</td> <td>12.0</td> </tr> <tr> <td>American Bobtail</td> <td>11.0</td> <td>15.0</td> </tr> <tr> <td>American Curl</td> <td>12.0</td> <td>16.0</td> </tr> <tr> <td>American Curl</td> <td>12.0</td> <td>16.0</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Cat CSV</p> <h5 id="loading-and-formatting-6">Loading and Formatting</h5> <p>As mentioned previously, to load and read in the dataset, we will need to create a DataFrame component named frame. Using the frame, we must use the Load function and type in the file path of the insurance CSV. Recall that a CSV is a comma separated text file that holds in data.</p> <pre><code>use Libraries.Compute.Statistics.DataFrame use Libraries.Interface.Controls.Charts.ViolinPlot /* This is an example of a simple violin plot in quorum. The data collected is about chicks' weight that depends on their sex and the type of feed they were consuming. */ // create dataframe to read in data DataFrame frame frame:Load("../Data/Animals/Cats.csv")</code></pre> <p>Note that, we stored this dataset in a Data folder, and contained in that folder is an inner folder named Animals.</p> <p>Once the data has been loaded in, we will now extract this data to use in the data chart. We will be using two functions from our frame component, AddSelectedColumns(text header) and AddSelectedFactors(text header) where the columns will be used to label our x axis, signifying the groups we are observing and the factor will be used to label our y axis, signifying the change over time. AddSelectedColumn(text header) and AddSelectedFactor(text header) take in a parameter of either the column number or the column label in the CSV file. We will be using the column number to demonstrate.</p> <p>Please note that for a Violin Plot, we will only be using the AddSelectedColumns(text header) because we would like to count the totals range of the minimum and maximum lifespan of cats. AddSelectedColumns(text header) will take a string as the parameter which represents the text header in the data file. Usage is shown below:</p> <table> <colgroup> <col style="width: 12%" /> <col style="width: 76%" /> <col style="width: 11%" /> </colgroup> <thead> <tr> <th>Function</th> <th>Description</th> <th>Usage</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>frame:AddSelectedColumns(text heading)</td> <td>AddSelectedColumns() takes in a string that matches a column heading from our dataset. This function is used to format our axises. For this tutorial, we will be calling this function twice and extract “Minimum Life Span” and “Maximum Life Span.”</td> <td>frame:AddSelectedColumns(“heading”)</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Adding CSV columns onto Charts</p> <p>We should have the following code:</p> <pre><code>// pull out selected data, for this we will be categorizing by life span frame:AddSelectedColumns("Minimum Life Span") frame:AddSelectedColumns("Maximum Life Span")</code></pre> <p>Now it is time to create the Violin Plot which can be done with the following code. This creates a chart object from our DataFrame component, frame. The rest of this lesson, we will be using the chart object we have created to change and format the rest of our line chart.</p> <pre><code>// using the data frame, format data by creating a violin plot chart component ViolinPlot chart = frame:ViolinPlot() chart:Display()</code></pre> <p>Calling the Display() function will give us a pop-up of our formatted data so far. We still need to give meaning to our data, therefore, the following steps will show us how to label and customize our chart.</p> <h5 id="labeling-the-violin-plot">Labeling the Violin Plot</h5> <p>In order for viewers to understand our data, labels give a clear comprehension of what is being presented. This means that we will be labeling the x axis, y axis, legend, and giving our chart a title that describes the dataset. To do so, we will call the following functions with our ‘chart’ object: SetTitle(), SetXAxisTitle(text title), SetYAxisTitle(text title), SetLegendTitle(text title), and SetSubtitle(text title). Here is a brief description on what each function does and what it takes in.</p> <table style="width:100%;"> <colgroup> <col style="width: 7%" /> <col style="width: 70%" /> <col style="width: 22%" /> </colgroup> <thead> <tr> <th>Function</th> <th>Description</th> <th>Usage</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>SetTitle(text name)</td> <td>SetTitle() takes in a string as a parameter, which would be the title of the chart. For this example, we will name the chart “Minimum and Maximum Life Expectancy for Various Cat Breeds”</td> <td>chart:SetTitle(“Minimum and Maximum Life Expectancy for Various Cat Breeds”)</td> </tr> <tr> <td>SetXAxisTitle(text name)</td> <td>SetXAxisTitle() takes in a string as a parameter, which would be the label of the x axis. For this example, we will label this section “Min/Max Lifespan”</td> <td>chart:SetXAxisTitle(“Min/Max Lifespan”</td> </tr> <tr> <td>SetYAxisTitle(text name)</td> <td>SetYAxisTitle() takes in a string as a parameter, which would be the label of the y axis. For this example, we will label this section “Type of Extrema.”</td> <td>chart:SetYAxisTitle(“Type of Extrema”)</td> </tr> <tr> <td>SetLegendTitle(text name)</td> <td>SetLegendTitle() takes in a string as a parameter, which would label the legend of the chart. The legend identifies the separate ages for the dots. For this example, we will label the legend “Age Group”</td> <td>chart:SetLegendTitle(“Age Group”)</td> </tr> <tr> <td>SetSubtitle(text title)</td> <td>SetSubtitle() takes in a string as a parameter which would set a subtitle under the title. This can be any short description or any other necessary information for our chart. For this example, we will label the subtitle “How long do cats live?”</td> <td>chart:SetSubtitle(“How long do cats live?”)</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Violin Plot Labeling Functions</p> <pre><code>// label your violin plot chart:SetXAxisTitle"Min/Max Lifespan") chart:SetYAxisTitle("Age") chart:SetLegendTitle("Type of Extrema") chart:SetSubtitle("How long do cats live?") chart:SetTitle("Minimum and Maximum Life Expectancy for Various Cat Breeds")</code></pre> <p>Note, if we would like to see the data chart so far, we can type “chart:Display()” to view it with the labels we created.</p> <h5 id="customizing-the-violin-plot">Customizing the Violin Plot</h5> <p>Now that we have our data labeled, we can customize our data to our liking, such as adjusting the intervals, changing starting values, and changing the color. We will be playing around with all these features and to do so, we will be again, using our chart object to call these functions. The functions we will be using for this would be: SetLegendLocation(text location), SetColorPaletteToDisurbing(), SetFontSize(integer size), and FlipOrientation(). Here are brief descriptions on what each function does and how to use it.</p> <table> <colgroup> <col style="width: 8%" /> <col style="width: 82%" /> <col style="width: 9%" /> </colgroup> <thead> <tr> <th>Function</th> <th>Description</th> <th>Usage</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>SetLegendLocationToBottom()</td> <td>SetLegendLocationToBottom() takes in no parameters, which would be the directions, but will place the legend in a specificed place. For this example, we will place the legend on the bottom. Alternatively, you could also use SetLegendLocationToTop(), SetLegendLocationToLeft() or SetLegendLocationToRight().</td> <td>chart:SetLegendLocationToBottom()</td> </tr> <tr> <td>SetFontSize(integer size)</td> <td>SetFontSize() takes in an integer as a parameter and will set the font size on all text based on the desired input. For this tutorial, we will insert 20 as the font size.</td> <td>chart:SetFontSize(20)</td> </tr> <tr> <td>SetColorPaletteToDisurbing()</td> <td>SetColorPaletteToDisurbing() takes in no parameters, but will adjust the color palette based off of yellows, browns, oranges, and greens</td> <td>chart:SetColorPaletteToDisturbing()</td> </tr> <tr> <td>FlipOrientation()</td> <td>FlipOrientation() takes in no parameters, and this function will swap the places of the x and y axis.</td> <td>chart:FlipOrientation()</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Other Useful Violin Plot Functions</p> <pre><code>// set the legend location, choices are left, right, top and bottom chart:SetLegendLocationToBottom() // color palette contains yellows, oranges, browns, and greens chart:SetColorPaletteToDisturbing() // adjust font size by preference, here we set it to 30 pt chart:SetFontSize(20) // if we would like to switch the x and y axis chart:FlipOrientation()</code></pre> <p>Congratulations, our Violin Plot is constructed! Now we can display our chart with the Display() function. There are two ways to do this, letting it automatically display and specifying a specific window size. By doing chart:Display() it will display in a size equal to the screen size. By doing chart:Display(num, num), it will display the chart in a respected constraint window size. We will be using the specified display.</p> <pre><code>chart:Display(1000, 750)</code></pre> <p>Now, feel free to clean, build, and run our program and we shortly should see a Game window pop-up. This is our Violin Plot! To view the entire code, click <a href="https://github.com/qorf/curriculum/blob/main/Reference/DataScience/Charts%20(New)/DataScienceCurric/SourceCode/ViolinExample1.quorum">here</a> to view the file.</p> <h5 id="try-it-yourself-23">Try it Yourself!</h5> <p>Press the blue run button to execute the code in the code editor. Press the red stop button to end the program. Your program will work when the console outputs “Build Successful!”</p> <h5 id="final-chart-6">Final Chart</h5> <h5 id="further-useful-box-plot-functions-1">Further Useful Box Plot Functions</h5> <table> <colgroup> <col style="width: 17%" /> <col style="width: 67%" /> <col style="width: 15%" /> </colgroup> <thead> <tr> <th>Function</th> <th>Description</th> <th>Usage</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>SetBandWidth(integer num)</td> <td>This function takes in an integer that will make a violin chart more or less exaggerated.</td> <td>chart:SetBandWidth(1)</td> </tr> <tr> <td>SplitPlot(boolean value)</td> <td>This function takes in a boolean that will split the violins if there are two violin charts in a group.</td> <td>chart:SplitPlot(false)</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Other Useful Violin Plot Actions</p> <p>To view more examples with charts, we can reference the Quorum Curriculum Repository for <a href="https://github.com/qorf/curriculum/tree/main/Reference/DataScience/Charts%20(New)/DataScienceCurric/SourceCode">charts</a>.</p> <h5 id="next-tutorial-121">Next Tutorial</h5> <p>In the next tutorial, we will discuss saving charts, which describes how to use the saving feature to save charts onto the desktop.</p> <p>Go BackNext Tutorial</p> <h5 id="on-this-page-139">On this page</h5> <h2 id="data-science">Data science</h2> <h3 id="descriptive-statistics-and-the-accessibility-features">Descriptive Statistics and the Accessibility Features</h3> <h5 id="descriptive-statistics-1">Descriptive Statistics</h5> <h5 id="accessibility-in-descriptive-statistics">Accessibility in Descriptive Statistics</h5> <p>When we discuss the idea of summaries, one category that often comes up is called Descriptive Statistics. The idea is that these kinds of statistics do not directly test a hypothesis, or make a prediction, but instead they give us some kind of information. Many of these are taught at relatively young ages. In this section, we provide sample code on how to run each of these statistics. In each case, we will provide a brief description of what the statistic is and then how to run code to calculate it. Finally, because different manufacturers use the same name to describe different types of calculations, we provide the equation used for each calculation in MathML format.</p> <p>One note on Accessibility. MathML is an accessible application we recommend for viewing the equations in this section. We especially recommend users of the NVDA screen reader to download Math Player 4. Math Player is optional and freely available at the following link:</p> <p><a href="https://docs.wiris.com/mathplayer/en/mathplayer-user-manual.html">Accessible Math Player</a></p> <h5 id="next-tutorial-122">Next Tutorial</h5> <p>In the next tutorial, we will discuss mean, which describes calculating the mean.</p> <p>Go BackNext Tutorial</p> <h5 id="on-this-page-140">On this page</h5> <h3 id="exporting-a-comma-separated-value-csv-file">Exporting a Comma Separated Value (CSV) File</h3> <h5 id="data-science-1">Data Science</h5> <p>This tutorial tells you how to export a Comma Separated Value (CSV) file from Google Sheets or Excel</p> <h5 id="exporting-from-google-sheets">Exporting from Google Sheets</h5> <p>We assume that all data has been finalized to how we want it and are now ready to export our data to use for further analysis. This would be done by uploading an XLXS (Excel file) or by entering data in each box. How we can have our data be saved as a CSV is fairly simple on Google Sheets.</p> <p>When we have our sheet file open, we would want to click on the ‘File’ tab on the left hand corner. Under ‘Files’ we now want to scroll down to ‘Download’ where it will pop-up a sub-menu on various file extensions which we can choose from. We want to navigate to the second to last option called ‘Comma Separated Value’ CSV and click it. This will prompt a download in which our file will be located in the ‘Downloads’ folder within our computers.</p> <h5 id="exporting-from-mircosoft-excel">Exporting from Mircosoft Excel</h5> <p>We assume that all data has been finalized to how we want it and are now ready to export our data to use for further analysis. This would be done by uploading an XLXS (Excel file) or by entering data in each box. How we can have our data be saved as a CSV is fairly simple on Microsoft Excel.</p> <p>When we have our sheet file open, we would want to click on the ‘File’ tab on the left hand corner. It should take us onto a new screen where we have many different saving options. We then want to go to the ‘Save As’ tab.</p> <p>Through there, we can specify the file location on where we want our newly created CSV file to live. Underneath where we can change the file name, we can choose the specific file extension with the pop-up drop down menu. From there, we want to select CSV (comma delimited) (*.csv) as our extension type. Then click the save button following on the right side of the file extension.</p> <h5 id="next-tutorial-123">Next Tutorial</h5> <p>In the next tutorial, we will discuss file loading, which describes how to load in a file using DataFrames.</p> <p>Go BackNext Tutorial</p> <h5 id="on-this-page-141">On this page</h5> <h3 id="filtering-data-in-a-dataset">Filtering Data in a Dataset</h3> <h5 id="filtering-data-1">Filtering Data</h5> <h5 id="filtering-the-data">Filtering the data</h5> <p>Being able to look at specific sections of our data may be useful when we have large amounts of entries in our dataset. For example, say that we have a survey sample of 2000 entries on music and we are wanting to look at data based off of entries that contain “indie pop” within the genre category. Instead of having to manually go through our data and find the individual rows containing “indie pop” we can simply make it easier on ourselves by filtering.</p> <p>The example we will be looking at is about dog breeds. In this dataset, it lists over 100 entries of different dog breeds and describes their life span, weight, height, temperament, etc. Now, looking at all these different dogs could be a bit overwhelming and right now, we want to only focus on dogs that may be good in an apartment, so it would make sense to possibly find smaller dogs. Instead of scrolling through every row to manually look for small dogs, we can now filter by the “Breed Group.” To do we would be able to filter all the dog breeds we want using the Filter(text source) function within the DataFrames library.</p> <p>Here is a brief description of how the Filter() function works.</p> <table> <colgroup> <col style="width: 7%" /> <col style="width: 69%" /> <col style="width: 23%" /> </colgroup> <thead> <tr> <th>Function</th> <th>Description</th> <th>Usage</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>frame:Filter(text source)</td> <td>This function takes in a string expression similar to writing an expression in Quorum. This function will filter out specific rows based on columns. The expression will evaluate to true or false on each row and either filter that row or not.</td> <td>text dq = ” dq = dq:GetDoubleQuote() frame:Filter(“Breed =” + dq + “Toy” + dq)</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Filter Helper Function</p> <p>Let’s try an example and retrieve all rows that contain “Toy” as the breed group. Doing so will create a copy of our data frame and contain ONLY the rows with “Toy,” hence we are filtering our dataset. Please note that in the Quorum Language, there is a flaw in the programming language in regard to usability and double quotes (notably, Quorum lacks escape characters), so we must manually make our double quotes as shown above.</p> <pre><code>//We need the DataFrame class to load in files for Data Science operations. use Libraries.Compute.Statistics.DataFrame use Libraries.Compute.Statistics.Transforms.RemoveUndefinedRowsTransform //Create a DataFrame, which is essentially a table that understands //more information about the data that is being loaded. DataFrame frame //This loads data relative to the project, so put the AskAManager.csv file in the Data/Miscellaneous folder frame:Load("../Data/Animals/Dogs.csv") text dq = "" dq = dq:GetDoubleQuote() //it's annoying, but we need to manually put in the double quotes, so //Quorum interprets the word "toy" as text //this then compares the value in the row Breed with //the constant text value "Toy" frame:Filter("Breed = " + dq + "Toy" + dq) //We can save the frame or output it to the console, like we are doing here. output frame:ToText()</code></pre> <h5 id="try-it-yourself-24">Try it Yourself!</h5> <p>Press the blue run button to execute the code in the code editor. Press the red stop button to end the program. Your program will work when the console outputs “Build Successful!”</p> <p>Congratulations! We have successfully filtered the data from a dataset. To view the code we just ran, we can reference it <a href="https://github.com/qorf/curriculum/blob/main/Reference/DataScience/Data%20Frames/FilterData.quorum">here</a>.</p> <h5 id="on-this-page-142">On this page</h5> <h3 id="introduction-to-data-science">Introduction to Data Science</h3> <h5 id="data-science-2">Data Science</h5> <p>This tutorial introduces the concept of DataFrames in Quorum.</p> <h5 id="what-is-a-dataframe">What is a DataFrame?</h5> <p>The key component in loading data is to use a DataFrame. A DataFrame is a series of rows and columns, like a table, except that the columns inside of this table understand information about their data and can transform it in a variety of ways. For example, one column might contain text, another might contain numbers, and another might contain integers. DataFrames can have selections, kind of like selecting a row or column in a spreadsheet, and can do operations on top of that selection.</p> <p>We use DataFrames for everything in our library and always load and save it the same way. By default, Quorum data frames use the “Comma Separated Files” method for loading into DataFrame objects. Second, if we want to, we can load a DataFrame by hand, meaning we can inject and use values in a table manually.</p> <h5 id="creating-a-dataframe">Creating a DataFrame</h5> <p>To create a DataFrame, the way that we create it is defining it like a normal variable such as: DataType variableName. In this case, the data type would be of type DataFrame and we can name the DataFrame as any meaningful name. Typically, the easiest name for a DataFrame is to call it ‘frame.’ In many of our tutorials using DataFrames we use the naming convention ‘frame’ for consistency.</p> <h6 id="code-example">Code Example</h6> <p>Once we have this DataFrame object created, we can now use these to access any datasets we have uploaded, create charts, compute data statistics, and much more.</p> <pre><code>DataFrame frame</code></pre> <h5 id="try-it-yourself-25">Try it Yourself!</h5> <p>Press the blue run button to execute the code in the code editor. Press the red stop button to end the program. Your program will work when the console outputs “Build Successful!”</p> <h5 id="next-tutorial-124">Next Tutorial</h5> <p>In the next tutorial, we will discuss tidy data, which describes how quorum organizes data with tidy data.</p> <p>Go BackNext Tutorial</p> <h5 id="on-this-page-143">On this page</h5> <h3 id="learn-about-calculating-the-interquartile-range">Learn About Calculating the Interquartile Range</h3> <h5 id="descriptive-statistics-2">Descriptive Statistics</h5> <h5 id="calculating-the-interquartile-range">Calculating the Interquartile Range</h5> <p>In data science, the Interquartile Range (IQR) is a measure of variability, based on dividing a data set into quartiles. Specifically, IQR will describe the spread of the middle half of the distribution. For example, say we have a box plot of four quartiles, the IQR would calculate the two middle quartiles, notably Q1 through Q3. The interquartile range provides us a spread between regions of the data.</p> <p><em>I<strong>Q</strong>R</em> = <em>Q</em>₃ − <em>Q</em>₁</p> <p>The Interquartile Range is calculated by using a helper action within the DataFrame’s class. We will calculate the Interquartile Range (IQR) for the ‘Area’ column. To do this, we will use our ‘frame’ object and call the function InterQuartileRange (). In this case we will be calculating the IQR of the area of dry bean classifications. Here is a brief description on how InterQuartileRange() works.</p> <table style="width:100%;"> <colgroup> <col style="width: 13%" /> <col style="width: 73%" /> <col style="width: 13%" /> </colgroup> <thead> <tr> <th>Function</th> <th>Description</th> <th>Usage</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>frame:InterQuartileRange()</td> <td>This action sorts the following selected column and calculates the IQR of the column. Note that it can only calculate the IQR of one column at a time.</td> <td>frame:InterQuartileRange()</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>IQR Function</p> <p>Here are other functions that we use in the example:</p> <table> <colgroup> <col style="width: 29%" /> <col style="width: 43%" /> <col style="width: 27%" /> </colgroup> <thead> <tr> <th>Function</th> <th>Description</th> <th>Usage</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>InterQuartileRange range = frame:InterQuartileRange()</td> <td>Initializes the IQR class named range to the frame we created earlier</td> <td>InterQuartileRange range</td> </tr> <tr> <td>range:GetMinimum()</td> <td>Returns the minimum value that is not an outlier, that is inside the IQR range</td> <td>output “Minimum:” + range:GetMinimum()</td> </tr> <tr> <td>range:GetMaximum()</td> <td>Returns the maximum value that is not an outlier, that is inside the IQR range</td> <td>output “Maximum:” + range:GetMaximum()</td> </tr> <tr> <td>range:GetInterQuartileRange()</td> <td>Returns the range of the IQR calculated from a given dataset</td> <td>output “Range:” + range:GetInterQuartileRange()</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Helper Functions for IQR</p> <p>Here is some code on how to calculate the IQR:</p> <pre><code>//We need the DataFrame class to load in files for Data Science operations. use Libraries.Compute.Statistics.DataFrame //This is the calculation for the arithmetic mean use Libraries.Compute.Statistics.Calculations.InterQuartileRange //Create a DataFrame, which is essentially a table that understands //more information about the data that is being loaded. //Using the default loader is enough for our purposes DataFrame frame frame:Load("../Data/Miscellaneous/DryBeans.csv") //Tell the frame we want the first column selected frame:AddSelectedColumn(0) InterQuartileRange range = frame:InterQuartileRange() output "Minimum: " + range:GetMinimum() output "Maximum: " + range:GetMaximum() output "Range: " + range:GetInterQuartileRange()</code></pre> <h5 id="try-it-yourself-26">Try it Yourself!</h5> <p>Press the blue run button to execute the code in the code editor. Press the red stop button to end the program. Your program will work when the console outputs “Build Successful!”</p> <p>Congrats! We have just learned how to calculate the Interquartile Range! To view the whole file, we can click <a href="https://github.com/qorf/curriculum/blob/main/Reference/DataScience/Summarizing/SourceCode/CalculateInterquartile.quorum">here</a>.</p> <h5 id="next-tutorial-125">Next Tutorial</h5> <p>In the next tutorial, we will discuss standard deviation from the mean, which describes calculating the standard deviation from the mean (z-score).</p> <p>Go BackNext Tutorial</p> <h5 id="on-this-page-144">On this page</h5> <h3 id="learn-about-calculating-the-kurtosis">Learn About Calculating the Kurtosis</h3> <h5 id="descriptive-statistics-3">Descriptive Statistics</h5> <h5 id="calculating-the-kurtosis">Calculating the Kurtosis</h5> <p>In data statistics, kurtosis is a phrase used to indicate how heavy or light the tails of our data are. By heavy tails, we mean that our data might be flatter around the edges. By light tails, it is the opposite. A dataset might be largely flat across the board. One reason we care about this is because as data is distributed in different ways, it can cause problems in data analysis. Put simply, we use kurtosis to make sure the distribution of our data is fairly balanced.</p> <p><span class="math display">$$\text{Kurtosis=}\frac{n\left( n\operatorname{} + \operatorname{}1 \right)\operatorname{}}{\left( n\operatorname{} - \operatorname{}1 \right)(n - 2)(n - 3)\operatorname{}s^{4}}\underset{i = 1}{\overset{n}{\sum\operatorname{}}}\left( {x - \overline{x}} \right)^{4}\operatorname{} - \operatorname{}\frac{3(n - 1)^{2}}{(n - 2)\operatorname{}\*\operatorname{}(n - 3)}$$</span></p> <p>While one might assume that the equations for kurtosis are standardized, in practice different statistical packages provide slightly different answers. In our case, we document the equations we used in MathML. All statistical packages provide similar answers and our equations match those used in the <a href="https://commons.apache.org/proper/commons-math/">Apache Commons mathematical packages</a>.</p> <p>The kurtosis can be calculated by calling the helper action, Kurtosis() contained within the DataFrame’s class. To do this, we will use our ‘frame’ object and call the function Kurtosis(). In this case we will be calculating the mean of the area of dry bean classifications. Here is a brief description on how Kurtosis() works.</p> <table> <colgroup> <col style="width: 11%" /> <col style="width: 79%" /> <col style="width: 8%" /> </colgroup> <thead> <tr> <th>Function</th> <th>Description</th> <th>Usage</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>dataFrameObject:Skew()</td> <td>This action takes the column that you have passed and calculates the kurtosis of that column. Note that it can only calculate the kurtosis of one column at a time.</td> <td>frame:Kurtosis()</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Kurtosis Function</p> <p>Here is some code on how to calculate the kurtosis:</p> <pre><code>//We need the DataFrame class to load in files for Data Science operations. use Libraries.Compute.Statistics.DataFrame //Create a DataFrame, which is essentially a table that understands //more information about the data that is being loaded. //Using the default loader is enough for our purposes DataFrame frame frame:Load("../Data/Miscellaneous/DryBeans.csv") //Tell the frame we want the first column selected frame:AddSelectedColumn(0) output frame:Kurtosis()</code></pre> <h5 id="try-it-yourself-27">Try it Yourself!</h5> <p>Press the blue run button to execute the code in the code editor. Press the red stop button to end the program. Your program will work when the console outputs “Build Successful!”</p> <p>Congrats! We have just learned how to calulate the kurtosis! To view the whole file, we can click <a href="https://github.com/qorf/curriculum/blob/main/Reference/DataScience/Summarizing/SourceCode/CalculateKurtosis.quorum">here</a>.</p> <h5 id="end-of-lesson-15">End of Lesson</h5> <p>You have reached the end of the lesson for Descriptive Statistics. To view more tutorials, press the button below or you can go back to the previous lesson pages.</p> <p>Go BackBack to Tutorials</p> <h5 id="on-this-page-145">On this page</h5> <h3 id="learn-about-calculating-the-mean">Learn About Calculating the Mean</h3> <h5 id="descriptive-statistics-4">Descriptive Statistics</h5> <h5 id="calculating-the-mean">Calculating the Mean</h5> <p>In data science, the arithmetic mean is known as the average. It is the central value in a finite data set of numbers. We can calculate the mean by finding the sum of all values in a dataset and divide it by the number of values.</p> <p><span class="math display">$$\overline{x} = \frac{1}{n}\left( {\sum\limits\_{i = 0}^{n}x\_{i}} \right)$$</span></p> <p>The arithmetic mean can be calculated in Quorum by using the helper action, Mean() within the DataFrame’s class. To do this, we will use our ‘frame’ object and call the function Mean(). In this case we will be calculating the mean of the perimeter and the area of dry bean classifications. Here is a brief description on how Mean() works.</p> <table> <colgroup> <col style="width: 13%" /> <col style="width: 78%" /> <col style="width: 7%" /> </colgroup> <thead> <tr> <th>Function</th> <th>Description</th> <th>Usage</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>dataFrameObject:Mean()</td> <td>This action calculates the mean of the column selected from the frame. Note that it can only calculate the mean of one column at a time.</td> <td>frame:Mean()</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Mean Function</p> <p>Here is some code on how to calculate the mean:</p> <pre><code>//We need the DataFrame class to load in files for Data Science operations. use Libraries.Compute.Statistics.DataFrame //Create a DataFrame, which is essentially a table that understands //more information about the data that is being loaded. DataFrame frame //This loads data relative to the project, so put the dryBeans file in the Data/Miscellaneous folder frame:Load("../Data/Miscellaneous/DryBeans.csv") //Tell the frame we want the first column selected frame:AddSelectedColumn(0) text someText = "Mean of the first column (Area) of dry beans:" output someText output frame:Mean()</code></pre> <h5 id="try-it-yourself-28">Try it Yourself!</h5> <p>Press the blue run button to execute the code in the code editor. Press the red stop button to end the program. Your program will work when the console outputs “Build Successful!”</p> <p>Congrats! We have just learned how to calulate the mean! To view the whole file, we can click <a href="https://github.com/qorf/curriculum/blob/main/Reference/DataScience/Summarizing/SourceCode/BeanMean.quorum">here</a>.</p> <h5 id="next-tutorial-126">Next Tutorial</h5> <p>In the next tutorial, we will discuss median, which describes calculating the median.</p> <p>Go BackNext Tutorial</p> <h5 id="on-this-page-146">On this page</h5> <h3 id="learn-about-calculating-the-median">Learn About Calculating the Median</h3> <h5 id="descriptive-statistics-5">Descriptive Statistics</h5> <h5 id="calculating-the-median">Calculating the Median</h5> <p>In data statistics, the median is the middle number of a sorted (either ascending or descending) numerical dataset. Depending on context, a median may describe a dataset better than the average because it is not skewed by possible outliers in our datasets. The median basically is the separating factor between the upper and lower halves of a dataset.</p> <p><span class="math display">$$median = \left\\ \frac{n + 1}{2} \right\\^{th}$$</span></p> <p>The median is calculated using the helper action Median() which is within the DataFrame’s class. We again calculate this for the survival column. To do this, we will use our ‘frame’ object and call the function Median(). In this case we will be calculating the median of the perimeter and the area of dry bean classifications. Here is a brief description on how Median() works.</p> <table> <colgroup> <col style="width: 12%" /> <col style="width: 79%" /> <col style="width: 7%" /> </colgroup> <thead> <tr> <th>Function</th> <th>Description</th> <th>Usage</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>dataFrameObject:Median()</td> <td>This action sorts the following selected column and calculates the middle value of that column. Note that it can only calculate the median of one column at a time.</td> <td>frame:Median()</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Median Function</p> <p>Here is some code on how to calculate the median:</p> <pre><code>//We need the DataFrame class to load in files for Data Science operations. use Libraries.Compute.Statistics.DataFrame //Create a DataFrame, which is essentially a table that understands //more information about the data that is being loaded. DataFrame frame //This loads data relative to the project, so put the dryBeans file in the Data/Miscellaneous folder frame:Load("../Data/Miscellaneous/DryBeans.csv") //we can also grab by the header name as well and calculate the mean/average frame:AddSelectedColumns("MinorAxisLength") text someText1 = "Median of the column Minor Axis Length of dry beans:" output someText1 output frame:Median()</code></pre> <h5 id="try-it-yourself-29">Try it Yourself!</h5> <p>Press the blue run button to execute the code in the code editor. Press the red stop button to end the program. Your program will work when the console outputs “Build Successful!”</p> <p>Congrats! We have just learned how to calulate the median! To view the whole file, we can click <a href="https://github.com/qorf/curriculum/blob/main/Reference/DataScience/Summarizing/SourceCode/BeanMedian.quorum">here</a>.</p> <h5 id="next-tutorial-127">Next Tutorial</h5> <p>In the next tutorial, we will discuss mode, which describes calculating the mode.</p> <p>Go BackNext Tutorial</p> <h5 id="on-this-page-147">On this page</h5> <h3 id="learn-about-calculating-the-mode">Learn About Calculating the Mode</h3> <h5 id="descriptive-statistics-6">Descriptive Statistics</h5> <h5 id="calculating-the-mode">Calculating the Mode</h5> <p>In data science, the mode is typically the number that occurs the most frequently in a dataset. Mode is unique because in a numerical dataset, there can be three types of modes: no mode, one mode, or multiple modes. In mode allows scientists to know what values would be most sampled in a dataset.</p> <p><span class="math display">$$mode = L + h\*\frac{(f\_{m} - f\_{1})}{(f\_{m} - f\_{1}) + (f\_{m} - f\_{2})}$$</span></p> <p>The mode is calculated similarly to the others. We create the Mode class, then pass it to the column. Like the others, undefined values are automatically removed. One difference is that with Mode, if the column has more than one value that has an equally high frequency in the data set, like 1,1,2,2,3,3, then all three modes are returned. If we have a case where there are no duplicates at all, like 1,2,3,4,5,6, then the modes are technically all values in the column and this is returned. We can detect this case by calling the HasDuplicates() action by calling it inside the Mode class.</p> <p>This method we are doing will find all modes in a single column. In order to get the mode of a single column, we first need to extract it and store it inside a DataFrame column, named col. For this example, we will grab the ‘Perimeter’ column by calling GetColumn(int columnNumber) and insert 1 as the perimeter.</p> <pre><code>DataFrameColumn col = frame:GetColumn(1)</code></pre> <p>Then, we need to create a mode class object, and note that this mode object takes account of any missing data so 0’s would not be counted. We then use our col and call Calculate where we insert the mode object we also made as the parameter.</p> <pre><code>col:Calculate(mode)</code></pre> <p>Then, we want to create a number array, called ‘modes’ and store all the modes found from our previous calculation and then sort it using the Sort() function on the array. This is so we can check if there are any duplicates as mentioned previously. To check for duplicates, we iterate through the ‘modes’ array with a repeat loop and output any of the modes with the most duplicates, so in this case we may result in many modes as the result. We can verify if the dataset contains duplicates with the function HasDuplicates() which is called from the mode object.</p> <p>Here are brief descriptions of the objects and functions we have used throughout this tutorial:</p> <table> <colgroup> <col style="width: 20%" /> <col style="width: 60%" /> <col style="width: 19%" /> </colgroup> <thead> <tr> <th>Function / Class</th> <th>Description</th> <th>Usage</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>Mode objectName</td> <td>This is the mode object used to calculate all the possible modes within a dataset.</td> <td>Mode mode</td> </tr> <tr> <td>modeObjectName:GetModes()</td> <td>Using an array, it retrieves all the modes found in a dataset.</td> <td>Array modes = mode:GetModes()</td> </tr> <tr> <td>modeObjectName:HasDuplicates()</td> <td>This checks the mode object for any duplicate values to determine if there are multiple modes.</td> <td>mode:HasDuplicates()</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Mode helper Function</p> <p>Here is some code on how to calculate the mode:</p> <pre><code>//We need the DataFrame class to load in files for Data Science operations. use Libraries.Compute.Statistics.DataFrame use Libraries.Compute.Statistics.DataFrameColumn use Libraries.Compute.Statistics.Calculations.Mode use Libraries.Containers.Array //Create a DataFrame, which is essentially a table that understands //more information about the data that is being loaded. DataFrame frame //This loads data relative to the project, so put the dryBeans file in the Data/Miscellaneous folder frame:Load("../Data/Miscellaneous/DryBeans.csv") //Get the column we want, in this case "perimeter" DataFrameColumn col = frame:GetColumn(1) //The calculation for means automatically takes missing data into account Mode mode //we pass the Mean class to the column, which does the calculation and stores the answer //We can then get the answer in code or do something else with it, like output it to the screen col:Calculate(mode) Array modes = mode:GetModes() modes:Sort() i = 0 repeat while i < modes:GetSize() output modes:Get(i) i = i + 1 end output mode:HasDuplicates()</code></pre> <h5 id="try-it-yourself-30">Try it Yourself!</h5> <p>Press the blue run button to execute the code in the code editor. Press the red stop button to end the program. Your program will work when the console outputs “Build Successful!”</p> <p>Congrats! We have just learned how to calulate the mode! To view the whole file, we can click <a href="https://github.com/qorf/curriculum/blob/main/Reference/DataScience/Summarizing/SourceCode/BeanMode.quorum">here</a>.</p> <h5 id="next-tutorial-128">Next Tutorial</h5> <p>In the next tutorial, we will discuss variance and standard deviation, which describes calculating the variance and standard deviation.</p> <p>Go BackNext Tutorial</p> <h5 id="on-this-page-148">On this page</h5> <h3 id="learn-about-calculating-the-skew">Learn About Calculating the Skew</h3> <h5 id="descriptive-statistics-7">Descriptive Statistics</h5> <h5 id="calculating-the-skew">Calculating the Skew</h5> <p>In data statistics, skewness can be thought of as a lack of symmetry in the data. When analyzing data, mathematical properties about that data can be useful in understanding it. Two rather useful metrics are skew and, in the next section, kurtosis. We measure skew as a number, positive or negative, which references whether the data set is shifted in one direction or the other. A skew of 0 means that the data is symmetrical around the mean. A positive skew, or right skew, indicates the tail of the data is longer above the mean. A negative skew, or left skew, is the opposite. For calculating skew, we use an equation that is common in statistical packages, called the “Fisher-Pearson Standardized Moment Coefficient.”</p> <p><span class="math display">$$\text{Skew=}\frac{n}{(n - 1)(n - 2)}\sum\limits\_{i = 1}^{n}\left( \frac{x\_{i} - \overline{x}}{s} \right)^{3}$$</span></p> <p>The skew is calculated using the helper action Skew() which is within the DataFrame’s class. To do this, we will use our ‘frame’ object and call the function Skew(). In this case we will be calculating the skew of the area of dry bean classifications. Here is a brief description on how Skew() works.</p> <table> <colgroup> <col style="width: 12%" /> <col style="width: 80%" /> <col style="width: 7%" /> </colgroup> <thead> <tr> <th>Function</th> <th>Description</th> <th>Usage</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>dataFrameObject:Skew()</td> <td>This action takes the column that you have passed and calculates the skew of that column. Note that it can only calculate the skew of one column at a time.</td> <td>frame:Skew()</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Skew Function</p> <p>Here is some code on how to calculate the skew:</p> <pre><code>//We need the DataFrame class to load in files for Data Science operations. use Libraries.Compute.Statistics.DataFrame //Create a DataFrame, which is essentially a table that understands //more information about the data that is being loaded. //Using the default loader is enough for our purposes DataFrame frame frame:Load("../Data/Miscellaneous/DryBeans.csv") //Tell the frame we want the first column selected frame:AddSelectedColumn(0) output frame:Skew()</code></pre> <h5 id="try-it-yourself-31">Try it Yourself!</h5> <p>Press the blue run button to execute the code in the code editor. Press the red stop button to end the program. Your program will work when the console outputs “Build Successful!”</p> <p>Congrats! We have just learned how to calulate the skew! To view the whole file, we can click <a href="https://github.com/qorf/curriculum/blob/main/Reference/DataScience/Summarizing/SourceCode/CalculateSkew.quorum">here</a>.</p> <h5 id="next-tutorial-129">Next Tutorial</h5> <p>In the next tutorial, we will discuss kurtosis, which describes calculating the kurtosis.</p> <p>Go BackNext Tutorial</p> <h5 id="on-this-page-149">On this page</h5> <h3 id="learn-about-calculating-the-standard-deviation-from-mean">Learn About Calculating the Standard Deviation from Mean</h3> <h5 id="descriptive-statistics-8">Descriptive Statistics</h5> <h5 id="calculating-the-standard-devation-from-mean">Calculating the Standard Devation from Mean</h5> <p>In data science, the standard deviations from the mean is a way to determine whether a data set has outliers. Outliers are data points that have an abnormal distance from the other values in a dataset.
