One reason we do this is because if we observe very extreme outliers, it is rational to consider whether the data could have been coded incorrectly or whether the data is real. One easy way to do this is to calculate the number of standard deviations away from the mean. In statistics, the technical term for this is ‘z-scores.’ This is why the equation below uses z as a label.</p> <p><span class="math display">$$z = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}$$</span></p> <p>We can calculate z-scores, or the number of standard deviations from the mean, for an entire column using the StandardDeviationsFromMean class. In addition, this class has an action, CalculateStandardDeviationFromMean, which can return us the answer for a specific value. This returns to us a new column with numbers in it. Notably, a score of 0 means that the value for that data point was at the mean. A score of 1, or -1, means that the data point was one standard deviation above or below the mean, respectively. Having these values for a column lets us quickly skim them, or filter them, looking for points that may not belong.</p> <p>The standard deviations from mean can be calculated in Quorum by using the StandardDeviationsFromMean class and passing it to a column. To do this, we will use our ‘frame’ object and will get the column by calling frame:GetColumn() function. In this case we will be calculating the standard deviations from mean of the area of dry bean classifications. Here is a brief description on how StandardDeviationsFromMean () works.</p> <table> <colgroup> <col style="width: 10%" /> <col style="width: 63%" /> <col style="width: 25%" /> </colgroup> <thead> <tr> <th>Function</th> <th>Description</th> <th>Usage</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>Calculate(zscores)</td> <td>Calculates the Standard Deviations from Mean and stores the answer in the variable that is inside the parentheses</td> <td>col:Calculate(zscores)</td> </tr> <tr> <td>GetResultColumn()</td> <td>Returns a column with all of the calculated standard deviations</td> <td>NumberColumn result = zscores:GetResultColumn</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Z-Scores Function</p> <p>Here is the full code on how to find the standard deviations from the mean of a numerical dataset:</p> <pre><code>//We need the DataFrame class to load in files for Data Science operations. use Libraries.Compute.Statistics.DataFrame use Libraries.Compute.Statistics.DataFrameColumn //This is the calculation for the arithmetic mean use Libraries.Compute.Statistics.Calculations.StandardDeviationsFromMean use Libraries.Compute.Statistics.Columns.NumberColumn //Create a DataFrame, which is essentially a table that understands //more information about the data that is being loaded. //Using the default loader is enough for our purposes DataFrame frame frame:Load("../Data/Miscellaneous/DryBeans.csv") //Get the column we want, in this case "survival" DataFrameColumn col = frame:GetColumn(0) //The calculation automatically and take missing data into account StandardDeviationsFromMean zscores //we pass the Mean class to the column, which does the calculation and stores the answer //We can then get the answer in code or do something else with it, like output it to the screen col:Calculate(zscores) NumberColumn result = zscores:GetResultColumn() output result:ToText()</code></pre> <h5 id="try-it-yourself-32">Try it Yourself!</h5> <p>Press the blue run button to execute the code in the code editor. Press the red stop button to end the program. Your program will work when the console outputs “Build Successful!”</p> <p>Congrats! We have just learned how to calulate the z-score! To view the whole file, we can click <a href="https://github.com/qorf/curriculum/blob/main/Reference/DataScience/Summarizing/SourceCode/CalculateStandardDeviationsFromMean.quorum">here</a>.</p> <h5 id="next-tutorial-130">Next Tutorial</h5> <p>In the next tutorial, we will discuss skew, which describes calculating the skew.</p> <p>Go BackNext Tutorial</p> <h5 id="on-this-page-150">On this page</h5> <h3 id="learn-about-calculating-the-variance-and-standard-deviation">Learn About Calculating the Variance and Standard Deviation</h3> <h5 id="descriptive-statistics-9">Descriptive Statistics</h5> <h5 id="calculating-the-variance-and-standard-deviation">Calculating the Variance and Standard Deviation</h5> <p>In data science, standard deviation measures the variability of a set of numerical values. Having a low standard deviation means that values are more clumped whereas a higher standard deviation means that the values are spread out in a wider range. Standard deviation is the square root of variance. Variance is simply the average of the squares of the deviations. What that means is that it describes the variability of observations from its arithmetic mean. This is done by calculating the difference between each number and the mean then squaring the differences to divide them by the sum of squares. Here are the equations of standard deviation and variance:</p> <p><strong>Standard Deviation:</strong></p> <p><span class="math display">$$s\_{x} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n - 1}\sum\limits\_{i = 1}^{n}\left( \left( x\_{i} - \overline{x} \right)^{2} \right)}$$</span></p> <p><strong>Variance:</strong></p> <p><span class="math display">$$s\_{x}^{2} = \frac{1}{n - 1}\sum\limits\_{i = 1}^{n}\left( \left( x\_{i} - \overline{x} \right)^{2} \right)$$</span></p> <p>While the mean and median are measures of central tendency, variance and standard deviation are measures of dispersion. Put another way, variance and standard deviation are different measures of how the data points are compared to a center point. The standard deviation is the square root of the variance. This example shows using both the Variance() function and the StandardDeviation() function, even though they are mathematically related.</p> <p>After loading the data, to calculate the standard deviation and variance, we want to call the two actionss from our DataFrame, frame Variance() and StandardDeviation() from one column out of our dataset. Here are brief descriptions of how these functions work:</p> <table> <colgroup> <col style="width: 22%" /> <col style="width: 60%" /> <col style="width: 16%" /> </colgroup> <thead> <tr> <th>Function</th> <th>Description</th> <th>Usage</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>dataFrameObject:StandardDeviation()</td> <td>This action will calculate the standard deviation from a single column of data within the dataset.</td> <td>frame:StandardDeviation()</td> </tr> <tr> <td>dataFrameObject:Variance()</td> <td>This action will calculate the variance from a single column of data within the dataset.</td> <td>frame:Variance()</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Standard Devation and Variance Function</p> <p>Here is some code on how to calculate the variance and SD:</p> <pre><code>//We need the DataFrame class to load in files for Data Science operations. use Libraries.Compute.Statistics.DataFrame //Create a DataFrame, which is essentially a table that understands //more information about the data that is being loaded. //Using the default loader is enough for our purposes DataFrame frame //This loads data relative to the project, so put the dryBeans file in the Data/Miscellaneous folder frame:Load("../Data/Miscellaneous/DryBeans.csv") //Tell the frame we want the roundness column which is received through the text header frame:AddSelectedColumns("roundness") //When we call Variance or StandardDeviation, the frame now knows //we are referencing the first column. output "Variance: " + frame:Variance() output "Standard Deviation: " + frame:StandardDeviation()</code></pre> <h5 id="try-it-yourself-33">Try it Yourself!</h5> <p>Press the blue run button to execute the code in the code editor. Press the red stop button to end the program. Your program will work when the console outputs “Build Successful!”</p> <p>Congrats! We have just learned how to calulate the variance and standard deviation! To view the whole file, we can click <a href="https://github.com/qorf/curriculum/blob/main/Reference/DataScience/Summarizing/SourceCode/BeanVarianceAndSD.quorum">here</a>.</p> <h5 id="next-tutorial-131">Next Tutorial</h5> <p>In the next tutorial, we will discuss IQR, which describes calculating the interquartile range.</p> <p>Go BackNext Tutorial</p> <h5 id="on-this-page-151">On this page</h5> <h3 id="loading-a-dataset-by-hand">Loading a dataset “by Hand”</h3> <h5 id="data-science-3">Data Science</h5> <p>This tutorial tells use the DataFrame to load data “by Hand”</p> <h5 id="loading-data-by-hand">Loading data “by Hand”</h5> <p>While normally we load data from a file or another source, we can also create it by hand. We recommend making our data in excel or other sources, but document this possibility here for completeness. By default, there are six column types we can add, NumberColumn, BooleanColumn, IntegerColumn, TextColumn, AudioColumn, and DateColumn. Here are brief explanations on each valid column data entry we can use.</p> <table> <colgroup> <col style="width: 5%" /> <col style="width: 65%" /> <col style="width: 28%" /> </colgroup> <thead> <tr> <th>Object</th> <th>Description</th> <th>Usage</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>NumberColumn</td> <td>NumberColumns allow us to insert both integers and decimal values into our data sets.</td> <td>NumberColumn numCol numCol:Add(“1”) numCol:Add(“1.5”)</td> </tr> <tr> <td>BooleanColumn</td> <td>BooleanColumns allow us to insert true and false values into our data sets.</td> <td>BooleanColumn boolCol boolCol:Add(true) boolCol:Add(false)</td> </tr> <tr> <td>IntegerColumn</td> <td>IntegerColumns allow us to insert whole numbers into our data sets.</td> <td>IntegerColumn intCol integerCol:Add(5) integerCol:Add(8)</td> </tr> <tr> <td>TextColumn</td> <td>TextColumns allow us to insert strings/text into our data sets.</td> <td>TextColumn txtCol txtCol:(“Mickey”) txtCol:(“Mouse”)</td> </tr> <tr> <td>AudioColumn</td> <td>AudioColumns allow us to insert audio files into our data sets. It takes in a string which is the file path of the audio file. AudioColumn* will accept both .ogg files and .wav files.</td> <td>AudioColumn aCol aCol:Add(“...mp4”) aCol:Add(“...mp4”)</td> </tr> <tr> <td>DateColumn**</td> <td>DateColumns allow us to insert dates into our data sets.</td> <td>DateColumn dCol dCol:Add(“11/2/2022”) dCol:Add(“11/3/2022”)</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Column Types</p> <p>**DateColumn was added in Quorum 10.0.</p> <p>For this example, we will be creating a dataset that incorporates a selection of the data types we can insert. What we want to start off is creating a DataFrame object to load our dataset. We will go ahead and name it ‘frame.’ Now, let us create the columns of the data types: number, boolean, integer, and text.</p> <p>We should have the following code:</p> <p><strong>*Note that AudioColumns cannot be used with the ToText() function with DataFrames.</strong></p> <h5 id="code-example-1">Code Example</h5> <pre><code>//We need the DataFrame class to load in files for Data Science operations. use Libraries.Compute.Statistics.DataFrame use Libraries.Compute.Statistics.Columns.NumberColumn use Libraries.Containers.Array use Libraries.Compute.Statistics.DataFrameColumn use Libraries.Compute.Statistics.Columns.TextColumn use Libraries.Compute.Statistics.Columns.BooleanColumn use Libraries.Compute.Statistics.Columns.IntegerColumn //Create a DataFrame, which is essentially a table that understands //more information about the data that is being loaded. DataFrame frame NumberColumn numCol TextColumn textCol BooleanColumn boolCol IntegerColumn intCol</code></pre> <p>Now that we have our data columns, we can simply use the Add(type element) with the respective column object we have created. Our Add(type element) can be used with all the different columns and will add our element of the respective data type within the data set. Here, we will add two elements to each column.</p> <pre><code>numCol:Add(1.4) textCol:Add("Fruit") boolCol:Add(true) intCol:Add(6) numCol:Add(3.5) textCol:Add("Vegetable") boolCol:Add(false) intCol:Add(10)</code></pre> <p>Now that we have populated our dataset, we would like to insert them into the DataFrame. Doing this step actually helps construct the elements and form it into a CSV-style type of dataset. We can achieve this by calling the AddColumn(dataColumn type) function with our DataFrame ‘frame’ object. Here is a brief description of how AddColumn(dataColumn type) works.</p> <table> <colgroup> <col style="width: 11%" /> <col style="width: 55%" /> <col style="width: 33%" /> </colgroup> <thead> <tr> <th>Function</th> <th>Description</th> <th>Usage</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>frame:AddColumn(dataColumn type)</td> <td>This function takes in a data column of either: text, boolean, number, audio, integer, or date and constructs the column. It forms one column each instance it is called.</td> <td>booleanColumn boolCol boolCol:Add(true) boolCol:Add(true) boolCol:Add(false) frame:AddColumn(boolCol)</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>AddColumn Function</p> <p>For our case, calling AddColumn() will add the two elements of each type into a DataFrame. Afterwards, we can view our data set onto the console by calling the ToText() function with our ‘frame’ object as well. We will now be inserting the elements we have added onto our data frame as follows and displaying them onto the console:</p> <pre><code>frame:AddColumn(numCol) frame:AddColumn(textCol) frame:AddColumn(boolCol) frame:AddColumn(intCol) output frame:ToText()</code></pre> <h5 id="try-it-yourself-34">Try it Yourself!</h5> <p>Press the blue run button to execute the code in the code editor. Press the red stop button to end the program. Your program will work when the console outputs “Build Successful!”</p> <p>Congratulations! We have successfully created our first dataset. To view another example of loading data by hand we can reference it <a href="https://github.com/qorf/curriculum/blob/main/Reference/DataScience/Data%20Frames/FileLoadByHand.quorum">here</a>. To add on, here is another example of using the AudioColumn <a href="https://github.com/qorf/curriculum/blob/main/Reference/DataScience/Data%20Frames/FileLoadByHandAudio.quorum">here</a>.</p> <h5 id="next-tutorial-132">Next Tutorial</h5> <p>In the next tutorial, we will discuss file saving, which describes how to save data back using DataFrames.</p> <p>Go BackNext Tutorial</p> <h5 id="on-this-page-152">On this page</h5> <h3 id="loading-a-dataset-from-a-file">Loading a dataset from a file</h3> <h5 id="data-science-4">Data Science</h5> <p>This tutorial tells use the DataFrame to load a file</p> <h5 id="loading-from-a-file">Loading from a File</h5> <p>By far the easiest way to load a file into a DataFrame is to load it from a comma separated file (CSV). Recall that a CSV is a plain text file that contains data, with commas separating each cell in the table.This is the default setting in DataFrames and calling Load automatically detects these file types. Here is a brief explanation of what our Load(text filepath) function does.</p> <table> <colgroup> <col style="width: 12%" /> <col style="width: 62%" /> <col style="width: 24%" /> </colgroup> <thead> <tr> <th>Function</th> <th>Description</th> <th>Usage</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>frame:Load(text filepath)</td> <td>This function takes in a string which is the location of the file path (inside the file explorer) of the dataset we want to read in.</td> <td>frame:Load(“../Data/Food/FastFoodRestaurants.CSV”)</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Load Helper Function</p> <p>What we want to start off is creating a DataFrame object to load our dataset. We will go ahead and name it ‘frame.’ Now, let us use the Load(text filepath) method in order for our data frame to properly locate and read in our dataset. Then, to confirm if we read all of our data, we can actually output all the contents on the terminal</p> <p>We should have the following code:</p> <h5 id="code-example-2">Code Example</h5> <pre><code>//We need the DataFrame class to load in files for Data Science operations. use Libraries.Compute.Statistics.DataFrame //Create a DataFrame, which is essentially a table that understands //more information about the data that is being loaded. DataFrame frame //This loads data relative to the project, so put the Population.csv file in the Data folder //If we deploy our program, this path is relative to the binary. frame:Load("../Data/Geography/US States.csv") //The system loaded the file, but can also output it a text value, or the console, if we want that. output frame:ToText()</code></pre> <h5 id="try-it-yourself-35">Try it Yourself!</h5> <p>Press the blue run button to execute the code in the code editor. Press the red stop button to end the program. Your program will work when the console outputs “Build Successful!”</p> <h5 id="next-tutorial-133">Next Tutorial</h5> <p>In the next tutorial, we will discuss data loading, which describes how to load data “by Hand” in a file using DataFrames.</p> <p>Go BackNext Tutorial</p> <h5 id="on-this-page-153">On this page</h5> <h3 id="loading-and-formatting-our-dataset">Loading and Formatting our Dataset</h3> <h5 id="descriptive-statistics-10">Descriptive Statistics</h5> <h5 id="formatting-and-loading-the-dry-bean-data">Formatting and Loading the Dry Bean Data</h5> <p>Before we run analysis on this data, let us examine it. This dry bean dataset comes from seven different classes of beans: Seker, Barbunya, Bombay, Cali, Horoz, Sira, and Dermason. From these beans, researchers collected data on 12 dimensions and 4 shape forms in order for systems to distinguish between seven different registered beans. The attributes recorded from the beans are: Area, Perimeter, Major axis length, Minor axis length, Aspect ratio, Eccentricity, Convex area, Equivalent diameter, Extent, Solidity, Roundness, Compactness, ShapeFactor1, ShapeFactor2, ShapeFactor3, ShapeFactor4, and Class. In terms of classification, these attributes are important because they help scientists understand the natural world. Here is a sample of our dataset:</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Area</th> <th>Perimeter</th> <th>MajorAxisLength</th> <th>MinorAxisLength</th> <th>AspectRation</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>28395</td> <td>610.291</td> <td>208.1781</td> <td>173.8887</td> <td>1.197191</td> </tr> <tr> <td>28734</td> <td>638.018</td> <td>200.5248</td> <td>182.7344</td> <td>1.097356</td> </tr> <tr> <td>29380</td> <td>624.11</td> <td>212.8261</td> <td>175.9311</td> <td>1.209713</td> </tr> <tr> <td>30008</td> <td>645.884</td> <td>210.558</td> <td>182.5165</td> <td>1.153638</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Snippet of DryBeans.csv</p> <p>Oftentimes, we need to transform our data before we can use it and here is no exception. From the UCI repository, the dry bean dataset can be downloaded as a zip file, and within the zip file, the dataset itself, it is saved as an XLSX, however Quorum only accepts datasets that are of CSV type. Recall that a CSV is a plain text file that contains data separated by commas. To fix this issue, we need to save the file in any spreadsheet program (e.g., Excel, Google Sheets). From there, we simply would want to keep the file name relating to the dry beans and be sure to save as ‘CSV (comma delimited) *.csv.’ Now that we have the correct file format, we can use this dataset to analyze.</p> <p>For easier access, we have the converted dataset readily available <a href="https://github.com/qorf/curriculum/blob/main/Reference/DataScience/Charts%20(New)/Data/Miscellaneous/DryBeans.csv">here</a></p> <p>Now that our dataset is prepared, we are going to load it into a DataFrame. A DataFrame is the object that will hold in our data. To do this, we create the DataFrame and call it ‘frame.’ From there we use ‘frame’ like a regular variable and now have access to many functions on loading, formatting, etc. and for this purpose, we will be using the Load(text filepath) function and AddSelectedColumns(text heading). Here is a brief explanation of what our Load(text filepath) and our AddSelectedColumns(text heading) functions do.</p> <table> <colgroup> <col style="width: 16%" /> <col style="width: 61%" /> <col style="width: 22%" /> </colgroup> <thead> <tr> <th>Class / Action</th> <th>Description</th> <th>Usage</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>frame:Load(text filepath)</td> <td>This action takes in a string which is the location of the file path (inside the file explorer) of the dataset we want to read in.</td> <td>frame:Load(“../Data/Food/FastFoodRestaurants.CSV”)</td> </tr> <tr> <td>frame:AddSelectedColumns(text heading)</td> <td>This action takes in a string which is an exact text header within the dataset.</td> <td>frame:AddSelectedColumns(“Heading 1”)</td> </tr> <tr> <td>frame:AddSelectedColumn(integer colNum)</td> <td>Alternatively, we can add the corresponding integer column in the dataset. This function takes in an integer which is the column number starting from 0.</td> <td>frame:AddSelectedColumn(0) frame:AddSelectedColumn(1)</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Helper Actions to Load Our Files</p> <p>Now that we have this ‘frame’ object, we can call the Load function which will locate the file and read all data entries in. To confirm that our data has been read, we can output our CSV file using the function call, ToText(). If we wanted to only output a specified column (because datasets can become quite large), we can also call the function ToText(integer) that allows us to print out the row based on the integer inside the parameter. This will only print one row at a time rather than the entire dataset.</p> <p>Luckily, for this dataset, there is no missing data, however as we have seen in the data science world, some datasets are messy and would require preprocessing. Typically after loading in a dataset, we would want to clean it, meaning, getting rid of empty rows or columns. In Quorum, this is how we would properly read in our data:</p> <pre><code>//We need the DataFrame class to load in files for Data Science operations. use Libraries.Compute.Statistics.DataFrame use Libraries.Compute.Statistics.Transforms.RemoveUndefinedRowsTransform //Create a DataFrame, which is essentially a table that understands //more information about the data that is being loaded. DataFrame frame //This loads data relative to the project, so put the dryBeans file in the Data/Miscellaneous folder frame:Load("../Data/Miscellaneous/DryBeans.csv") //We can save the frame or output it to the console, like we are doing here. output frame:ToText()</code></pre> <h5 id="try-it-yourself-36">Try it Yourself!</h5> <p>Press the blue run button to execute the code in the code editor. Press the red stop button to end the program. Your program will work when the console outputs “Build Successful!”</p> <h5 id="next-tutorial-134">Next Tutorial</h5> <p>In the next tutorial, we will discuss descriptive statistics, which describes descriptive statisics and how to make them accessible.</p> <p>Go BackNext Tutorial</p> <h5 id="on-this-page-154">On this page</h5> <h3 id="overview-of-summarizing-our-data">Overview of Summarizing Our Data</h3> <h5 id="descriptive-statistics-11">Descriptive Statistics</h5> <h5 id="overview-51">Overview</h5> <p>While the field of data science is filled with tests, procedures for managing data, and sometimes some brain bending ideas, some ideas in data science are harder than others. For example, we might want to know more information about how centralized or dispersed data is. These types of relatively simple things are often called descriptive statistics.</p> <p>Most data science toolkits have built in a number of equations out of the box to handle these operations. In this section, we provide code samples for each summary. Further, we have provided the specific equations Quorum uses and have placed these in an accessible format in the documentation.</p> <h5 id="gathering-data">Gathering Data</h5> <p>Often when learning about data analysis, it can be helpful to look at multiple datasets during the learning process. The reason is because different scientists format their data in different ways, make different assumptions, and we need to adapt to these to do our analysis correctly. In this section, we are going to be looking at new data, specifically from bean classification. Thus, this data set is regarding blood flow in the heart and the data we will be using is looking at patients with heart difficulties. The data can be found from a broader collection of data from the <a href="https://archive.ics.uci.edu/ml/index.php">University of California, Irvine Machine Learning Repository</a>.</p> <p>The citation for all of these data sets is this one:</p> <p><strong>Dua, D. and Graff, C. (2019). UCI Machine Learning Repository [<code>http://archive.ics.uci.edu/ml\</code>]. Irvine, CA: University of California, School of Information and Computer Science.</strong></p> <p>We are going to be going over the dry bean data set, which can be found here: <a href="https://archive.ics.uci.edu/ml/datasets/Dry+Bean+Dataset">Dry Beans Dataset [1]</a>.</p> <h5 id="references-2">References</h5> <p>[1]: KOKLU, M. and OZKAN, I.A., (2020), ‘Multiclass Classification of Dry Beans Using Computer Vision and Machine Learning Techniques.’ Computers and Electronics in Agriculture, 174, 105507. DOI: <code>https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compag.2020.105507.https://archive.ics.uci.edu/ml/datasets/Dry+Bean+Dataset</code>.</p> <h5 id="next-tutorial-135">Next Tutorial</h5> <p>In the next tutorial, we will discuss loading file, which describes loading the dataset using dataframes.</p> <h5 id="on-this-page-155">On this page</h5> <h3 id="reading-and-writing-data-overview">Reading and Writing Data Overview</h3> <h5 id="reading-and-writing-javascript-object-notation-json-data-1">Reading and Writing JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) Data</h5> <h5 id="overview-52">Overview</h5> <p>JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) is a human-readable way to format data and is commonly used for transmission between a server and web applications. JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) is a more “lightweight” and understandable format than another commonly used alternative known as Extensible Markup Language (XML). Because of these advantages and the fact that it is understood natively by the JavaScript programming language used in browsers, it is generally the preferred format today.</p> <p>JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) objects are a set of unordered key-value pairs, separated by a colon (“:“) and encapsulated with curly brackets (“{“ “}”), also called braces. The key portion of the pair is a name in double quotes and the value can be a text, integer, number, boolean or array value. Each of the pairs is separated by a comma (“,”) and any whitespace is ignored.</p> <p>In the following example, the first key name is “firstName” with a text value of “Joe”, the second key name is “lastName” with a text value of “Smith”, the third key name is “age” with an integer value of 15, and the fourth key name is “student” with a boolean value of true.</p> <p>Example JavaScript Object Notation format:</p> <pre><code>{ "firstName" : "Joe", "lastName" : "Smith", "age" : 15, "student" : true }</code></pre> <h5 id="json-in-quorum">JSON in Quorum</h5> <p>In order to access the JavaScriptObjectNotation class we must add the “use Libraries.Data.Formats.JavaScriptObjectNotation” statement at the beginning of our class definitions when working with JavaScript Object Notation (JSON).</p> <h5 id="next-tutorial-136">Next Tutorial</h5> <p>In the next tutorial, we will discuss JavaScript Object Notation Using Primitives, which describes an introduction to creating JavaScriptObjectNotation objects with primitive value types..</p> <h5 id="on-this-page-156">On this page</h5> <h3 id="reading-in-javascript-object-notation-formatted-data-from-text-values-or-from-a-">Reading in JavaScript Object Notation Formatted Data from Text Values or from a File</h3> <h5 id="reading-and-writing-javascript-object-notation-json-data-2">Reading and Writing JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) Data</h5> <h5 id="overview-53">Overview</h5> <p>If you have data which is already in JavaScript Object Notation format, with { “name” : value } pairs in curly braces, then the data can be read in and stored as a JavaScriptObjectNotation object. This data can be read in as a text value or from a file.</p> <h5 id="reading-in-from-a-text-value">Reading in from a Text Value</h5> <p>In this example, we are using the JavaScript Object Notation formatted text “myValue” with the key name “data” and its associated array value.</p> <pre><code>use Libraries.Data.Formats.JavaScriptObjectNotation class Main action Main //sets myValue = {“data” : [21.5, 22.7, 23.9]} text dq = "" dq = dq:GetDoubleQuote() text myValue = "{" + dq + "data" + dq + ": [21.5, 22.7, 23.9]}" //creates a JavaScriptObjectNotation object “json” to store //“myValue” and outputs the JavaScript Object Notation formatted object JavaScriptObjectNotation json json:Read(myValue) output json:ToText() end end</code></pre> <p>The output should look like this:</p> <pre><code>{ "data" : [21.5, 22.7, 23.9] }</code></pre> <h5 id="reading-in-from-a-file">Reading in from a File</h5> <p>To read in formatted JavaScript Object Notation data from a file we need to use the additional “Libraries.System.File” library and connect to the file containing the data. The file response.json is available for you to download for testing in this next example.</p> <pre><code>use Libraries.Data.Formats.JavaScriptObjectNotation use Libraries.System.File class Main action Main JavaScriptObjectNotation json //Creates a File object “myFile”, Sets the Path for “myFile” //(where you will be reading the JavaScript Object Notation data from) //and Reads from the specified file path. File myFile //be sure to use the file path that you have set your response.json file to myFile:SetPath("files/data/response.json") json:Read(myFile) output json:ToText() end end</code></pre> <p>Since the file” response.json” that we are reading in from contained the following JavaScript Object Notation formatted data:</p> <pre><code>{ "item1": 22, "item2": 33.2, "item3": true }</code></pre> <p>The output to the screen should look like this:</p> <pre><code>{ "item1": 22, "item2": 33.2, "item3": true }</code></pre> <h5 id="next-tutorial-137">Next Tutorial</h5> <p>In the next tutorial, we will discuss Writing JavaScript Object Notation Data Overview, which describes how to write JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) formatted data as a text value or to a file.</p> <p>Go BackNext Tutorial</p> <h5 id="on-this-page-157">On this page</h5> <h3 id="saving-data-back-to-disk">Saving data back to disk</h3> <h5 id="data-science-5">Data Science</h5> <p>This tutorial tells use the DataFrame to save data back to disk</p> <h5 id="loading-data-by-hand-1">Loading data “by Hand”</h5> <p>Just like with loading, we can save DataFrame objects back to disk if we want to. Copying data is plausibly useful, but where this becomes more helpful is after cleaning. For example, in a typical data set in data science, we often gather data, clean it up to remove problems, and then make a copy of that cleaned data. We can automate that process in code, then save it back, so that we can then reproduce our results later. We will be showing two examples of how to save the data we have created using our DataFrames.</p> <p>The first way is possibly the easiest way to save our data, which uses the Load(text fileLocation) function to read in a preexisting file such as:</p> <pre><code>//We need the DataFrame class to load in files for Data Science operations. use Libraries.Compute.Statistics.DataFrame //Create a DataFrame, which is essentially a table that understands //more information about the data that is being loaded. DataFrame frame //This loads the project relative to the project, so the Population.csv file in the Data folder //If we deploy our program, this path is relative to the binary. frame:Load("../Data/Geography/US States.csv")</code></pre> <p>And in this program, we end up manipulating the data by either removing unnecessary columns or adding more to our dataset. In order to save our modified dataset without changing the preexisting one, we can use the Save(text fileDestination) function in order to create a new copy of our new data. Here is a brief description of what our Save(text fileDestination) function does:</p> <table> <colgroup> <col style="width: 13%" /> <col style="width: 72%" /> <col style="width: 13%" /> </colgroup> <thead> <tr> <th>Function</th> <th>Description</th> <th>Usage</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>frame:Save(text fileDestination)</td> <td>This function takes in a string which is the file path of where we want this new dataset to be located in our file explorer. Note that the extension of our dataset must be a CSV file.</td> <td>frame:Save(“...csv”)</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Save Helper Function</p> <p>Here is an example of changing our loaded dataset and saving it onto a new dataset:</p> <pre><code>//We can now save this. This is not very useful in this example, //but can be if we have data frames we have generated or transformed frame:Save("../Data/Geography/US States.csv")</code></pre> <h5 id="try-it-yourself-saving-a-file">Try it Yourself: Saving a File</h5> <p>Press the blue run button to execute the code in the code editor. Press the red stop button to end the program. Your program will work when the console outputs “Build Successful!”</p> <h5 id="code-example-saving-a-file-by-hand">Code Example: Saving a File by Hand</h5> <p>The other method is to use our data creation “by hand” and save the data we made within Quorum onto our computer. To do this, let’s take an example program:</p> <pre><code>//We need the DataFrame class to load in files for Data Science operations. use Libraries.Compute.Statistics.DataFrame use Libraries.Compute.Statistics.Columns.NumberColumn use Libraries.Containers.Array use Libraries.Compute.Statistics.DataFrameColumn use Libraries.Compute.Statistics.Columns.TextColumn use Libraries.Compute.Statistics.Columns.BooleanColumn use Libraries.Compute.Statistics.Columns.IntegerColumn //Create a DataFrame, which is essentially a table that understands //more information about the data that is being loaded. DataFrame frame //This creates a TextColumn, which contains strings/text TextColumn txtColumn txtColumn:SetHeader("Names") txtColumn:Add("Daniel") txtColumn:Add("Yuria") txtColumn:Add("Kristine") txtColumn:Add("Yuri") txtColumn:Add("Rebecca") txtColumn:Add("Brianna") TextColumn txtColumn1 txtColumn1:SetHeader("Favorite Ice Cream") txtColumn1:Add("Vanilla") txtColumn1:Add("Matcha") txtColumn1:Add("Birthday Cake") txtColumn1:Add("Rocky Road") txtColumn1:Add("Chocolate") txtColumn1:Add("Strawberry") //This creates a NumberColumn, which contains decimal values NumberColumn numColumn numColumn:SetHeader("Cost") numColumn:Add(3.40) numColumn:Add(3.50) numColumn:Add(4.00) numColumn:Add(4.10) numColumn:Add(2.80) numColumn:Add(2.50) //This will add the data we added into a formal column //Adding more columns will create the comma separation similar to a CSV frame:AddColumn(txtColumn1) frame:AddColumn(txtColumn) frame:AddColumn(numColumn) //The system loaded the file, but can also output it a text value, or the console, if we want that. output frame:ToText()</code></pre> <h5 id="try-it-yourself-saving-a-file-by-hand">Try it Yourself: Saving a File by Hand</h5> <p>Press the blue run button to execute the code in the code editor. Press the red stop button to end the program. Your program will work when the console outputs “Build Successful!”</p> <p>To view the whole code, we can click this <a href="https://github.com/qorf/curriculum/blob/main/Reference/DataScience/Data%20Frames/FileSaveExample2.quorum">link</a>.</p> <h5 id="end-of-lesson-16">End of Lesson</h5> <p>You have reached the end of the lesson for Data Science. To view more tutorials, press the button below or you can go back to the previous lesson pages.</p> <p>Go BackBack to Tutorials</p> <h5 id="on-this-page-158">On this page</h5> <h3 id="tidy-data">Tidy Data</h3> <h5 id="data-science-6">Data Science</h5> <p>This tutorial introduces Tidy Data and why we use it in the Quorum Programming Language.</p> <h5 id="what-is-tidy-data">What is Tidy Data?</h5> <p>There are many ways to create datasets for analysis. In practice, while anything goes, there are advantages to having consistent formats. Notably, keeping our data consistent makes it possible for 1) humans reading the data to know ahead of time how it is structured and 2) computers ahead of time to use that structure to its advantage when running statistical and charting actions. For this reason, Quorum has adopted what <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hadley_Wickham">Hadley Wickham</a> calls the <a href="https://r4ds.had.co.nz/tidy-data.html">tidy data format</a>.</p> <p>The basic idea behind Tidy is that data must have three properties:</p> <ul> <li>Variables must be in columns</li> <li>Observations must be in rows</li> <li>Individual cells must represent only one value</li> </ul> <p>In Quorum, all charts, statistical tests, and actions related to data all assume that data are in a tidy format. This means that sometimes some systems must convert data to other formats to conduct tests, or other such operations, but this can be done automatically. Here is an example of data in Tidy Format:</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>y</th> <th>x1</th> <th>x2</th> <th>x3</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>2</td> <td>4</td> <td>-9</td> <td>9</td> </tr> <tr> <td>6</td> <td>7</td> <td>-19</td> <td>19</td> </tr> <tr> <td>3</td> <td>4</td> <td>-18</td> <td>18</td> </tr> <tr> <td>9</td> <td>8</td> <td>-16</td> <td>16</td> </tr> <tr> <td>15</td> <td>17</td> <td>-2</td> <td>2</td> </tr> <tr> <td>1</td> <td>3</td> <td>-4</td> <td>4</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Tidy Format Example</p> <p>In this example, y, x1, x2, and x3 are all variables and the first row is a header representing the name of those variables. The remaining rows contain all of the data points for each variable. Each cell contains only one value.</p> <h5 id="next-tutorial-138">Next Tutorial</h5> <p>In the next tutorial, we will discuss csv exporting, which describes how to export a csv from excel and google sheets.</p> <p>Go BackNext Tutorial</p> <h5 id="on-this-page-159">On this page</h5> <h3 id="tutorial-actions">Tutorial: Actions</h3> <h5 id="statistical-tests-1">Statistical Tests</h5> <h5 id="compare-means">Compare Means</h5> <p>The CompareMeans class is ultimately getting at a tricky question in statistics. In English, we often think of this as whether separate distributions of data, like columns in a spreadsheet, are statistically significantly different from each other.</p> <p>Consider an example. Suppose we have two columns of data in a spreadsheet. In the first column, the average is higher than the second. We can declare that and it might be true, but that data also has variation in it. Statistical tests at their core often try to balance 1) measures of centricity, 2) measures of dispersion, and 3) how much evidence is available. Intuitively, this makes sense. If the second group has a higher mean, but there is a lot of variation in the data and a small sample, this might indicate the result is less reliable than if there were more evidence or less variation. Statistical tests, while imperfect, try to balance these ideas and assign a number to them.</p> <p>Quorum implements multiple parametric and non-parametric tests. It has the ability to measure differences in means or variables for data that is normally distributed and not normally distributed.</p> <p>Listed below are functions that allow you to customize the statistical tests that you run. For example, the Ranked() function would be called when you want the results to be ranked or the call the RepeatedMeasures() function for tests that use repeated measures.</p> <table> <colgroup> <col style="width: 23%" /> <col style="width: 76%" /> </colgroup> <thead> <tr> <th><strong>Custom Functions</strong></th> <th><strong>Purpose</strong></th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>Ranked()</td> <td>Set the ranked boolean to true for ranked samples observations. Default is false</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Paired()</td> <td>Set the ranked boolean to true for ranked samples observations. Default is false.</td> </tr> <tr> <td>RepeatedMeasures()</td> <td>Set the paired boolean to true for paired samples in a Two-Sample Test. Default is false.</td> </tr> <tr> <td>TestVarianceAssumption()</td> <td>Set the repeatedMeasures boolean to true in an N-sample test. Default is false.t</td> </tr> <tr> <td>TestDistributionAssumption()</td> <td>Set the testVarianceAssumption boolean to true to test variance assumptions. Default is false.</td> </tr> <tr> <td>AssumeEqualVariances()</td> <td>Set the assumeEqualVariances boolean to true to assume variances are equal. Default is false.</td> </tr> <tr> <td>AssumeNormalDistribution()</td> <td>Set the assumeNormalDistribution boolean to true to assume normal distribution.Default is false.</td> </tr> <tr> <td>CorrectFamilyWiseError()</td> <td>Set the correctFamilyWiseError boolean to false in N-sample pairwise tests. Default is true.</td> </tr> <tr> <td>SetMean()</td> <td>Set the mean in tests where it is applicable.</td> </tr> <tr> <td>SetMedian()</td> <td>Set the median in tests where it is applicable</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Custom Functions for the Compare Means Class</p> <h5 id="one-group">One Group</h5> <p>The tests listed below are used with a single sample group.</p> <table> <colgroup> <col style="width: 55%" /> <col style="width: 44%" /> </colgroup> <thead> <tr> <th><strong>Formal Test</strong></th> <th><strong>Action in CompareMeans Class</strong></th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>Parametric: One-Sample T-Test</td> <td>CompareMeans</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Non-Parametric: Wilcoxon Signed Rank Test</td> <td>CompareRelatedRankedMeans</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Tests For One Group</p> <h6 id="compare-mean-with-a-given-value">Compare Mean with a Given Value</h6> <h6 id="technical-test-name-one-sample-t-test">Technical Test Name: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Student%27s_t-test">One Sample T-Test</a></h6> <p>We can test whether the mean of a population is different from a proposed value in Quorum by using a One Sample T-Test.</p> <p>Let’s say you had a snack that claimed it had 25 grams of protein. You can compare whether it really does. To do this, collect a sample of the same energy bars from different stores and record the grams of protein in each one. Then run compare it to 25 to determine if it is true or not.</p> <p>An example of how the test is implemented in Quorum is shown below.</p> <h6 id="compare-ranked-median-with-a-given-value">Compare Ranked Median with a Given Value</h6> <h6 id="technical-test-name-wilcoxon-signed-rank">Technical Test Name: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilcoxon_signed-rank_test">Wilcoxon Signed Rank</a></h6> <p>Using a Wilcoxon Signed Rank Test, we can test the median of a group of numbers of a single sample with a given median for data that is not normally distributed to determine if it is different or not. Such data does not have a bell shaped curve or has really big values.</p> <p>For example, you want to see if a new medicine influences driving abilities. You would randomly pick a group of drivers for your group that took the medicine and then compare their driving abilities to the basic driving abilities for drivers that have not taken any medicine.</p> <p>An example of how the test is implemented in Quorum is shown below.</p> <h5 id="two-groups-different-subjects-per-group">Two Groups: Different Subjects Per Group</h5> <p>The tests listed below are used with two sample groups from different populations.</p> <table> <colgroup> <col style="width: 74%" /> <col style="width: 25%" /> </colgroup> <thead> <tr> <th><strong>Formal Test</strong></th> <th><strong>Action in CompareMeans Class</strong></th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>Parametric: Two-Sample T-Test for Equal Variances, Welch’s Two-Sample T-Test for Unequal Variances</td> <td>CompareMeans</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Non-Parametric: Mann-Whitney U-Test (Wilcoxon Rank Sum Test)</td> <td>CompareRankedMeans</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Tests For Two Groups: Different Subjects</p> <h6 id="compare-means-of-two-samples-with-equal-variances">Compare Means of Two Samples With Equal Variances</h6> <h6 id="technical-test-name-two-sample-t-test">Technical Test Name: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Student%27s_t-test">Two-Sample T-Test</a></h6> <p>We can use a Two-Sample T-test to determine if the means of two samples are equal assuming that the sample groups have equal variances or in other words, the data is spread out equally.</p> <p>One example where this test could be used is comparing the average scores on a quiz for students from two different schools.</p> <p>Below is an example of how to run it in Quorum</p> <h6 id="compare-means-of-two-samples-with-unequal-variances">Compare Means of Two Samples With Unequal Variances</h6> <h6 id="technical-test-name-welchs-two-sample-t-test">Technical Test Name: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welch%27s_t-test">Welch’s Two-Sample T-Test</a></h6> <p>We can test data samples that have unequal variances to determine if the means of two populations are equal through a Welch’s Two-Sample T-Test. This is the default test in Quorum.</p> <p>Suppose that we want to improve the reading ability of elementary students through a series of activities for reading. Two groups of students would be needed - one group participating in the reading activities and one group not participating. At the end of the trial period, all students take a test to see if their reading abilities have improved or not. We can then compare if the activities helped from all the student’s scores.</p> <p>To implement this test in Quorum, refer to the example below.</p> <h6 id="compare-sample-populations">Compare Sample Populations</h6> <h6 id="technical-test-name-mann-whitney-u-test-or-wilcoxon-rank-sum-test">Technical Test Name: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mann%E2%80%93Whitney_U_test">Mann-Whitney U-Test or Wilcoxon Rank-Sum Test</a></h6> <p>We can determine if two different independent samples are from the same population through a Mann-Whitney U-Test. This test is for data that is not normally distributed, so it doesn’t have a bell shaped curve.</p> <p>As an example, suppose we are trying to see if exercise or healthy eating is better at lowering sugar levels. One group would exercise and the other group would eat healthy to determine at the end of the study which one lowered sugar more.</p> <p>To do this test in Quorum, refer to the example below.</p> <h5 id="two-groups-different-subjects-per-group-1">Two Groups: Different Subjects Per Group</h5> <p>The tests listed below are used with two sample groups from different populations.</p> <table> <colgroup> <col style="width: 55%" /> <col style="width: 44%" /> </colgroup> <thead> <tr> <th><strong>Formal Test</strong></th> <th><strong>Action in CompareMeans Class</strong></th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>Parametric: Paired T-Test</td> <td>CompareRelatedMeans</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Non-Parametric: Wilcoxon Signed Rank Test</td> <td>CompareRelatedRankedMeans</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Tests For Two Groups: Same Subjects</p> <h6 id="compare-means-of-two-dependentpaired-groups-with-a-given-value">Compare Means of Two Dependent/Paired Groups with a Given Value</h6> <h6 id="technical-test-name-paired-two-sample-t-test">Technical Test Name: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Student%27s_t-test">Paired Two-Sample T-Test</a></h6> <p>We can determine if the means of two paired groups are different from a proposed mean. To use this test in Quorum, refer to the example below.</p> <p>One scenario for this test to be used would be seeing the effect of two different study methods on the average exam scores of students in the same class.</p> <p>Below is an example of how to run it in Quorum</p> <h6 id="compare-ranked-medians-of-two-paired-samples-with-a-given-value">Compare Ranked Medians of Two Paired Samples With a Given Value</h6> <h6 id="technical-test-name-wilcoxon-signed-rank-test---two-groups">Technical Test Name: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilcoxon_signed-rank_test">Wilcoxon Signed Rank Test - Two Groups</a></h6> <p>We use a Wilcoxon Signed Rank Test to determine if the ranked medians of two paired samples is different from a proposed median. It is the same as the one previously mentioned, just with two groups now.</p> <p>For example, imagine you are a student in an 8th-grade science class, and your teacher wants to see if a new way of teaching helps students learn better. She decides to split the class into two groups - one group will be taught using the traditional method, and the other group will be taught using the new method. Both groups will take a pre-test to see what they already know, and then they will be taught using their assigned methods. After a certain period of time, both groups will take a post-test to see how much they have learned. The Wilcoxon Signed Rank Test can be used to compare the scores of the two groups. Since the same students are taking both tests, we can pair up their scores and see if there is a significant difference between the two groups.</p> <p>To implement this test factorin Quorum, refer to the example below.</p> <h5 id="n-groups---different-subjects-per-group">N Groups - Different Subjects Per Group</h5> <p>The tests listed below are used for a N (two or more) amount of different groups. Consider the post-hoc analysis tests after running the tests below.</p> <table> <colgroup> <col style="width: 64%" /> <col style="width: 35%" /> </colgroup> <thead> <tr> <th><strong>Formal Test</strong></th> <th><strong>Action in CompareMeans Class</strong></th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>Parametric: One-Way ANOVA for Equal Variances, Welch’s One-Way ANOVA for Unequal Variances</td> <td>CompareMeans, CompareMeansAssumingEqualVariances</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Non-Parametric: Kruskal-Wallis H-Test</td> <td>CompareRankedMeans</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Tests For N Groups: Different Subjects</p> <h6 id="compare-means-of-two-or-more-different-groups-with-equal-variances">Compare Means of Two or More Different Groups with Equal Variances</h6> <h6 id="technical-test-name-one-way-anova">Technical Test Name: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One-way_analysis_of_variance">One-Way ANOVA</a></h6> <p>We can check if the means of two or more different groups are different from each other by using a One-Way ANOVA. It would work best with three or more groups.</p> <p>A scenario in which this test would be used is finding the difference between average headache relief given three different medicines.</p> <p>An example of how to implement this test in Quorum is shown below.</p> <p>We can use Tukey’s HSD Multiple Comparison Test as a followup to do some post-hoc analysis.</p> <h6 id="compare-means-of-two-or-more-different-groups-with-unequal-variances">Compare Means of Two or More Different Groups with Unequal Variances</h6> <h6 id="technical-test-name-welchs-anova">Technical Test Name: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One-way_analysis_of_variance">Welch’s ANOVA</a></h6> <p>We can use Welch’s ANOVA Test to check if the means of two or more different groups with unequal variances are different from each other.</p> <p>One scenario to use this test would be determining how outgoing different hair colors (brown, blonde, black, or red) are. It does not assume variances of the groups are equal meaning that there might be data that varies from the average.</p> <p>An example of how to implement this test in Quorum is shown below.</p> <p>The Games-Howell Multiple Comparison Test is most commonly used as the post-hoc analysis for this test.</p> <h6 id="compare-medians-of-two-or-more-different-groups">Compare Medians of Two or More Different Groups</h6> <h6 id="technical-test-name-kruskal-wallis-h-test">Technical Test Name: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kruskal%E2%80%93Wallis_one-way_analysis_of_variance">Kruskal-Wallis H-Test</a></h6> <p>We use a Kruskal-Wallis Test to compare the medians of two or more different groups to see if they are different. It is an ANOVA test for data that does not have a normal distribution.</p> <p>Suppose we want to measure the growth of a plant in different sunlight. We plant some seeds in five different spots with either lots of sunlight directly, medium sunlight, low sunlight, sunlight through a window, or no sunlight. After some time, we can measure the height of the plants that grew in each different sunlight. A Kruskal-Wallis test will help determine if sunlight impacts the growth of the plant using the median.</p> <p>An example of how to do this test in Quorum is shown below.</p> <h5 id="n-groups---same-subjects-per-group-repeated-measurementsobservations">N Groups - Same Subjects Per Group (Repeated Measurements/Observations)</h5> <p>The tests listed below are used with a N (two or more) amount of groups from the same population.</p> <table> <colgroup> <col style="width: 52%" /> <col style="width: 47%" /> </colgroup> <thead> <tr> <th><strong>Formal Test</strong></th> <th><strong>Action in CompareMeans Class</strong></th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>Parametric: Repeated Measures Anova</td> <td>CompareRelatedMeans</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Non-Parametric: Friedman Test</td> <td>CompareRelatedRankedMeans</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Tests For N Groups: Same Subjects</p> <h6 id="compare-means-of-several-similar-groups">Compare Means of Several Similar Groups</h6> <h6 id="technical-test-name-repeated-measures-anova-test">Technical Test Name: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Repeated_measures_design">Repeated Measures ANOVA Test</a></h6> <p>We can determine if the means of several similar groups are the same or not through repeated observations or trials over time.</p> <p>One scenario to use the Repeated Measures One-Way ANOVA test would be tracking the weight gain of a puppy after eating a specific dog food for 6 weeks. Weighing the puppy before starting the dog food and every week after that for 6 weeks would be the repeated measures part.</p> <p>Below is an example of how to run it in Quorum</p> <p>We can run a Bonferroni Pairwise Procedure as a post hoc analysis test.</p> <h6 id="compare-medians-of-several-similar-groups">Compare Medians of Several Similar Groups</h6> <h6 id="technical-test-name-friedman-test">Technical Test Name: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friedman_test">Friedman Test</a></h6> <p>We use a Friedman Test to compare the difference between the medians of three or more groups through repeated observations.</p> <p>An example scenario of when this test could be used is watching movies. We could have a group of people watch five different movies and rate how good it was. Every person will rate the five movies so a Friedman test could determine if there are any major differences in the ratings of the five movies.</p> <p>An example of how to do this test in Quorum is shown below.</p> <h5 id="factorial-anova-and-manova">Factorial ANOVA and MANOVA</h5> <p>A Factorial ANOVA is a type of ANOVA that looks at two or more factors at the same time and can be either balanced or unbalanced. A factor is just a category or group that we’re interested in.</p> <p>This test uses the factors that we are interested in and tries to see what changes they caused on one dependent variable. For example, let’s say we want to know if there’s a difference in test scores based on both the number of hours studied per day AND the type of study method used (flashcards, reading notes, or practicing problems). We could use a Factorial ANOVA to analyze this data and see if there are significant differences between the different groups. Basically, a Factorial ANOVA is a statistical test that looks at multiple factors at the same time and can either be balanced or unbalanced which is explained in more detail below.</p> <p>The tests listed below are used for a N (two or more) amount of different groups with more than one factor.</p> <table> <colgroup> <col style="width: 56%" /> <col style="width: 43%" /> </colgroup> <thead> <tr> <th><strong>Formal Test</strong></th> <th><strong>Action in CompareMeans Class</strong></th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>Parametric: Balanced Factorial ANOVA</td> <td>CompareMeans</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Non-Parametric: Unbalanced Factorial ANOVA</td> <td>CompareMeans</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Tests For N Groups: Multiple Factors</p> <h6 id="compare-several-means-with-same-number-of-groups">Compare Several Means With Same Number of Groups</h6> <h6 id="technical-test-name-balanced-factorial-anova">Technical Test Name: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-way_analysis_of_variance">Balanced Factorial ANOVA</a></h6> <p>In a Balanced Factorial ANOVA, each group has the same number of participants.</p> <p>We are going to use the example above to see what different study methods and different amounts of time affect test scores. For a Balanced Factorial ANOVA, if we have 3 different study methods and 3 different study hours (which are the factors), we would need the same number of participants in each of the 9 resulting groups. Then it would make the data balanced and we can then compare any differences between the groups.</p> <h6 id="compare-several-means-with-different-number-of-groups">Compare Several Means With Different Number of Groups</h6> <h6 id="technical-test-name-unbalanced-factorial-anova">Technical Test Name: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-way_analysis_of_variance">Unbalanced Factorial ANOVA</a></h6> <p>In an Unbalanced Factorial ANOVA, groups might have more participants than others. This happens mostly when there are not enough groups or not enough people to recruit.</p> <p>Let’s use the example above to see what different study methods and different amounts of time affect test scores. We might have three groups for studying time: one group that studies for 1 hour, another group that studies for 2 hours, and a third group that studies for 3 hours. With these, there might be more participants in one group than in another like we have 10 participants in the 1 hour group, 15 participants in the 2 hour group, and 8 participants in the 3 hour group. This unequal grouping makes it harder to see differences between the groups, but it can be done using an Unbalanced Factorial ANOVA!</p> <h6 id="factorial-manova">Factorial MANOVA</h6> <p>MANOVA stands for multivariate analysis of variance which is a type of statistical analysis that looks at the relationship between multiple variables.</p> <p>A Factorial MANOVA looks at the effects of multiple independent variables (factors) on multiple dependent variables at the same time. This test helps us compare groups of data based on different variables (factors or characteristics) to see if there are any differences between them. Our goal is to see how the independent variables or factors affect the dependent variables.</p> <p>The tests listed below are used for a N (two or more) amount of different groups with more than one factor.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th><strong>Formal Test</strong></th> <th><strong>Action in CompareMeans Class</strong></th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>Parametric: Factorial MANOVA</td> <td>CompareSeveralMeans</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Tests For N Groups: Multiple Dependent Variables</p> <h6 id="compare-means-of-several-groups-with-multiple-dependent-and-independent-variables">Compare Means Of Several Groups With Multiple Dependent and Independent Variables</h6> <h6 id="technical-test-name-factorial-manova">Technical Test Name: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multivariate_analysis_of_variance">Factorial MANOVA</a></h6> <p>In a Balanced Factorial ANOVA, each group has the same number of participants.</p> <p>Imagine you have a bunch of data about different things, like the height, weight, and age of a group of people. Now, you want to find out if certain factors, like gender and exercise, have an effect on people’s height or weight. A Factorial MANOVA lets you look at multiple factors together at the same time instead of looking at them one at a time.</p> <h5 id="next-tutorial-139">Next Tutorial</h5> <p>In the next tutorial, we will discuss Compare Distributions, which describes how to check the distributions of data.</p> <p>Go BackNext Tutorial</p> <h5 id="on-this-page-160">On this page</h5> <h3 id="tutorial-adding-a-javascriptobjectnotation-value-type-to-a-javascriptobjectnotat">Tutorial: Adding a JavaScriptObjectNotation Value Type to a JavaScriptObjectNotation Object (Nesting)</h3> <h5 id="reading-and-writing-javascript-object-notation-json-data-3">Reading and Writing JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) Data</h5> <h5 id="nesting">Nesting</h5> <p>In this tutorial, we will create a JavaScriptObjectNotation object “data” which will be nested in another JavaScriptObjectNotation object “json” and then output the final result. We begin by creating the JavaScriptObjectNotation object that we plan on nesting, “data” and “Add”ing the necessary { name : value } pairs to the nested JavaScriptObjectNotation object “data.”</p> <pre><code>use Libraries.Data.Formats.JavaScriptObjectNotation class Main action Main JavaScriptObjectNotation data data:Add("item1", "a") data:Add("item2", "b") data:Add("item3", "c")</code></pre> <p>We then create the JavaScriptObjectNotation object, which will encapsulate the nested object, “json” and “Add” the necessary { name : value } pairs. To add the JavaScriptObjectNotation object to a { name : value } pair we change the value to the object to be nested, in this case “data.”</p> <pre><code> json:Add("detail", data)</code></pre> <p>Here is the complete code section which will create a nested JavaScriptObjectNotation object and output the formatted JavaScriptObjectNotation objects.</p> <pre><code>use Libraries.Data.Formats.JavaScriptObjectNotation class Main action Main JavaScriptObjectNotation data data:Add("item1", "a") data:Add("item2", "b") data:Add("item3", "c") JavaScriptObjectNotation json json:Add("data1", "A") json:Add("data2", "B") json:Add("detail", data) output json:ToText() end end</code></pre> <p>The output should look something like this, with the nested JavaScriptObjectNotation object enclosed by an inner pair of curly braces following its corresponding key name “detail”:</p> <pre><code>{ "data1": "A", "data2": "B", "detail": { "item1": "a", "item2": "b", "item3": "c" } }</code></pre> <h5 id="next-tutorial-140">Next Tutorial</h5> <p>In the next tutorial, we will discuss JavaScript Object Notation Using Arrays, which describes how to use array values with JavaScriptObjectNotation objects.</p> <p>Go BackNext Tutorial</p> <h5 id="on-this-page-161">On this page</h5> <h3 id="tutorial-adding-an-array-value-type-to-a-javascriptobjectnotation-object">Tutorial: Adding an Array Value Type to a JavaScriptObjectNotation Object</h3> <h5 id="reading-and-writing-javascript-object-notation-json-data-4">Reading and Writing JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) Data</h5> <h5 id="adding-an-array-value-type-to-a-javascriptobjectnotation-object">Adding an Array Value Type to a JavaScriptObjectNotation Object</h5> <p>In this tutorial we will create an array using JavaScriptObjectNotation which we will call “array.” We will use “array” as a corresponding value for the key name “detail” in a JavaScriptObjectNotation object called “json.” We will then output the final result. We begin by adding the necessary JavaScriptObjectNotation library and creating our JavaScriptObjectNotation object “array” to be used as a value in our JavaScriptObjectNotation object “json”.</p> <pre><code>use Libraries.Data.Formats.JavaScriptObjectNotation class Main action Main //creates a JavaScriptObjectNotation object "array" JavaScriptObjectNotation array //sets the JavaScriptObjectNotation object "array" to type Array. array:SetArray() //Adds the values of "project1" and "project2" to "array" array:Add("arrayValue1") array:Add("arrayValue2")</code></pre> <p>Finally, we need to “Add” the JavaScriptObjectNotation object value “array” to the JavaScriptObjectNotation object “json”.</p> <pre><code> JavaScriptObjectNotation json json:Add("data1", 10) json:Add("data2", 11) json:Add("myArray", array)</code></pre> <p>Here is the complete code section which will add an array value to a JavaScriptObjectNotation object and output the { name : value } pairs in JavaScript Object Notation format.</p> <pre><code>use Libraries.Data.Formats.JavaScriptObjectNotation class Main action Main JavaScriptObjectNotation array array:SetArray() array:Add("arrayValue1") array:Add("arrayValue2") JavaScriptObjectNotation json json:Add("data1", 10) json:Add("data2", 11) json:Add("myArray", array) json:SetPrettyPrint(true) output json:ToText() end end</code></pre> <p>The final result should look like this, with the “array” values separated by commas and enclosed within square brackets:</p> <pre><code>{ "data1": 10, "data2": 11, "myArray": ["arrayValue1", "arrayValue2"] }</code></pre> <h5 id="next-tutorial-141">Next Tutorial</h5> <p>In the next tutorial, we will discuss Reading JavaScript Object Notation Data Overview, which describes an overview into reading in JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) data from text values and files.</p> <p>Go BackNext Tutorial</p> <h5 id="on-this-page-162">On this page</h5> <h3 id="tutorial-adding-primitive-values-to-a-javascriptobjectnotation-object">Tutorial: Adding Primitive Values to a JavaScriptObjectNotation Object</h3> <h5 id="reading-and-writing-javascript-object-notation-json-data-5">Reading and Writing JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) Data</h5> <h5 id="primitives">Primitives</h5> <p>In this tutorial we will go over how to add key names and their associated primitive type values to a JavaScriptObjectNotation object, including:</p> <ul> <li><strong>Integer Values</strong> : such as (1, 2, 3)</li> <li><strong>Number Values</strong> : such as (1.0, 2.2, 3.7)</li> <li><strong>Boolean Values</strong> : true or false</li> <li><strong>Text Values</strong> : such as (“name”, “John”, “Smith”)</li> </ul> <p>Although integer value types are not standardly used in JavaScript Object Notation, we have added the integer value type as an added convenience for the user.</p> <h5 id="adding-an-integer-value-to-a-javascriptobjectnotation-object">Adding an Integer Value to a JavaScriptObjectNotation Object</h5> <p>We start by creating a JavaScriptObjectNotation object, called “json” in this example.</p> <pre><code>use Libraries.Data.Formats.JavaScriptObjectNotation class Main action Main JavaScriptObjectNotation json</code></pre> <p>We then have to “Add” the text key, and associated integer value to the JavaScriptObjectNotation object json.</p> <pre><code> json:Add("item1", 1) json:Add("item2", 2)</code></pre> <p>Here is the complete code section, which outputs our formatted JavaScriptObjectNotation object to the screen, allowing us to view each of the { name : value } pairs within the curly braces that encapsulate the object:</p> <pre><code>use Libraries.Data.Formats.JavaScriptObjectNotation class Main action Main JavaScriptObjectNotation json json:Add("item1", 1) json:Add("item2", 2) output json:ToText() end end</code></pre> <p>Where the output should look something like this:</p> <pre><code>{ "item1": 1, "item2": 2 }</code></pre> <h5 id="adding-other-value-types-to-a-javascriptobjectnotation-object">Adding Other Value Types to a JavaScriptObjectNotation Object</h5> <p>Similar to the way in which we added an integer value to the JavaScriptObjectNotation we start by creating a JavaScriptObjectNotation object. However, when “Add”ing our { name : value } pairs to the object we will change the value type accordingly to a number, boolean, or text type.</p> <p>Adding a number type value to the JavaScriptObjectNotation object:</p> <pre><code>use Libraries.Data.Formats.JavaScriptObjectNotation class Main action Main JavaScriptObjectNotation json json:Add("item1", 1.1) json:Add("item2", 2.2) output json:ToText() end end</code></pre> <p>Adding a boolean type value to a JavaScriptObjectNotation object:</p> <pre><code>use Libraries.Data.Formats.JavaScriptObjectNotation class Main action Main JavaScriptObjectNotation json json:Add("item1", true) json:Add("item2", false) output json:ToText() end end</code></pre> <p>Adding a text type value to a JavaScriptObjectNotation object:</p> <pre><code>use Libraries.Data.Formats.JavaScriptObjectNotation class Main action Main JavaScriptObjectNotation json json:Add("firstName", "Joe") json:Add("lastName", "Smith") output json:ToText() end end</code></pre> <h5 id="next-tutorial-142">Next Tutorial</h5> <p>In the next tutorial, we will discuss JavaScript Object Notation Using Nesting, which describes how to nest a JavaScriptObjectNotation object as a value within another JavaScriptObjectNotation object.</p> <p>Go BackNext Tutorial</p> <h5 id="on-this-page-163">On this page</h5> <h3 id="tutorial-data-science-introduction">Tutorial: Data Science Introduction</h3> <h5 id="data-science-7">Data Science</h5> <p>This is an introduction to Data Science and why it is important.</p> <h5 id="introduction-1">Introduction</h5> <p>This guide is designed to provide an overview of documentation for data science libraries in Quorum. In it, we discuss the major features, like loading data, analyzing it, and generating charts from it. The goal of this set of tutorials is practical in the sense that it provides how to use the libraries and interpret the results, but it is not intended as a fully data science curriculum or statistics tutorial. While some equations on how the system works will be included, the goal here is to describe how to use the system, not to provide a deep dive of the math.</p> <p>Thus, perhaps the first question to answer is what this set of tutorials are for, which in turn gets at what data science is for. In plain English, data science, statistics, and similar areas are designed to help us understand certain kinds of questions. Namely, we have a data set, in it is some kind of information structured in any way we can imagine, and the goal is to answer a question about that data. In a sense, we want to turn that data into information that we can practically use.</p> <p>In order to better understand what we do in data science, it sometimes helps to have data. While we could gather some, and generating our own data in scientific ways is fun and exciting, we are going to rely here on <code>https://www.data.gov</code>. Specifically, we are going to be looking at data on several topics. In each case, our goal is to learn something different about data science. Thus, across these tutorials we will load data, filter it, adjust it, test it, or anything else to try and understand it. The datasets we will be using are all free and public.Once we have finished with these tasks, we will examine how to manipulate our data even more such as incorporating our data into statistics or charts. All items in this track use examples that we have stored on Github in the <a href="%20https://github.com/qorf/curriculum">Quorum curriculum repository</a>.</p> <h5 id="overview-into-saving-and-loading-dataframes">Overview into Saving and Loading DataFrames</h5> <p>In any kind of data science application, whether it be to answer a question, create a model, or create charts, we first need to load our data. There are many ways to load data and Quorum has adopted an “opinionated” approach, similar to TidyVerse in the language R. We did this in part because the approach is consistent in how it stores data, but also because using the same way of loading data across the board for all data sets makes analysis easier. To understand this, we first need to talk about data frames, which are basically fancy tables we can load from a spreadsheet.</p> <h5 id="next-tutorial-143">Next Tutorial</h5> <p>In the next tutorial, we will discuss data frames, which describes Introduction to data frames.</p> <h5 id="on-this-page-164">On this page</h5> <h3 id="tutorial-returning-key-names-and-values-from-a-javascriptobjectnotation-object">Tutorial: Returning Key Names and Values from a JavaScriptObjectNotation Object</h3> <h5 id="reading-and-writing-javascript-object-notation-json-data-6">Reading and Writing JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) Data</h5> <h5 id="returning-a-list-of-key-names-from-a-javascriptobjectnotation-object">Returning a List of Key Names from a JavaScriptObjectNotation Object</h5> <p>In order to return a list of all the key names included in a JavaScriptObjectNotation object we will use an Array container to manage the key names and then output those key names to the screen. We will start by adding the necessary libraries and creating a JavaScriptObjectNotation object “json” with nested JavaScriptObjectNotation object values.</p> <pre><code>use Libraries.Data.Formats.JavaScriptObjectNotation use Libraries.Containers.Array class Main action Main JavaScriptObjectNotation json JavaScriptObjectNotation joe JavaScriptObjectNotation jill joe:Add("First Name", "Joe") joe:Add("Last Name", "Smith") joe:Add("Age", 15) joe:Add("GPA", 3.89) jill:Add("First Name", "Jill") jill:Add("Last Name", "Miller") jill:Add("Age", 14) jill:Add("GPA", 3.65) json:Add("Student1", joe) json:Add("Student2", jill) json:Add("School", "Elm Creek High School") json:Add("City", "Jackson") json:Add("State", "MS") json:Add("Zip Code", 12345)</code></pre> <p>Now that we have a JavaScriptObjectNotation object “json” to gather key names from, we will create an Array of text values called “keys,” and set that Array to collect all of the key names in our JavaScriptObjectNotation object “json” by using the “GetKeys()” action.</p> <pre><code> //creates the Array of text values "keys"and assigns "keys" to the text values of the //key names in out JavaScriptObjectNotation object "json" Array<text> keys = json:GetKeys() //loop to continue "Get"ting "key's" key names one at a time and output each key //name until there are no more key names to "Get" i = 0 repeat keys:GetSize() times key = keys:Get(i) output key i = i + 1 end</code></pre> <p>The entire code section should look like this:</p> <pre><code>use Libraries.Data.Formats.JavaScriptObjectNotation use Libraries.Containers.Array class Main action Main JavaScriptObjectNotation json JavaScriptObjectNotation joe JavaScriptObjectNotation jill joe:Add("First Name", "Joe") joe:Add("Last Name", "Smith") joe:Add("Age", 15) joe:Add("GPA", 3.89) jill:Add("First Name", "Jill") jill:Add("Last Name", "Miller") jill:Add("Age", 14) jill:Add("GPA", 3.65) json:Add("Student1", joe) json:Add("Student2", jill) json:Add("School", "Elm Creek High School") json:Add("City", "Jackson") json:Add("State", "MS") json:Add("Zip Code", 12345) Array<text> keys = json:GetKeys() i = 0 repeat keys:GetSize() times key = keys:Get(i) output key i = i + 1 end end end</code></pre> <p>The output should look similar to this:</p> <pre><code>Student1 Student2 School City State Zip Code</code></pre> <p>Notice how there is no indication that “Student1” and “Student2” contain nested JavaScriptObjectNotation object values. All that we have returned to us are the key names connected to the values, which can be very helpful when trying to sort through large amounts of data for relevant information. In the next section we will go over how to return the values associated with specific key names in a JavaScriptObjectNotation object.</p> <h5 id="returning-values-from-a-javascriptobjectnotation-object">Returning Values from a JavaScriptObjectNotation Object</h5> <p>Once you have a list of all the key names in a JavaScriptObjectNotation object, you can use those key names to determine which specific key name values you would like to have returned for viewing, rather than having all of the key name and value pairs returned to you at once. In order to return a specific key name’s value we will use the “GetValue()” action which takes one text type value as a parameter. This parameter should be the key name associated with the value(s) that you wish to have returned. In the example below, we will use the JavaScriptObjectNotation object “json” with the nested JavaScriptObjectNotation object values “joe” and “jill” that we used in the previous tutorial. We will be using the list of key names that was returned to us to determine which of their values we would like to “Get”.</p> <p>In order to specify which value(s) we wish to have returned, we will pass in the value’s key name as a parameter to the “GetValue()” action. In this example we are going to have the “School” value and the “Student1” value returned to us. Since “Student1” has a nested JavaScriptObjectNotation object as its value, the “GetValue()” action will return the entire JavaScriptObjectNotation object “joe” value. You can add the following lines of code to your existing code section from the previous tutorial.</p> <pre><code> output "Student1: " + json:GetValue("Student1") output "School: " + json:GetValue("School")</code></pre> <p>The complete code section to create a Nested JavaScriptObjectNotation object and return specific values located within that JavaScriptObjectNotation object looks like this:</p> <pre><code>use Libraries.Data.Formats.JavaScriptObjectNotation class Main action Main JavaScriptObjectNotation json JavaScriptObjectNotation joe JavaScriptObjectNotation jill joe:Add("First Name", "Joe") joe:Add("Last Name", "Smith") joe:Add("Age", 15) joe:Add("GPA", 3.89) jill:Add("First Name", "Jill") jill:Add("Last Name", "Miller") jill:Add("Age", 14) jill:Add("GPA", 3.65) json:Add("Student1", joe) json:Add("Student2", jill) json:Add("School", "Elm Creek High School") json:Add("City", "Jackson") json:Add("State", "MS") json:Add("Zip Code", 12345) output "Student1: " + json:GetValue("Student1") output "School: " + json:GetValue("School") end end</code></pre> <p>The output should look similar to this:</p> <pre><code> Student1: {"First Name": "Joe", "Last Name": "Smith", "Age": 15, "GPA": 3.89} School: Elm Creek High School</code></pre> <h5 id="end-of-lesson-17">End of Lesson</h5> <p>You have reached the end of the lesson for Reading and Writing JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) Data. To view more tutorials, press the button below or you can go back to the previous lesson pages.</p> <p>Go BackBack to Tutorials</p> <h5 id="on-this-page-165">On this page</h5> <h3 id="writing-javascript-object-notation-formatted-data-as-a-text-value-or-to-a-file">Writing JavaScript Object Notation Formatted Data as a Text Value or to a File</h3> <h5 id="reading-and-writing-javascript-object-notation-json-data-7">Reading and Writing JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) Data</h5> <h5 id="writing-javascript-object-notation-objects-as-a-text-value">Writing JavaScript Object Notation Objects as a Text Value</h5> <p>To write formatted JavaScript Object Notation data as a text value we will use the “ToText()” action on the JavaSciptObjectNotation object which will output the associated JavaScriptObjectNotation object to the screen by default. Using just the “ToText()” action on its own will output the JavaScriptObjectNotation object as a single line of text with the {name : value} pairs separated only by a comma. To output the JavaScriptObjectNotation with the {name : value} pairs separated by a comma and a carriage return, we must also use the “SetPrettyPrint()” action with the boolean parameter set to true. In the following example we begin by creating a JavaScriptObjectNotation object “json” and adding a few { name : value } pairs to the object.
